s1.why: Without an instructions file, the model re-figures the stack, structure, and rules in every new conversation — the first lost minutes and a risk of breaking your conventions. CLAUDE.md provides that context once and automatically.
instructions: Remember the key point: [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] reads CLAUDE.md at the start of EVERY conversation — without reminders.
It's the project's "character": stack, conventions, important paths, commands, and taboos in one place.
Without the file you repeat the same things in every request — with it you write only the task itself.
CLAUDE.md speeds up not one answer but every one: it's a permanent part of the context.
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why repeating conventions in every request is worse than keeping them in CLAUDE.md.
s1.tip: Think of CLAUDE.md as Custom Instructions, but for code and for a specific project.

s2.title: How to create it and where it lives
s2.why: Writing the file from scratch by hand is slow and easy to forget things. The /init command inspects the repo and assembles a draft for you — you just polish it.
instructions: Fastest path: run [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] in the project root — Claude scans the code and generates a base CLAUDE.md.
Alternative: create CLAUDE.md manually in the repo root with a plain text editor.
Check the location: the project CLAUDE.md sits in the root (next to package.json / .git).
Open the resulting file and read it — /init often writes extra you should remove.
s2.validate: There's a CLAUDE.md file in the project root, and Claude Code picks it up in a new conversation.
s2.tip: After /init, always re-read the file by hand — auto-generation gives a base, not a final.

s3.title: What to write inside
s3.why: The value of CLAUDE.md isn't in describing the obvious but in what the model can't guess: your commands, non-standard paths, conventions, and explicit prohibitions. That turns the file from a brochure into a working tool.
instructions: Stack and versions — briefly: what's actually used (e.g. React 18 + Vite), if it affects decisions.
Commands: how to build, run tests, lint — exact lines Claude can execute.
Important paths: where the code is, where configs are, where NOT to change anything.
Conventions: naming, style, patterns the team follows.
Taboos: what's NOT allowed — "don't use any", "don't touch migrations without asking".
s3.validate: The file has commands, paths, and at least 2-3 explicit taboos — not just a description of "what this project is".
s3.tip: Simple rule: if Claude can learn it from the code itself — don't write it; if it can't or often gets it wrong — write it.

s4.title: Hierarchy and scope
s4.why: CLAUDE.md comes in several levels, and they stack rather than conflict. Understanding the hierarchy lets you keep personal rules separate from team ones and avoid committing extras.
instructions: Global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — your personal rules for ALL projects (e.g. response language).
Project CLAUDE.md in the repo root — shared team rules, goes into git.
CLAUDE.local.md — personal settings just for you in this project; add it to .gitignore.
Levels stack: global + project + local apply together.
Imports: long blocks can be moved to separate files and linked from CLAUDE.md.
s4.validate: You understand which rule to put in global, which in project, and which in CLAUDE.local.md.
s4.tip: Secrets, personal paths, and experiments go in CLAUDE.local.md (outside git), not the shared CLAUDE.md.

s5.title: Keep it short and current
s5.why: The longer the file, the worse the model holds priorities, and a stale rule is worse than no rule — it actively harms. A short, fresh CLAUDE.md beats a big, forgotten one.
instructions: Don't put human docs in CLAUDE.md — that's what the README is for.
Don't duplicate the README, changelog, or feature descriptions — only instructions for the model.
Don't store secrets, tokens, or keys — those go in the environment or CLAUDE.local.md.
Clean up regularly: changed a tool or path? Fix the file right away.
If the file grows large — move topics into separate files and link them via imports.
s5.validate: The file fits a manageable size, with no stale items and no copies of the README.
s5.tip: Every couple of weeks, re-read CLAUDE.md as a newcomer: is it all still true?

s6.title: Common mistakes and a check
s6.why: Most CLAUDE.md problems are walls of text and stale rules. A quick check in a live conversation shows whether the file actually works or just sits in the repo.
instructions: Check for a wall of text: if the file scrolls forever — trim it to the essentials.
Check for staleness: is every rule still true? Delete what stopped being true.
Check for obviousness: remove what Claude can already see in the code.
Live test: open a new conversation in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] and give a task touching your rule — is it respected?
If a rule is ignored — rephrase it shorter and clearer, with no fuzzy wording.
s6.validate: In a new conversation Claude respects your conventions and taboos without reminders in the request itself.
s6.tip: Keep current Claude Code settings and commands handy in the [[node:cc-config|config]] and [[node:cc-install|install]] — CLAUDE.md works together with them.

sys-rag-architecture.title: RAG architecture — how the "retrieve + generate" system is built
sys-rag-architecture.subtitle: We treat RAG not as an idea but as a system: which components are inside, how they connect, and which pattern to choose
sys-rag-architecture.whatItIs: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) as an architecture is a pipeline of three parts: the index (a base of preprocessed documents), the retriever (finds relevant chunks for a query), and the generator (the LLM that assembles an answer from what was found). This course isn't about "why RAG" — it's about HOW it's built inside and where its limits are.
sys-rag-architecture.approach: We go from the overall diagram to the details. First we see the whole pipeline (query → retrieval → generation), then we break down each component separately, then we look at patterns of varying complexity (naive / hybrid / re-rank) and decide which one fits the task. We finish by assembling a minimal system, reviewing risks, and a production-readiness checklist.
outcomes: You understand the RAG pipeline as a set of components, not as "search magic"
You can name and separate the roles: index, retriever, generator
You choose a pattern (naive / hybrid / re-rank) deliberately, based on data volume and quality
You see where the system breaks: garbage in the index, poor retrieval, hallucinations on top of what was found
You can use a checklist to assess whether a RAG system is production-ready

applyIn.title: Documentation support bot
applyIn.description: You design a system where a customer asks a question and the bot finds doc chunks and answers with links. Architectural understanding helps decide: is naive search enough, or is re-ranking needed.

applyIn.title: Internal knowledge base assistant
applyIn.description: An employee asks about policies and history — the system pulls from heterogeneous sources. Here it's crucial to separate index and retriever to understand why the right thing isn't found.

applyIn.title: Evaluating an existing RAG solution
applyIn.description: You're handed a ready system or a vendor product. Knowing the components and patterns, you ask the right questions: how do they chunk, which search, is there re-rank, do they show sources.

pitfalls: Treating RAG as one black box of "search" — then it's impossible to tell which component produces the bad answer
Thinking the LLM determines answer quality rather than retrieval — in reality a poor retriever kills even a strong model
Building a complex re-ranking pattern right away when naive would suffice for the data volume — needless complexity and cost
Ignoring preprocessing: chunking and index quality matter more than model choice (see [[node:sys-chunking-strategies|Chunking strategies]])
Not designing source citation into the architecture — it's costlier to add later, and without sources nobody trusts the system

exercises.question: Take any RAG product you know (support bot, AI doc search) and break it into three components: what acts as the index, what as the retriever, what as the generator?
exercises.hint: Index — where preprocessed documents live. Retriever — what returns the top-N chunks for a query. Generator — the LLM composing the final text. If you can't separate retriever and generator — that's exactly the "black box".

exercises.question: You have a base of 500 short FAQ articles and simple queries. Which pattern would you pick — naive, hybrid, or re-rank — and why?
exercises.hint: Small volume + simple queries = naive often suffices (one vector search, top-3). Re-rank and hybrid are justified when there are many documents, specific terms, or top precision matters.

exercises.question: The system returns relevant chunks, but the answer is still inaccurate. On which pipeline component do you look for the problem?
exercises.hint: If retrieval found the right thing but the answer is bad — the problem is in the generator: the prompt, missing "answer only from context" instruction, or the model improvising. It's not a search problem.

s1.title: RAG as architecture: seeing the whole pipeline
s1.why: Before fixing details, you need to see the system as a data flow. RAG isn't "smart search" — it's a pipeline: the query passes through retrieval and reaches generation together with the found context. Without this picture you can't tell where things break.
instructions: Draw three blocks in a row: Index → Retriever → Generator, and a query arrow entering the Retriever
Trace the data path: documents go into the index in advance; the query goes to the retriever; the retriever pulls top-N chunks; chunks + query go to the LLM; the LLM produces an answer with links
Note there are two run times: offline (filling the index) and online (answering a query) — these are often confused
Compare with the intro node [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]]: there RAG is the idea "find and answer"; here it's a system with component boundaries
Write in one sentence what enters the generator besides the query (answer: the found context)
s1.validate: You can name from memory the path from query to answer through all three components and say what happens offline versus online.
s1.tip: Keep the "offline vs online" split in mind: 80% of quality problems are born offline (bad index) and show up online (bad answer).

s2.title: The three components: index, retriever, generator
s2.why: Each component solves its own task and breaks in its own way. If you don't separate them, you'll blame every error on "dumb AI" when the cause is the index or the search. Role separation is the basis of diagnosis.
instructions: Index: documents arrive here already cut into chunks and turned into vectors; index quality = chunking quality + data freshness (see [[node:sys-vector-stores|Vector stores]])
Retriever: returns top-N relevant chunks for a query; its metric is whether it found the right thing at all (recall) and whether it's in the top (precision)
Generator: the LLM that's given the query + found chunks and asked to assemble an answer strictly from them with links
For each component write its main failure: index — garbage/stale; retriever — didn't find / found the wrong thing; generator — invented beyond the context
Link to chunking: how documents are cut directly determines what the retriever can find ([[node:sys-chunking-strategies|Chunking strategies]])
s2.validate: For each of the three components you can name its input, output, and characteristic way of breaking.
s2.tip: Diagnose by layers: first check whether the retriever returned the right chunk (eyeball the top-N). If yes — the generator is at fault. If not — the index/retriever is.

s3.title: Patterns: naive, hybrid, re-rank
s3.why: RAG comes in varying complexity, and grabbing the complex one right away is a mistake in cost and maintenance. Three base patterns cover almost all cases; the task is to understand how they differ and what each is for.
instructions: Naive RAG: one vector search for the query → top-N chunks → into the LLM. Simple, cheap, enough for small volumes and simple queries
Hybrid search: you combine vector search (by meaning) and keyword search (by exact words/terms), merging results — saves you where codes, SKUs, names matter ([[node:sys-hybrid-search|Hybrid search]])
Re-ranking: you pull more candidates (e.g. top-20), then re-sort with a separate model and keep the best top-3-5 — top precision rises, but latency and cost are added
Map the pattern to the task: small volume → naive; specific terms → hybrid; many noisy candidates and precision needed → re-rank
Remember the quality ladder from the node: naive ~50-60%, with relevance checks 75-85%, with re-ranking 90%+ good answers
s3.validate: For a concrete task you can justify the pattern choice and name what you pay for the added complexity (latency, cost, maintenance).
s3.tip: Don't jump to re-rank. Start with naive, measure where it misses, and add complexity only against a real quality gap.

s4.title: How to assemble: a minimal end-to-end pipeline
s4.why: Understanding components isn't enough — you need to see them assembled. A minimal working RAG is simpler than it seems: it can be described in 5 steps. This is the base on top of which hybrid and re-rank are later layered.
instructions: Offline stage: gather documents → cut into chunks → turn into vectors → put into the index/vector store
Online stage, step 1: turn the user query into a vector the same way as the documents
Online stage, step 2: the retriever searches the index for the top-N nearest chunks by this vector
Online stage, step 3: assemble the prompt = instruction + found chunks + query; the instruction explicitly demands "answer only from the context and give links"
Online stage, step 4: the LLM generates the answer; you must pass through the sources of the found chunks into the answer
s4.validate: You can describe step by step a minimal RAG from filling the index to an answer with links, without peeking.
s4.tip: The generator instruction "use only the provided context; if there's no answer, say so" is the cheapest defense against hallucinations. Build it in from day one.

s5.title: Architecture limits and risks
s5.why: RAG is no silver bullet. The architecture has built-in weak spots: they're predictable, and knowing them you design the system to be resilient rather than patching it after complaints.
instructions: Garbage in = garbage out: stale, duplicate, draft documents in the index → the retriever confidently finds noise. Build a process for removing the outdated
Retrieval is the bottleneck: if the needed chunk isn't in the top-N, the generator won't see it and either stays silent or invents; answer quality is capped by search quality
Hallucinations on top of context: even with the right chunks the LLM can improvise — cured by a strict instruction and showing sources for verification
Chunking tears meaning: too fine a cut loses context, too coarse dilutes relevance — this is an architectural, not a "tuning" risk ([[node:sys-chunking-strategies|Chunking strategies]])
Lack of sources kills trust: without a "where from" link users re-check with a human, and the system's value drops
s5.validate: You can name at least 3 built-in RAG risks and, for each, an architectural (not cosmetic) solution.
s5.tip: Remember the priority rule: data and retrieval quality matter more than model choice. Swapping the LLM without fixing the index is treating a symptom.

s6.title: Readiness checklist and verification
s6.why: You need to be able to verify the architecture before launch. The checklist turns component understanding into concrete "ready / not ready" questions and guards against typical gaps.
instructions: Index: is the data current, are duplicates and drafts removed, is chunking deliberate (not blind defaults)?
Retriever: did you eyeball the top-N on a set of real queries — does the right thing actually make it into the output?
Pattern: chosen deliberately for the task (naive/hybrid/re-rank), not "by fashion"; is the added complexity justified by a measured gap?
Generator: does the prompt forbid answering outside context and require links; have you tested "no answer in the base" cases?
Sources: does the answer always show where it came from; can the user click through and verify?
s6.validate: You ran the system through all 5 checklist items on a set of real queries and for each item gave a "yes" with proof, not a "probably yes".
s6.tip: The main check is cheap: take 10-15 real questions and eyeball the retrieval top-N for each. If search finds the right thing — the system is almost ready; if not — no model will save it.

sys-context-passing.title: How to pass context between workflow steps
sys-context-passing.subtitle: What to hand the next AI step — everything, only what's needed, or a summary
sys-context-passing.whatItIs:
When a workflow is several AI steps (see [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|Prompt Chaining]]), the key question isn't "what to ask" but "what to pass on". Pass too much and every step is slow, expensive, and sometimes overflows the limit. Pass too little and the next step loses the thread and starts guessing.

This course teaches the four passing strategies (full / compressed / structured / referential) and how to pick one for a given task.
sys-context-passing.approach: Context isn't "attach everything just in case". It's an engineering decision: for each transition between steps, explicitly decide what the next step needs to work, and pass only that. Less noise means a faster, more accurate answer.
outcomes: Understand why "pass everything" is an expensive habit, not a safe default
Know the 4 passing strategies: full, compressed (summary), structured, referential
Can pick a strategy based on the size and volatility of the context
See the risks — context bloat and losing what matters — and how to catch them
Have a checklist to review context passing in any workflow

applyIn.title: Long customer conversations
applyIn.description: A 50+ message thread: the first step makes a summary, the rest get summary + last few messages instead of the whole history.

applyIn.title: Multi-step research
applyIn.description: Each step searches and analyzes. Pass structured findings (facts, links), not the raw text of every source.

applyIn.title: Data processing pipelines
applyIn.description: In systems from [[node:ai-data-systems|AI Data Systems]], pass a reference to a document rather than its full content — the step fetches the part it needs.

pitfalls: "I'll pass everything to be safe" — every step becomes slow and expensive, and the AI gets distracted by irrelevant content.
Regenerating the summary at every step when context hasn't changed — paying for the same work many times.
Compressing so aggressively that an important detail is lost — the next step runs on incomplete data.
Passing raw IDs and references while forgetting the step has no access to their content ([[node:cap-memory|Memory]] isn't unlimited).
Not checking whether the final input fits the model's limit — the workflow breaks silently on long cases.

exercises.question: Take your 4-5 step workflow. For each transition, list what the next step actually needs versus what's passed out of habit. What can you drop?
exercises.hint: If a step doesn't use a chunk of its input in its answer, it doesn't need that chunk.

exercises.question: Compare two versions of step 5: full history on input vs. summary + last 3 messages. Compare speed, input length, and answer quality.
exercises.hint: Quality often improves with compression — the AI stops drowning in noise.

exercises.question: Find a spot in your workflow where you can swap "pass the content" for "pass a reference". What must the step be able to do for that to work?
exercises.hint: The referential strategy only works if the step has a tool to fetch data by reference.

s1.title: Why pass context carefully
s1.why: Without a deliberate passing decision, context snowballs: by step 5 the input holds the entire history of prior steps. That's slow, costly, and hits the model limit. Under-passing is just as bad — the step loses the thread.
instructions: Open any of your multi-step AI workflows (see [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|Prompt Chaining]]).
Look at what reaches the last step's input. Is it the whole history, or only what's needed?
Estimate the cost: a long input means more tokens, so more money and time on every run.
Lock in the idea: passing context is a decision, not "attach everything just in case".
s1.validate: You can state how much context actually reaches the last step of your workflow and why that's a lot or a little.
s1.tip: "I'll pass everything just in case" is the most expensive habit in multi-step workflows.

s2.title: The four passing strategies
s2.why: There's no single right strategy — there are four, each for its own case. Knowing them lets you choose deliberately instead of passing everything by default.
instructions: Full: pass the entire previous output as-is. Simple but expensive. Good for 2-3 short steps.
Compressed (summary): the AI shrinks the context into a short summary, and the summary moves forward. For long conversations and research.
Structured: pass extracted fields (customer, plan, status) instead of text. The step gets clean data without noise.
Referential: pass a link/ID rather than the content; the step fetches what it needs (relevant for systems in [[node:ai-data-systems|AI Data Systems]]).
s2.validate: You can describe all 4 strategies in your own words and give an example where each fits.
s2.tip: Strategies combine: a structured profile + a history summary + a document reference in one input.

s3.title: How to pick a strategy for the task
s3.why: The choice comes down to two things: how big the context is and how much it changes from step to step. Those two questions give you a ready answer.
instructions: 2-3 steps and small context → full. Don't overcomplicate.
Large, dynamic context (long conversations, multi-step research) → summary, refreshed as it grows.
You know exactly which fields the step needs → structured: pass only those.
Data is large and lives in a source the step can reach → referential.
s3.validate: For each transition in your workflow you can name the chosen strategy and one reason for the choice.
s3.tip: Start with the simplest thing that works. Add complexity only when you hit cost or a limit.

s4.title: Example: a long customer conversation
s4.why: One concrete example shows how the strategies save money and improve quality at the same time.
instructions: Given: a workflow processes a 50+ message thread. The bad version gives every step the whole history (tens of thousands of words).
Step 1: the AI reads the whole conversation and makes a ~200-word summary ("complains about X, tried Y, ready for Z").
Steps 2-5: get the summary (compressed) + the last 5 messages (full, for freshness) + the customer profile (structured).
Result: each step's input is far shorter, cost drops many times over, and answers are sharper — the AI doesn't drown in noise.
s4.validate: You understand which three strategies are combined in this example and why each is there.
s4.tip: Almost always pass the most recent messages in full — that's where the new meaning is, while the summary holds the background.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: Each strategy has its own cost of failure. Knowing the risks up front is cheaper than catching them in production.
instructions: Context bloat: "pass everything" makes each step slower and pricier, plus the risk of overflowing the model limit.
Losing what matters: an over-aggressive summary drops a detail the next step needs to be right.
Wasted work: regenerating a summary when context didn't change is pointless (memory isn't unlimited, see [[node:cap-memory|Memory]]).
Broken references: the referential strategy fails if the step has no tool to fetch data by the link.
s5.validate: For your workflow you can name the main risk of the chosen strategy and how to spot it.
s5.tip: If context is stable between steps — cache the summary and reuse it instead of recomputing.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final pass turns intuition into a repeatable rule: run the list for each transition and your context stays under control.
instructions: For each transition: what does the next step actually need? Drop everything extra.
A strategy is chosen (full / summary / structured / referential) and the reason is recorded.
The longest step's final input fits the model limit with room to spare.
The summary isn't regenerated where context hasn't changed.
Run the workflow on your longest real case and compare cost/speed against "pass everything".
s6.validate: The workflow runs on a long case without overflowing the limit, and every transition has a deliberate strategy.
s6.tip: Make this checklist part of reviewing any new multi-step workflow — it's cheap and catches expensive mistakes.

sys-vector-stores.title: Vector stores: how to choose
sys-vector-stores.subtitle: From selection criteria to a checklist: pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma for your use case
sys-vector-stores.whatItIs: A practical course on choosing a vector store for RAG and semantic search. A vector store is a database for embeddings with fast ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) search. The course goes from "do you even need one" through comparing solution classes (managed / self-hosted / embedded in Postgres) to a justified choice for your specific scale, latency, and budget. Builds on [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]] and [[node:af-vector-db|Vector DB]].
sys-vector-stores.approach: The decision is made not by hype but along three axes: operational complexity, latency at scale, and cost. We start from your real numbers (vector count, QPS, whether you have an ops team, whether you already run Postgres), not from "what's popular." Each step gives concrete thresholds and a check that the choice won't break as you grow.
outcomes: You understand what a vector store solves and when you actually need one (>10k documents or RAG in production)
You distinguish three classes: embedded (pgvector), managed SaaS (Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud), self-hosted (Qdrant, Weaviate)
You estimate latency, cost, and operational load using 2026-05 baseline numbers
You pick a store for your specific task via a decision tree, not by fashion
You know the limits and risks: lock-in, re-indexing on model change, multi-tenant isolation

applyIn.title: Launching RAG in production
applyIn.description: A team moves a Chroma PoC into a real product and needs a store that survives growth to millions of vectors without a migration in six months.

applyIn.title: Semantic search in an existing product
applyIn.description: You already run Postgres and need meaning-based search. The course shows when pgvector covers the task without new infrastructure.

applyIn.title: Multi-tenant SaaS with search
applyIn.description: Several customers in one product: the course teaches isolating tenant data via namespaces/partitions and filtering so nobody's documents leak.

pitfalls: Picking Pinecone "because it's popular" at 50k vectors with Postgres on hand — paying $70/mo for what pgvector does free and faster
Running Chroma in production: at 1M+ vectors and >50 QPS there's no HA, managed backup, or mature replication
Ignoring metadata filtering — search returns similar texts from other products and the user sees noise
One index across all tenants without namespace/partition — one customer sees another's data, a security incident
Changing the embedding model without full re-indexing — old vectors are incompatible with new ones and results degrade

exercises.question: You have a B2B SaaS on Postgres RDS, 200k support docs, 50 QPS, an ops team of 2. Which store do you choose and why?
exercises.hint: Map the numbers to the thresholds: < 5M vectors, < 100 QPS, Postgres already there. What does that mean for "new infrastructure"?

exercises.question: A year later the base grows to 5M chunks and p95 latency rises to 120ms on pgvector. What do you do, and how do you minimize migration pain?
exercises.hint: Think about a dedicated engine with metadata as payload, and why an early correct choice makes the migration a days-long task, not weeks.

exercises.question: A team wants hybrid search (vector + keywords) out of the box and self-host. Which two options do you consider?
exercises.hint: One engine has hybrid search built in; for the other you assemble it by hand on top of an existing DB.

s1.title: Why a vector store and the selection criteria
s1.why: Without a clear grasp of what a vector store solves and which axes you choose it on, it's easy to grab a trendy tool and overpay — or hit a ceiling. Three axes — operational complexity, latency, cost — drive everything that follows.
instructions: Pin down the task: RAG, semantic search, or semantic cache — this shapes the filtering and latency requirements
Write down your input numbers: how many vectors now and in a year, expected QPS, embedding dimension (often 1536)
Answer honestly: do you have an ops team and how many hours a month can it spend on maintenance
Check whether you already run Postgres — this shifts the whole equation toward pgvector
Tie the task to architecture via [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]
s1.validate: You have three numbers on paper (vector count, QPS, budget) plus answers on ops team and Postgres.
s1.tip: Most selection mistakes are born here: the numbers are eyeballed. Take real metrics or at least a conservative one-year estimate.

s2.title: Managed vs self-hosted vs embedded
s2.why: This is the first and main fork. The solution class decides who carries the operational load: you (self-host), the provider (managed), or your existing DB (embedded).
instructions: Embedded — pgvector: a Postgres extension, transactions, joins, role-based access, ~0 extra infra, scales to ~10M vectors
Managed SaaS — Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud: 0 ops, simple API, you pay money to avoid the chores
Self-hosted — Qdrant, Weaviate: maximum control and filtering, but backups, upgrades, and monitoring are on you (4-8h/mo)
Map each class to your ops-team answer from step 1
Browse the [[node:af-vector-db|Vector DB]] overview for engine details
s2.validate: You can explain in one sentence who carries the operational load in each of the three classes.
s2.tip: "Managed" doesn't mean "better" — it means "more money instead of hours." If you already have Postgres and a DBA, embedded often beats managed on both speed (no network hop) and cost.

s3.title: Scale, latency, and cost
s3.why: The class is chosen; now you need numbers. Without a latency and cost baseline it's easy to take either something too expensive or something that can't handle the load. The numbers below are a 2026-05 baseline; the landscape moves fast.
instructions: Latency (single query, top-10, 1M vectors): pgvector+HNSW 20-80ms p95, Pinecone serverless 50-150ms (network round-trip), Qdrant self-host 10-40ms, Weaviate 30-100ms
Cost (1M vectors of 1536-dim, 100 QPS): pgvector ~$0 over Postgres, Pinecone ~$70-300/mo, Qdrant Cloud ~$100-400/mo, self-host Qdrant ~$30-80/mo for a VM
Account for ops hours: managed = 0, self-host = 4-8h/mo on backups/upgrades/monitoring
Remember the ceilings: Chroma is not for hundreds of millions of vectors or >50 QPS; pgvector is comfortable up to ~10M
Add the money cost and the cost of ops hours — that's the full TCO
s3.validate: You have an estimate of p95 latency and monthly cost (money + hours) for 2-3 candidates.
s3.tip: Self-host looks cheaper on money ($30-80 for a VM), but 4-8h/mo of an engineer often costs more than a managed plan. Count the full TCO, not just the hosting bill.

s4.title: How to choose for your task
s4.why: All the data is gathered — time to walk the decision tree. The goal is one justified choice, not a list of "either way works."
instructions: Postgres already there + < 5M vectors + < 100 QPS -> pgvector (no new infra)
No ops team, want managed, budget OK -> Pinecone or Qdrant Cloud
Complex filters (metadata + vector) and self-host -> Qdrant
Need hybrid search out of the box -> Weaviate (or pgvector + BM25 by hand)
PoC on a laptop -> Chroma, but with a migration plan for going to prod
s4.validate: You can name one engine and three reasons for the choice, tied to your numbers from steps 1 and 3.
s4.tip: If you're torn between pgvector and managed while you have Postgres — start with pgvector. Migrating up is cheaper than paying for unused capabilities from day one.

s5.title: Limits and risks: lock-in and re-indexing
s5.why: The right engine choice doesn't save you from strategic traps. Lock-in, vector incompatibility on model change, and multi-tenant leaks are the most expensive mistakes — and all are predictable.
instructions: Lock-in: a managed solution's proprietary API makes moving harder — keep an abstraction layer over the store client
Re-indexing: changing the embedding model makes old vectors incompatible -> you need a full re-index, ideally parallel indexes with A/B routing
Multi-tenant: one index for all = data leakage between customers; use namespaces (Pinecone) / partitions (Qdrant) / WHERE tenant_id (pgvector)
Always apply metadata filtering (tenant_id, product, lang, date_range) BEFORE the vector search, otherwise the results contain noise from other data
Budget time for re-indexing in advance — it's nearly inevitable as models evolve
s5.validate: For your choice you can name a tenant isolation strategy and an action plan for changing the embedding model.
s5.tip: Re-indexing is not "if" but "when." Teams that build a parallel-index pipeline upfront change models with no downtime; the rest take result degradation.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final review turns reasoning into a launch-ready decision. The checklist catches what's easy to forget under deadline pressure.
instructions: The choice is justified by numbers (volume, QPS, budget, ops hours), not by engine popularity
The candidate's p95 latency fits your budget at the scale a year out, not just today
Metadata filtering and tenant isolation are configured (namespace / partition / WHERE)
There's a re-indexing plan for an embedding-model change and an abstraction layer against lock-in
It's connected to the data pipeline in [[node:ai-data-systems|AI data systems]] and to architecture in [[node:systems|System Design]]
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked, and you can defend the choice to the team in one sentence with numbers.
s6.tip: If even one item is open, it's not a blocker for a PoC but a mandatory TODO before production. Record the open items explicitly so they don't get lost.

sys-chunking-strategies.title: Chunking strategies for RAG
sys-chunking-strategies.subtitle: How document splitting decides retrieval quality
sys-chunking-strategies.whatItIs:
Chunking is splitting documents into pieces (chunks) before embedding. It is the foundational step of a [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG pipeline]]: what the model finds and cites depends on chunking more than on the vector store or embedding model choice.

Four core strategies: fixed-size (N tokens with overlap), recursive splitter (paragraph→sentence→word), semantic chunking (boundary where the topic shifts) and document-aware (by structure: headings, code blocks, tables). This course teaches you to pick a strategy by content type and to avoid breaking retrieval at chunk boundaries.
sys-chunking-strategies.approach: Don't memorize numbers — test on your own data. Take a real corpus, run 2-3 chunk_size and overlap variants, measure recall on an eval set. Intuition for the right size only comes from A/B testing on your own content.
outcomes: Understand why chunking is the main cause of poor RAG (60-70% of diagnoses)
Tell fixed-size, recursive, semantic and document-aware apart and know when to use each
Choose chunk_size and overlap by content type deliberately, not by default
Recognize over- and under-chunking from retrieval symptoms
Build a pre-indexing checklist so you don't have to re-index later

applyIn.title: Launching a new RAG system
applyIn.description: From day one you pick the strategy by source_type and bake in metadata — this saves a full re-index later.

applyIn.title: Diagnosing "RAG answers poorly"
applyIn.description: Check chunking before swapping the model — in most cases the culprit is chunk size and missing overlap.

applyIn.title: Mixed corpus (docs + code + PDF)
applyIn.description: Apply different strategies to different block types in one pipeline, without splitting tables and code blocks.

pitfalls: One chunk_size for the whole corpus — a PDF contract and an FAQ need different treatment.
Splitting with no overlap — a boundary fact is lost between two vectors, neither is relevant.
Splitting structured blocks — a table or code block torn into pieces becomes meaningless.
Chunks without metadata — no citations and no filtering by tenant/language/date.
Changing strategy without a full re-index — old and new vectors of different sizes give unstable recall.

exercises.question: Take one of your documents (an article or markdown doc) and split it with a recursive splitter at chunk_size=256 and 512. Eyeball 3-4 chunks of each variant.
exercises.hint: Watch the boundaries: where is a fact cut in half? That is the argument for overlap.

exercises.question: Build a mini eval set of 5-10 questions against the corpus and measure recall@5 for two chunk_size values. Record which wins.
exercises.hint: If both are <70%, the problem isn't the size — it's overlap or blocks being split.

exercises.question: Find a document in your corpus with a table or code block and check whether the splitter tore it apart.
exercises.hint: If it did, that's a candidate for a document-aware strategy that protects blocks.

s1.title: Why chunking decides RAG quality
s1.why: Bad chunking breaks everything downstream, yet it gets fixed last — people swap the model first, even though chunk size is the culprit 60-70% of the time.
instructions: Learn the mechanics: a too-large chunk → the embedding dilutes into an "average meaning" vector, top-N pulls in garbage.
A too-small chunk → context is lost and the model has no idea what the fragment is about.
Tie this to [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: chunking sits before embedding and decides what is retrievable at all.
Adopt the rule: when someone says "RAG answers poorly," check chunking first, not the model.
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words why both a too-large and a too-small chunk hurt retrieval.
s1.tip: Keep the 60-70% figure in mind: that's the share of diagnoses rooted in chunking. It saves hours of "model tuning."

s2.title: The four splitting strategies
s2.why: Without understanding the differences you'll default to fixed-size — the simplest and most context-losing strategy.
instructions: Fixed-size: N tokens (usually 256-512) with 10-20% overlap. Simple and fast, but tears context at boundaries.
Recursive splitter (LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter): splits by paragraph → sentence → word until a piece fits. The best default for prose.
Semantic chunking: adjacent sentences are compared by embedding similarity, the boundary lands where similarity drops (topic shift). Costlier to ingest, more precise retrieval.
Document-aware: respects structure (markdown headings, HTML tags, code blocks). A chunk is a logical section, not an arbitrary window.
Remember the role of overlap: it preserves a fact that straddles two chunks.
s2.validate: You can name all four strategies and, in a word, each one's main trade-off (speed / context / cost / structure).
s2.tip: Overlap isn't a separate strategy but a parameter layered on fixed-size and recursive. 10-20% is the working range.

s3.title: How to choose a strategy by content
s3.why: The choice follows content type, not fashion: the wrong strategy bakes in weak retrieval that model tuning won't cure.
instructions: Prose / articles / docs → recursive splitter, chunk_size 256-512. Fast and sufficient.
Mixed format (code + text) → document-aware with per-block-type splitting.
Long structured documents (contracts, research papers) → semantic chunking.
Tabular / structured data → row-based splitting, not text-based.
FAQ-style content → smaller chunk_size (128-256), technical docs → larger (512-1024).
s3.validate: For three of your content types you can name a strategy and an approximate chunk_size with justification.
s3.tip: If you're torn between two options, that's a signal to A/B test, not to guess. An eval set answers more precisely than intuition.

s4.title: Example: a mixed corpus in practice
s4.why: A real corpus is almost always mixed (docs + Slack + PDF), and one strategy for everything is the most common mistake.
instructions: Markdown docs: recursive splitter with separators on headings (\n## , \n### ), chunk_size=512, overlap=80, length measured in tokens (tiktoken).
Slack threads: preserve message boundaries — don't split an individual message into pieces.
PDF contracts: SemanticChunker with a percentile breakpoint — it cuts on topic shifts.
Add universal metadata to every chunk: source_id, source_type, section, lang, updated_at, tenant_id.
Connect to the broader topic of [[node:ai-data-systems|AI data systems]]: chunking is one layer of the data infrastructure.
s4.validate: You have a plan: which strategy for which source and which metadata fields go on every chunk.
s4.tip: Bake metadata in from day one. Adding it later means re-indexing the whole corpus.

s5.title: Limits and risks: too large / too small
s5.why: Over- and under-chunking symptoms are easily mistaken for a "dumb model" — reading the signs saves a diagnostic cycle.
instructions: Under-chunking signs (too small): one document occupies 8 of the top-10, context is fragmented, the answer cites text mid-sentence.
Over-/large-chunking signs: retrieved chunks answer "almost your question," the embedding is diluted, irrelevant noise appears in results.
Cost risk: semantic chunking is 2-5x more expensive to ingest due to extra embedding calls for boundary detection.
Staleness risk: a doc is removed at the source but its chunks stay in the index — tied to [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]] and pipeline refresh.
If recall is <70% on the eval set — A/B chunk_size (256/512/1024) and overlap (10%/20%) usually gains +10-15% without swapping the model.
s5.validate: Given a retrieval symptom you can say which way to turn chunk_size and estimate the cost of the semantic variant.
s5.tip: Don't confuse semantic chunking's expense with its necessity: for prose, recursive is almost always enough.

s6.title: Checklist and validation before indexing
s6.why: Most chunking mistakes are fixable only by a full re-index — it's cheaper to catch them on a checklist before launch.
instructions: Strategy chosen by source_type, not one for the whole corpus.
Overlap set (at least 10%) for fixed-size and recursive.
Structured blocks (tables, code) are kept intact.
Every chunk carries metadata: source_id, source_type, section, lang, updated_at, tenant_id.
An eval set exists and recall@5 is measured; on a strategy change a full re-index is planned, not a partial one.
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked and you have a baseline recall before going to production.
s6.tip: Keep this checklist next to the ingestion code — it outlives team and model changes.

sys-hybrid-search.title: Hybrid search: sparse + dense
sys-hybrid-search.subtitle: Keywords and meaning together — more accurate than either alone
sys-hybrid-search.whatItIs:
Hybrid search combines two signals: **sparse** (BM25 — exact words, names, versions, error codes) and **dense** ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] — meaning, paraphrases, concepts). Each compensates for the other's weakness: dense loses exact terms, BM25 does not get "cancel sub" = "subscription termination". Together they give +10-25% recall@10 on typical RAG benchmarks vs pure dense.

This course is about the retrieval layer of [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: how to fuse two methods (RRF or weighted sum), when to add reranking, and how not to break everything without measuring quality.
sys-hybrid-search.approach: Do not believe that "dense is modern, BM25 is obsolete." They are not replacements — they are two different signals. Turn on hybrid with evaluation: first an eval set of 50-200 queries with ground truth, then measure recall@10 before and after. Without measurement you cannot tell whether hybrid helped or chunking broke.
outcomes: Understand that sparse and dense catch different query types and why you need both
Can fuse results via RRF (by rank) or weighted sum (by score with normalization)
Know when to add reranking and why only on the top 50-100, not the whole corpus
Can pick a setup: built-in hybrid (Weaviate, Qdrant) or pgvector + BM25 by hand
Can measure the gain via recall@10 / precision@5 and avoid turning hybrid on blindly

applyIn.title: Search over technical documentation
applyIn.description: Model names, versions, API methods, error codes — BM25 catches exact matches, dense catches paraphrased questions.

applyIn.title: Multilingual knowledge base
applyIn.description: Embeddings link query and document across languages, BM25 keeps exact terms and identifiers.

applyIn.title: Production RAG with short queries
applyIn.description: Users type keywords ("pgvector hnsw m parameter") — here the sparse signal is critical for quality.

pitfalls: Dense-only "because it is modern": a query "sonnet-4-5-20250929 deprecation" gets paraphrased to "model retirement" and loses the exact match — BM25 captures it.
Weighted sum without normalization: BM25 scores 0-15, cosine 0-1, the sum is dominated by BM25. Normalize (min-max) or use RRF (rank-based).
Reranking the whole corpus: a cross-encoder on 1M documents = $1000+ per query. Rerank only the top 50-100 after the first stage.
Hybrid without evaluation: you turn it on, recall does not grow, and the cause is unknown. Always use an eval set before/after, measure recall@10 and precision@5.
Ignoring filters: hybrid without `WHERE tenant_id = X` mixes tenant data. Search and metadata filters are orthogonal — you need both.

exercises.question: Take 10 real queries to your base. Split them into "exact" (names, versions, codes) and "semantic" (paraphrases, questions). Which method would win on each?
exercises.hint: Exact terms -> sparse (BM25). Paraphrases and concepts -> dense. A mix in the corpus -> you need hybrid.

exercises.question: Explain in plain terms why a weighted sum with BM25=12 and cosine=0.7 without normalization gives a bad result.
exercises.hint: Add the numbers directly: 12 vs 0.7. BM25 fully overrides the dense signal — α stops meaning anything.

exercises.question: You have recall@10 = 78% on dense-only. You turn on hybrid — it becomes 80%. Should you add a reranker, and what to check first?
exercises.hint: A small gain (< 5%) signals the problem may be in chunking, not search. Check document chunking first.

s1.title: Why hybrid: keywords + meaning
s1.why: A single signal always misses part of the queries. Dense loses exact terms, BM25 misses paraphrases. Hybrid closes both gaps at once.
instructions: Write down 2 failure cases for dense: exact terms (model names, error codes, person names) and rare words (out-of-vocabulary for the embedder).
Write down 2 failure cases for BM25: paraphrases ("cancel sub" vs "subscription termination") and conceptual queries.
Fix the benchmark number: hybrid gains +10-25% recall@10 vs pure dense on typical RAG benchmarks.
Tie it to [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: hybrid is the retrieval layer, before answer generation.
s1.validate: You can explain with two examples which query dense fails and which BM25 fails.
s1.tip: BM25 is what Google did for 20 years before neural search. "Old" does not mean "useless": on exact terms it beats embeddings.

s2.title: Sparse vs dense in plain terms
s2.why: To fuse two methods you must understand what each one measures and why their scores are not directly comparable.
instructions: Sparse (BM25): matches exact tokens, accounts for word frequency and rarity. Scores in roughly 0-15, not normalized.
Dense ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]]): query and document become vectors, closeness = cosine similarity in 0-1.
Key difference: BM25 sees letters and words, dense sees meaning. "MCP" and "Model Context Protocol" are different strings for BM25, close points for dense.
Remember the asymmetry: dense blurs exact-token matches that BM25 takes literally.
s2.validate: You can state the score ranges of BM25 and cosine, and why they cannot be added directly.
s2.tip: You will need this in the fusion step: the incomparability of scores is exactly why RRF is often simpler and more robust than weighted sum.

s3.title: How to fuse: fusion and re-rank
s3.why: Two result lists must merge into one ranking. The fusion method directly affects quality and how much tuning you will need.
instructions: RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion): each method returns top-N, ranks merge by `score = Σ 1/(k + rank_i)`, k=60. Works on ranks, not scores — no normalization needed.
Weighted sum: `final_score = α × dense_score + (1-α) × sparse_score`, α≈0.5 as a start. You must normalize scores (min-max), otherwise BM25 dominates.
Default start is RRF: simpler, no weights to tune, robust to different score scales.
Reranking (optional, +5-15% precision@5): feed the top 50-100 to a cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker), keep the top 5-10.
A cross-encoder reads query+document together — more accurate than the bi-encoder embedding, but more expensive and slower.
s3.validate: You can write RRF from memory and explain why weighted sum needs normalization while RRF does not.
s3.tip: The reranker is the most expensive part of the pipeline ($0.001/query with Cohere). So it goes last and works only over the already selected 50-100, not the whole corpus.

s4.title: How to apply in practice
s4.why: Architecture must land on a concrete stack. The choice depends on whether you have built-in hybrid or assemble it by hand.
instructions: Built-in hybrid: Weaviate, Qdrant (with FastEmbed), Elasticsearch + dense — hybrid out of the box, less code.
pgvector + BM25 by hand: `tsvector` for sparse + `pgvector` for dense, RRF in a SQL CTE — if you are already on Postgres.
Run BM25 and dense **in parallel**: latency ≈ max(times) ≈ 80-150ms, not the sum.
Add a reranker by budget: Cohere Rerank ($1/1k, 100-200ms, top quality) or BGE-reranker (self-host, free, slightly weaker). Total p95 ≈ 200-400ms.
This is part of the [[node:ai-data-systems|data systems]] and [[node:systems|systems]] around Claude — relevance retrieval before generation.
s4.validate: You have a chosen setup (built-in or pgvector) and a clear latency budget with and without reranker.
s4.tip: BM25 costs cents (CPU), a dense query is $0.00001. The real money goes to the reranker — enable it only if eval shows a precision@5 gain.

s5.title: Limits and risks
s5.why: Hybrid is not always a win. On some cases it adds nothing, and implementation mistakes silently break both quality and data safety.
instructions: When dense-only is enough: long natural-language questions, narrow domain with a fine-tuned embedder, < 10k documents (hybrid gain is small).
When hybrid is essential: technical content (names, versions, error codes), multilingual data, short keyword queries, recall < 80% on dense-only.
Risk #1 — weighted sum without normalization: BM25 overrides dense. Use RRF or normalize.
Risk #2 — reranker on the whole corpus: $1000+ per query. Top 50-100 only.
Risk #3 — ignoring filters: hybrid without `WHERE tenant_id = X` mixes tenant data. Search and metadata filters are both needed.
s5.validate: You can name a case where hybrid is not needed and three implementation mistakes that silently break the result.
s5.tip: The reranker landscape moves fast: Cohere is the 2026-05 baseline, but check current alternatives before choosing.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Hybrid without evaluation is faith, not engineering. An eval set turns "feels better" into measurable recall@10 and precision@5.
instructions: Build an eval set: 50-200 real helpful queries with ground truth (which document is correct).
Measure the baseline: recall@10 on dense-only.
Turn on hybrid (RRF), measure recall@10 again. Target norm > 85%.
If using a reranker — measure precision@5 after it (target > 70%) and p95 latency (< 400ms).
If the gain is < 5% — do not celebrate and do not blame search: check chunking, the problem is likely in document splitting.
s6.validate: You have recall@10 numbers before/after and a decision: hybrid helped, or the problem is in another RAG layer.
s6.tip: A/B without vs with hybrid on the same eval set is the only honest way to prove the gain. Without numbers any "it got better" is an illusion.

sys-document-pipelines.title: Document ingestion pipelines
sys-document-pipelines.subtitle: ETL for documents that feed RAG: from source to a vector in the index
sys-document-pipelines.whatItIs: A document ingestion pipeline is a continuously running conveyor that pulls documents from sources (Notion, Confluence, Drive, GitHub, Zendesk), parses, normalizes, deduplicates, chunks, computes embeddings, and writes them into a [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]]. Not a one-off script but a service with incremental sync, deletion handling, retries, and monitoring.
sys-document-pipelines.approach: We follow the real lifecycle of a document: first understand why a continuous pipeline is needed (rather than a one-shot script), then walk the full chain extraction → cleanup → chunking → embeddings → index, add incremental updates and deletion handling, build a minimal event-driven architecture, examine the limits and risks (garbage in, duplicates, drift), and close with a checklist of metrics.
outcomes: You understand why RAG degrades within weeks without a pipeline and how incremental sync differs from a nightly full re-sync
You know every stage of the chain: extraction, normalization, dedup, chunking, embedding, upsert — and what each one does
You can design incremental updates via webhooks + polling fallback and handle deletions correctly
You see the typical risks — garbage in, duplicates, no embedding version-tracking — and know how to close them
You have a metrics checklist (ingestion lag, parse-failure rate, dedup rate, deletion latency) to check pipeline health

applyIn.title: Production RAG over a corporate knowledge base
applyIn.description: Confluence + Zendesk + GitHub Wiki, where documents change daily and the index must reflect the current state without manual runs.

applyIn.title: A support bot with compliance requirements
applyIn.description: A deleted or stale document must not be cited: you need hard delete, tombstones, and a GDPR audit log.

applyIn.title: Migrating or switching the embedding model
applyIn.description: When the vectorization model changes and you need version-tracking so the index doesn't end up half on old and half on new vectors.

pitfalls: Nightly full re-sync as the only strategy: for 100k+ docs that's hours of compute and a stale index 23 hours a day — you need incremental + weekly full
Not handling deletions: a doc removed at the source stays in the index → answers linking to a 404 and a privacy issue
Parsing without error handling: one corrupted PDF breaks the whole batch — per-document try/except and a dead-letter queue are mandatory
No deduplication: the same FAQ from 3 sources returns 3 identical hits and erodes trust
Embeddings without version-tracking: after a model swap half the index is on old vectors, half on new → search degrades

exercises.question: You have 200k Confluence docs and ~500 change per day. Why is a nightly full re-sync a poor strategy, and what should you pick instead?
exercises.hint: Compare cost and freshness: how many compute hours 200k docs take and how long per day the index is stale. Think webhook-driven incremental + a rare full re-sync as catch-up.

exercises.question: A document was deleted at the source. Describe what must happen in the pipeline so it stops being cited, and the difference between soft and hard delete.
exercises.hint: A deletion signal (webhook or periodic diff) → an action in the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]]. Soft delete = tombstone + filter, hard delete = DELETE + audit for compliance.

exercises.question: RAG recall has slowly dropped for a month with no obvious cause. Which pipeline metrics do you check first?
exercises.hint: Drift often = the pipeline silently broke. Look at ingestion lag, parse-failure rate, connector status, embedding version-tracking, and dedup rate.

s1.title: Why you need a continuous pipeline
s1.why: Without understanding why a one-shot script fails in production, it's easy to build a demo that degrades within weeks. This step sets up the whole motivation of the course.
instructions: Examine three ways RAG degrades without a pipeline: new docs never reach the index, deleted ones answer like ghosts, updated ones return stale info
Articulate the difference: one-shot ingestion works for the demo, production needs incremental sync, deletion propagation, retries on flaky sources, and monitoring
List 4 signals of a broken pipeline: outdated info, citing a deleted document, duplicates in results, recall dropping with no cause (drift)
Place the pipeline in the system: it's the ingestion layer inside [[node:ai-data-systems|data systems]] under the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]
s1.validate: You can explain with one example exactly how a RAG answer becomes wrong if the pipeline stops for a week.
s1.tip: Plan the pipeline the moment RAG ships to production — "we'll add it later" almost never arrives.

s2.title: The chain: extraction → cleanup → chunking → embeddings → index
s2.why: Each stage solves its own task, and an error at an early stage (garbage parsing) poisons everything downstream. You need to see the whole conveyor.
instructions: Extraction: parse by type — PDF (PyMuPDF, Unstructured), HTML (BeautifulSoup, trafilatura), Office (python-docx), Markdown
Normalization: Unicode NFC, strip boilerplate (nav, footer), language detection, fix encoding
Deduplication: full-text hash + near-dup detection (MinHash / SimHash) for versioned copies of one document
Chunking → embeddings: split by the source's strategy (see [[node:sys-chunking-strategies|chunking strategies]]), then compute vectors in batches
Upsert to the index: write chunks with embeddings into the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]] along with metadata (source, doc_id, model version)
s2.validate: For each of the 5 stages you can name its input, output, and one characteristic failure mode.
s2.tip: Garbage in, garbage out: normalization quality directly determines search quality — don't skimp on stripping boilerplate.

s3.title: Incremental updates and deletion handling
s3.why: This is the heart of a production pipeline: incremental sync keeps the index fresh without full re-indexing, and deletion handling closes privacy/compliance gaps.
instructions: Webhook-driven (preferred): Notion, Linear, GitHub fire events → enqueue → process, source-to-index latency 1-10 minutes
Polling fallback for sources without webhooks: cursor by `updated_at` + diff, interval 5 min — 1 h depending on volume
Weekly full re-sync as catch-up for missed events and to fight data drift — expensive but mandatory
Deletion: soft delete (tombstone + filter `is_deleted = false`) for speed, hard delete (DELETE from the index) for GDPR with a mandatory audit
The mechanics of syncing sources are covered in [[node:sys-data-sync|data sync]]
s3.validate: You can draw the path of one update and one deletion from source to index with latency annotated.
s3.tip: Periodic reconciliation (diff against the source) catches deletions the webhook missed — without it your tombstones will be incomplete.

s4.title: How to build the pipeline (event-driven skeleton)
s4.why: Theory without a minimal skeleton doesn't run. Here we assemble the event-driven architecture that can scale.
instructions: Connectors publish events to a queue: `{source, doc_id, action: upsert|delete}` (e.g. via SQS)
Worker on `delete`: removes chunks by filter `{source, doc_id}` from the index and writes to audit_log
Worker on `upsert`: fetch → parse → normalize → compare the text sha256 with the previous hash, skip if equal
On change: chunk by source strategy → embed_batch → delete the document's old chunks → upsert new ones → save the new hash
Parse failures and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter queue with an alert when failure rate > 1%
s4.validate: You have a working loop where reprocessing an unchanged document writes nothing to the index (idempotent via hash).
s4.tip: Hashing the text before chunking is the cheapest way to avoid recomputing embeddings for unchanged documents.

s5.title: Limits and risks: garbage in, duplicates, drift
s5.why: Pipelines break quietly: a connector dies, embeddings split across versions, duplicates pile up. You need to know the limits and close the risks ahead of time.
instructions: Garbage in: one corrupted PDF must not kill the batch — per-document try/except + dead-letter queue, alert above 1% failures
Duplicates: exact hash match → drop; MinHash similarity > 0.95 → keep the newer one, mark as duplicate (normal dedup rate 5-15%)
Embedding versions: track `embedding_model_version` in metadata + a migration plan, otherwise half the index sits on the old model
Drift: weekly full re-sync + an alert on ingestion lag so a dead connector doesn't freeze the index unnoticed
Retries on flaky sources — exponential backoff so you don't slam into the source's rate limits
s5.validate: For each of the 4 risks (garbage, duplicates, embedding versions, drift) you can name a concrete defense mechanism.
s5.tip: The sneakiest risk is no embedding version-tracking: the problem isn't visible right away and shows up as search degradation weeks later.

s6.title: Checklist and pipeline health check
s6.why: A pipeline without metrics is a black box. The final step turns everything above into an observable system you can actually verify.
instructions: Freshness metric: ingestion lag (norm < 5 min from source to index)
Parsing reliability metric: parse-failure rate (< 1%), alert when exceeded
Dedup metric: dedup rate (norm 5-15%) — a sharp rise signals a new duplicating source
Deletion metric: deletion latency and matching the tombstone count with deletions at the source
Final run: update a document at the source and confirm the new RAG answer reflects the change within the SLA
s6.validate: You have a dashboard or list of 4+ metrics and can tell within a minute whether the pipeline is healthy.
s6.tip: Tie an alert not only to errors but to "silence": zero ingestion while sources are alive is a sign of a dead connector.

sys-multi-agent-patterns.title: Multi-Agent: 4 patterns of teamwork
sys-multi-agent-patterns.subtitle: When you need multiple agents and how to pick a pattern: supervisor-worker, parallel, pipeline, debate
sys-multi-agent-patterns.whatItIs: A course on how several AI agents work together instead of one. We break down the 4 core coordination patterns — supervisor-worker (boss + helpers), parallel fan-out, pipeline, and debate/critique — and learn to choose the right one for a task without creating needless complexity.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.approach: We move from the question "do you even need multiple agents" to a breakdown of each pattern, then to the selection rule, a live example, and the limits (cost, coordination). One principle: one main pattern per task, everything else is a tool inside it. We build on [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]] and [[node:systems|AI systems]].
outcomes: Tell the 4 multi-agent patterns apart and understand the purpose of each
Decide when a task truly needs multiple agents versus when one is enough
Pick a pattern by the task signal (splittability, differing viewpoints, iterative quality, external data)
Assess the cost of a scheme: call expense, coordination complexity, looping risk
Assemble a working multi-agent workflow from a checklist without mixing patterns

applyIn.title: Content and copy
applyIn.description: Landing pages, email campaigns, articles — the debate/critic pattern lifts a draft from "okay" to "almost done" in a couple of iterations.

applyIn.title: Large-scale data analysis
applyIn.description: 100 interviews, 5 competitors, a stack of documents — supervisor-worker and parallel split the work into independent chunks and assemble the result.

applyIn.title: Support and routing
applyIn.description: Classifying a request and routing it to a specialized agent — pipeline and supervisor-worker handle routine tickets predictably.

pitfalls: Mixing several patterns in one system — many parallel agents, expensive, impossible to tell what broke
Reflection/debate with no iteration limit — agents loop forever, set a cap of 2-3 rounds
Using debate for simple tasks — two agents arguing over the obvious is a waste of money
Jumping straight to a complex scheme instead of debugging one simple pattern over 5-10 tasks
Using multiple agents where one would do — extra cost and coordination with no quality gain

exercises.question: Your task: analyze 80 survey responses and extract common themes. Which pattern do you pick and why?
exercises.hint: Think about whether the task splits into independent chunks and who assembles the result. See [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]].

exercises.question: A team wants "AI writes → AI critiques → rewrites → critiques again..." with no limits. What's the risk and how do you close it?
exercises.hint: This is the reflection/debate pattern. What happens without a cap on the number of rounds?

exercises.question: Name one task signal for each of the 4 patterns in a single word or phrase.
exercises.hint: Splittability, differing viewpoints, iterative quality, external data — map them to supervisor-worker, debate, reflection, tool-using.

s1.title: When do you even need multiple agents
s1.why: Multi-agent always means more calls and more coordination. Before building a team of agents, make sure one agent genuinely can't do the job. Otherwise you pay for complexity with no gain.
instructions: State the task and ask: can one agent do this in a single pass at acceptable quality?
Check the 4 "team needed" signals: the task splits into independent chunks; differing viewpoints matter; quality improves with iteration; external data/tools are required
If none of the signals fire — stay with one agent, don't overcomplicate
If at least one fires — note which: it points to the pattern in step 3
s1.validate: You have a clear answer of "yes, multiple agents needed" with a concrete signal, or "no, one is enough".
s1.tip: The cost and complexity of multi-agent are justified by saving your time and raising quality — but not always. When in doubt, start with one agent.

s2.title: Breaking down the 4 patterns
s2.why: Without knowing the patterns, every project reinvents the wheel. With them, naming the scheme is enough for the team to know what to build. It's a shared vocabulary for agent coordination.
instructions: Supervisor-worker: a boss agent splits the task, specialist helpers do the parts, the boss assembles the result. See [[node:sys-supervisor-worker|supervisor-worker]]
Parallel (fan-out): one task is broken into identical chunks, agents process them in parallel, results are merged. See [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]]
Pipeline: agents are lined up in a conveyor — one's output is the next one's input (classify → process → format)
Debate/discussion: several agents produce different options or critique each other, a separate agent picks the best or merges the strengths
For each pattern, write one word for its purpose: splittability / scale / stages / quality-through-comparison
s2.validate: You can describe each of the 4 patterns in your own words and name what it's for.
s2.tip: Tool-using (an agent with tools) is often embedded inside any pattern — it's not a separate team but an agent's ability to pull external data.

s3.title: How to choose a pattern
s3.why: The wrong pattern makes a system expensive, slow and undebuggable. The right one makes it predictable and cheap to maintain. The choice flows from the task signal, not from trends.
instructions: Take the signal you found in step 1 and map it to a pattern
Task splits into different subtasks → supervisor-worker; splits into identical chunks at scale → parallel
Task passes through clear stages in sequence → pipeline; needs differing viewpoints or iterative quality → debate
Pick EXACTLY one main scheme. If you need more, add a second as a small tool inside the first, not as parallel work
Cross-check against orchestration principles: [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]]
s3.validate: You have one main pattern chosen for the task, justified by the signal, with no mixing of schemes.
s3.tip: If a task sounds like "both" — it almost always means one pattern on the outside and a second as a nested step, not two parallel systems.

s4.title: Example: walking through a working workflow
s4.why: A pattern only clicks on a concrete scenario. Running one example end to end cements how agents hand work off to each other.
instructions: Take a support task: an incoming request must be classified and routed to the right specialist — this is pipeline + supervisor-worker
Step 1: a coordinator agent receives the message and determines the type (password / billing / bug / complaint)
Step 2: routes to a specialized worker — each has its own data and instructions; complex cases and complaints → a human
Step 3: the worker does its part and returns the answer; the coordinator formats it and sends it to the customer
Trace where control passes between agents — that's the handoff protocol. See [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff protocols]]
s4.validate: You can sketch the example flow step by step and show the point where one agent hands work to another.
s4.tip: When classification breaks, debug the coordinator, not the whole system — that's the power of explicit role separation.

s5.title: Limits and risks: cost and coordination
s5.why: Several agents make more calls than one and require coordination. Ignore the limits and multi-agent becomes an expensive system you can't debug.
instructions: Estimate cost: each agent = separate calls; a team of 4 costs noticeably more than one
Set an iteration limit for debate/reflection (2-3 rounds), or agents loop for hours
Check observability: can you tell which agent failed without dissecting the whole system
Weigh the gain against the cost: quality rose from "okay" to "slight tweak", edit time dropped 1.5-2x — does that cover the higher cost
If coordination is harder than the task itself — simplify the scheme or go back to one agent
s5.validate: You have a cost estimate for the scheme, an iteration cap, and an answer on whether the system is debuggable.
s5.tip: Starting rule: begin with the simplest pattern (often tool-using or supervisor-worker), debug it over 5-10 tasks, then add complexity.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final pass over the checklist catches the main mistakes before launch: mixed patterns, missing limits, needless complexity. It's insurance before the system goes live.
instructions: The task signal is identified, and it genuinely requires multiple agents (one wouldn't do)
Exactly one main pattern is chosen; nested schemes only as a tool inside, not in parallel
An iteration cap is set for debate/reflection
Cost is estimated and justified by the gain in quality/time
The system is debuggable: it's clear which agent owns what and where control passes. Related to agents: [[node:agents|agents]]
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, and you can explain why you chose this scheme and where its limits are.
s6.tip: If even one item is "no" — don't launch. The failure usually hides in mixed patterns or a missing iteration limit.

sys-supervisor-worker.title: Supervisor-worker pattern
sys-supervisor-worker.subtitle: One orchestrator delegates subtasks to specialized agents
sys-supervisor-worker.whatItIs: Supervisor-worker is a [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|multi-agent]] architecture where one **supervisor** accepts a task, splits it into parts, and delegates them to domain-specific **worker agents**. Each worker is narrow: its own system prompt and 2-5 tools. The supervisor never does specialized work itself — it only decomposes, routes, and synthesizes the final answer. It is a form of [[node:ai-orchestration|orchestration]] with strictly separated roles.
sys-supervisor-worker.approach: Don't build a do-everything agent. Start with a supervisor that executes nothing itself plus 2-3 workers with clean boundaries. Routing goes through [[node:sys-branching-logic|branching logic]], task passing through a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]]. Test each worker in isolation first, then wire the loop and measure the bottleneck — the supervisor itself.
outcomes: Know when supervisor-worker is justified vs. when prompt chaining or fan-out suffices
Designed a supervisor: decompose → delegate → synthesize, with no specialized execution
Defined 2-3 workers with non-overlapping boundaries and narrow tool sets
Built the loop: plan → sequential worker calls → synthesis with an audit trail
Set the limits: max-depth, max-workers-per-turn, latency and cost control

applyIn.title: Research agent
applyIn.description: The supervisor delegates: web research → data analysis → writing the brief. Each stage is a separate worker with its own tools.

applyIn.title: Customer ops
applyIn.description: CRM lookup, ticket creation, email draft — three workers; the supervisor assembles the customer reply.

applyIn.title: Code assistant
applyIn.description: File search, test runs, code generation, linting. Natively implemented via [[node:cc-subagents|Claude Code sub-agents]].

pitfalls: The supervisor does worker tasks itself — the prompt bloats and orchestration focus is lost. Rule: delegate and synthesize only.
Workers with overlapping duties — the supervisor can't decide whom to call, duplicate calls, 2x cost. Draw clear domain/action boundaries.
Infinite recursive delegation — a worker becomes a supervisor with no limit. Hard max-depth = 2, usually 1.
Passing between workers as raw text with no schema — format drifts ~10% of the time. Use a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]] only.
Supervisor-worker on a simple task — the overhead isn't justified. One type of task = one agent with the right tools.

exercises.question: Take the task "build a B2B brief on a company" (financials + leadership + news + fit score). Lay out which workers you need and where the boundaries between them are.
exercises.hint: 4 workers with non-overlapping sources. If two workers fetch the same data, the boundaries are wrong.

exercises.question: For the same workers, estimate the latency of a sequential loop (~3s per call) and decide: is the pattern fit for interactive UX or do you need [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]]?
exercises.hint: Sequential latency = the sum of all calls. 4 × 3s = 12s — that's a lot for interactive.

exercises.question: Find a task in your project where you currently use one big agent with 10+ tools. Decide whether to split it into supervisor-worker and justify it.
exercises.hint: The test is 3+ different kinds of expertise AND steps that can't be rigidly fixed. Otherwise [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|prompt chaining]] is enough.

s1.title: What the pattern is and when to use it
s1.why: One agent with 20 tools and a 5000-token prompt confuses which tool to call and loses focus. Supervisor-worker is divide-and-conquer, but it isn't always justified — distinguishing it from neighboring patterns matters.
instructions: Memorize the essence: the supervisor decomposes and synthesizes; workers execute narrow tasks.
Check the applicability test: the task needs 3+ different kinds of expertise AND the steps can't be fixed up front.
Rule out alternatives: one type of task → one agent; rigid sequence → [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|prompt chaining]]; parallel identical tasks → [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]].
Fix in mind that the supervisor is a sequential dispatcher, not parallel.
s1.validate: You can state in one sentence why it's supervisor-worker and not chaining/fan-out/a single agent.
s1.tip: If the task's steps are always the same and run in order, it isn't supervisor-worker — it's a chain.

s2.title: The supervisor's role
s2.why: The supervisor is the orchestration brain. If it starts executing tasks itself, the prompt bloats and routing quality drops. Its job is strictly three actions: decompose, delegate, assemble.
instructions: Pick a stronger model: Sonnet/Opus — the supervisor reasons, it doesn't pinch tokens.
Describe in the system prompt (~1-2k tokens) the available workers and when to call which — this is [[node:sys-branching-logic|routing logic]].
Forbid the supervisor from doing specialized work: its tools are worker invocations (3-7), not subject-matter tools.
Add a synthesis mode: the supervisor aggregates worker outputs into the final answer.
s2.validate: The supervisor prompt contains no subject-matter tool — only delegation and synthesis.
s2.tip: A good supervisor reads like a dispatcher: "given X → call workers A and B → assemble the answer", with no "how" to do the subtask.

s3.title: The workers' role
s3.why: Workers are executors. Their strength is narrowness: short prompt, few tools, high accuracy on their domain. Fuzzy or overlapping workers break routing and double the cost.
instructions: Split responsibility by domain or action so the boundaries don't overlap.
Give each worker its own system prompt (500-1500 tokens) and 2-5 tools, no more.
Match the model to the task: simple lookup → Haiku, reasoning/analysis → Sonnet.
Give each worker its own eval set so you can test it in isolation (see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]]).
s3.validate: For any subtask it's unambiguous which single worker owns it.
s3.tip: If two workers fetch from the same data source, that's a signal to merge them or redraw the boundaries.

s4.title: How to wire the loop
s4.why: Wiring turns the supervisor and workers into a working system: plan → calls → synthesis. Without an audit trail you can't debug "why is the result weak."
instructions: Step 1: the supervisor returns a delegation plan from the input (which workers and with what input).
Step 2: call the workers from the plan sequentially, collecting results into a shared dict.
Step 3: pass results between workers and back via a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]], not raw text.
Step 4: the supervisor in synthesis mode builds the final answer; return it together with the full trail (plan + results) for [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]].
s4.validate: For a single request you can reconstruct: the plan, each worker call, retries, and the final synthesis.
s4.tip: Passing between workers is always by schema — otherwise the format drifts about 10% of the time.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: the supervisor bottleneck
s5.why: The supervisor is a sequential dispatcher, so it's also the bottleneck: latency accumulates, recursive delegation risks an infinite loop, and each extra worker adds cost.
instructions: Set a hard max-depth = 2 (usually 1): the supervisor doesn't call workers that are themselves supervisors.
