Cap max workers per turn at 3-5; if there are more, switch to [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]].
Compute latency: sequential = the sum of all worker calls (4 × 3s = 12s) — assess whether it fits interactive UX.
Budget the cost: supervisor reasoning + executions ≈ 1.5-2.5x one big agent, but quality is higher.
Add metrics ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]): delegation depth, worker success rate, retries per worker.
s5.validate: The system explicitly states max-depth, the per-turn worker cap, and the metrics you watch for degradation.
s5.tip: When latency grows and order isn't required, move the most independent workers into a parallel fan-out.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Before shipping you must confirm that roles are separated, boundaries are clean, limits are set, and the system is debuggable. This step closes all the pattern's typical mistakes.
instructions: Supervisor: does no specialized work, only decompose/delegate/synthesize — check the prompt.
Workers: boundaries don't overlap, each has a narrow tool set and its own eval.
Limits: max-depth and max-workers-per-turn are set; recursion is impossible.
Handoff: task and result passing is structured, not raw text.
Observability: there's a full trail and metrics ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]) for debugging.
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked, and you can explain why your supervisor-worker beats one big agent on this task.
s6.tip: If even one item is "no," it's a future production incident. Close it before shipping, not after.

sys-parallel-fan-out.title: Parallel fan-out (map-reduce)
sys-parallel-fan-out.subtitle: Split a task into independent chunks, process them in parallel, assemble the result
sys-parallel-fan-out.whatItIs: Map-reduce for AI: one large task is split into N independent subtasks (map), each processed in parallel by a separate model call, then the results are aggregated into a single answer (reduce). Canonical scenarios: corpus processing, multi-source research, multi-judge eval, variant generation. The pattern lives inside [[node:ai-orchestration|orchestration]] and relies on [[node:systems|production-systems]] discipline.
sys-parallel-fan-out.approach: The course goes from deciding whether you even need fan-out to a working map -> reduce pipeline with partial-failure handling. First we verify subtask independence, then build the map phase with a concurrency limiter, choose a reduce strategy, walk through a real example over 50 conversations, draw the boundaries (cost, duplicates, assembly), and close with a checklist that verifies coverage.
outcomes: Tell tasks where fan-out actually speeds things up from sequential chains where it is useless or harmful
Build a map phase with a concurrency limiter (semaphore) and exponential-backoff retries
Pick a reduce strategy — synthesis call, programmatic merge, or voting/averaging — by task type
Handle partial failures via a success threshold (80%) instead of all-or-nothing
Understand the economics: when to switch to the Message Batches API for a 50% discount and a separate limit pool

applyIn.title: Corpus processing
applyIn.description: 100+ pages, conversations, or tickets need summarize / classify / extract. Map is an independent call per item; reduce synthesizes the themes.

applyIn.title: Multi-source research and analytics
applyIn.description: 5-20 sources analyzed in parallel, then aggregated into one brief. Cheaper and faster than reading everything in one long context.

applyIn.title: Multi-judge evaluation
applyIn.description: Several critics score one output in parallel, results averaged. Diversity of perspective with no latency growth.

pitfalls: Running the map phase without a concurrency limiter: 100 simultaneous calls -> 429 storm -> retry amplification -> real throughput worse than sequential. A semaphore is mandatory.
Going sequential where subtasks are independent: a chain of 5 summaries takes 15s instead of 3s. Analyze dependencies explicitly.
Aggregating via plain concat with no synthesis call: 100 summaries glued into a document is a 'mix,' not insight.
All-or-nothing on failures: one crashed worker drops the whole job and loses the work of 99 successful ones. Use a success threshold.
Paying 100% for batch workloads: nightly classification, eval suites, bulk extraction belong in the Message Batches API (50% cheaper, separate limit pool).

exercises.question: You have 200 customer reviews; you need the theme and sentiment of each, then the top 10 pain points. Where is map and where is reduce here, and why is this not a sequential task?
exercises.hint: Extracting from one review does not depend on the others — that is map. The top 10 needs all themes at once — that is reduce. Subtask independence is the fan-out criterion.

exercises.question: You launched 100 parallel calls and got an avalanche of 429 errors; throughput dropped below sequential. What did you forget to add, and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: A concurrency limiter (semaphore around 10) + retry with exponential backoff. See [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]].

exercises.question: Out of 50 map calls, 6 failed. Should you fail the whole job? What rule applies?
exercises.hint: 44/50 = 88% > 80% threshold -> continue, note missing items in coverage. All-or-nothing would discard 44 good results.

s1.title: When you need fan-out: the independence check
s1.why: Fan-out only speeds things up if subtasks are truly independent. If B depends on A's result, there is nothing to parallelize — you get a race or garbage. A wrong call here breaks the whole pipeline.
instructions: Frame the task as a set of subtasks and draw the dependencies between them with arrows
Mark subtasks that can run knowing nothing about the others' results — those are map candidates
Check the scale: one small request does not justify orchestration overhead — fan-out pays off from ~10 items
If there are sequential chains (B after A), pull them outside fan-out; parallelize only the independent layer
s1.validate: You can name concrete subtasks, none of which reads another's output, and there are more than ~10 of them.
s1.tip: Independence test: if you shuffle the execution order of the subtasks, does the result change? No -> you can parallelize.

s2.title: Map phase: parallel processing with a limiter
s2.why: Map is N independent model calls. Without a concurrency limiter they drown the tier in 429s; with the right semaphore and backoff you get a near-free 10x speedup.
instructions: Set up an asyncio.Semaphore (or equivalent) with a sane cap — typically 10 concurrent calls
Wrap each worker in try/except and return an ok/failed status instead of crashing the whole batch
Add retry with exponential backoff for 429 and transient errors
Pick a cheap fast model (Haiku) for map — the volume of work here is large
Store the item's id/index in the result so you can restore order later
s2.validate: A run over 20-30 items causes no 429 flood, and each result carries an id and an ok/failed status.
s2.tip: The parallelism cap depends on tier ([[node:pl-rate|rate limits]]) — start at 10 and raise it while watching for 429s.

s3.title: Reduce phase: choosing the assembly strategy
s3.why: Reduce turns scattered partial results into one meaningful answer. The wrong strategy (just glue them) yields a 'mix' instead of insight. The strategy is chosen by task type.
instructions: Synthesis call — a separate strong-model call (Sonnet) that synthesizes all map results into a coherent answer: best quality, +1 LLM call
Programmatic merge — dedup, sort, top-N in code with no model: cheap, for structured outputs
Voting / averaging — for evaluation and classification: average several critics' scores
Before reduce, sort results by id/index — otherwise random order breaks reproducibility
s3.validate: For your task one reduce strategy is chosen and you can explain why the other two do not fit.
s3.tip: If the output is an insight in text — almost always a synthesis call. If a number or a list — programmatic merge.

s4.title: End-to-end example: 50 conversations -> themes and pains
s4.why: Tying map and reduce into one working pipeline with failure handling is the point of the course. A real example shows how the chunks fit together.
instructions: MAP: asyncio.gather over 50 conversations, each extract_themes under semaphore(10), Haiku, returns {conv_id, themes, status}
Check coverage: succeeded / total; if < 80%, fail the job, otherwise continue
REDUCE: collect all themes from the successes, sort them, one Sonnet call with a synthesize prompt
Return the report together with coverage (e.g. 47/50) so completeness is visible
For 1000+ items rewrite map onto the Message Batches API — submit, fetch in 1-2h
s4.validate: The pipeline returns a synthesized report and a coverage metric; a few worker failures do not bring down the whole run.
s4.tip: Coverage in the output is cheap trust insurance: the reader instantly sees how much data the conclusion rests on.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: cost, duplicates, assembly
s5.why: Fan-out is not magic: 100 parallel calls cost 100x in tokens. Without understanding the economics and failure modes the pattern turns into an expensive, fragile construct.
instructions: Cost: wall time drops but cost grows linearly with the number of calls — budget ahead, see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]]
Batches: for non-realtime workloads switch to the Message Batches API — 50% discount, separate limit pool, latency 5min-24h
Duplicates and order: parallel results arrive out of order — sort by id; dedup themes during reduce
Partial failures: set a success threshold (80-90%), log gaps, do not drop the whole job for one worker
Applicability boundary: under a tight cost budget or sequential dependencies fan-out is not needed — see [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|multi-agent patterns]] for more complex coordination
s5.validate: You can state the run's cost, the failure threshold, and the condition for switching to Batches for your task.
s5.tip: Rule: realtime and interactive -> plain parallelism; anything that can wait hours -> Batches API for the 50% saving.

s6.title: Checklist and pipeline verification
s6.why: A final pass catches the classic traps (no limiter, bare concat, all-or-nothing) before they get expensive in production.
instructions: Independence: map subtasks do not read each other's outputs — confirmed
Limiter: a semaphore and exponential-backoff retry on 429 are in place
Reduce: a strategy is chosen (synthesis / merge / voting), not a bare concat
Failures: a success threshold is set, gaps are logged, order is restored by id
Economics: cost is calculated, and for batch workloads the Message Batches API is considered
s6.validate: All five checklist items are closed, and a test run on a slice of the data gives correct coverage with no 429 storm.
s6.tip: Run the pipeline on 10% of the data as a smoke test before the full run — cheaper to find a problem on 5 items than on 5000.

sys-handoff-protocols.title: Hand tasks between agents without losing context
sys-handoff-protocols.subtitle: Structured handoff instead of passing the whole transcript
sys-handoff-protocols.whatItIs:
A handoff protocol is a formal way to transfer a task and its state from one agent to another. Without it, agent-to-agent work turns into a mess of tangled contexts: one agent ships its entire 50k-token transcript to the next, which burns half its context just reading it — more expensive, slower, unfocused.

There are two base formats. Transcript handoff: the receiver sees the sender's full conversation with every tool call — simple, nothing lost, but context bloats. Structured handoff: the sender explicitly builds a compact package {task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria} and the receiver reads only that. In practice the best option is a hybrid: a structured package plus references to artifacts for optional drill-down. This is a base building block of any [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]] and [[node:systems|agentic systems]].
sys-handoff-protocols.approach: Never pass the transcript "as is" — over 5 handoffs it grows to 100k tokens. Build a compact structured package and pass references to artifacts (ticket ID, document ID), not the values. Every handoff must carry the task, what is already done, the constraints, and a done-criterion — otherwise the receiver either redoes work or hallucinates.
outcomes: You understand why a formal handoff protocol beats forwarding the whole conversation
You know the 5 mandatory components of a handoff package: task, context, state, constraints, success_criteria
You can assemble a structured handoff message the receiver reads in seconds
You see the boundaries and risks: lost context, infinite A→B→A loops, private data leaking into logs
You have a checklist to validate a handoff before shipping it to production

applyIn.title: Supervisor-worker system
applyIn.description: A coordinator hands subtasks to workers — each dispatch and result collection goes through a structured package, see [[node:sys-supervisor-worker|supervisor-worker]].

applyIn.title: Sequential agent pipeline
applyIn.description: research agent → writer agent → editor agent: each passes a compact package with references to artifacts, not its whole context.

applyIn.title: Human-in-the-loop
applyIn.description: An agent prepares a result → a human reviews → the agent continues. Without an explicit package the human cannot tell what is done or where to stop.

pitfalls: Passing the full transcript: over 5 handoffs context grows to 100k tokens, cost 5x, focus 0.2x.
Handoff without success_criteria — the receiver does not know when to stop and either over-works or under-delivers.
Losing trace_id across handoffs: logs fall apart and debugging handoff failures takes far longer.
Putting PII and secrets straight into the package: they land in every agent's logs — pass references (IDs) and resolve values inside a trusted boundary.
Handoff without max-hops: A→B→A→B turns into infinite ping-pong. You need a hard hop limit (3–5) and escalation on overflow.

exercises.question: Take any multi-agent scenario of yours and write down exactly what one agent passes to another. Reduce it to {task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria} — what stayed in context, and what became artifact references?
exercises.hint: If context holds more than a couple of paragraphs, almost all of it should become an artifact reference, not text in the package.

exercises.question: Simulate a failure: remove completed_steps from the handoff and watch what the receiver does. Then remove success_criteria. Which of the two omissions is more dangerous in your scenario?
exercises.hint: Without completed_steps the receiver repeats work; without success_criteria it never knows when to stop. Compare the cost of each error.

exercises.question: Add max-hops and trace_id to your protocol. Replay a chain of three handoffs and check: can you reconstruct the full task history from a single trace_id?
exercises.hint: If logs from different agents cannot be stitched by one identifier, trace_id is being lost somewhere in the handoff.

s1.title: Why a formal handoff is needed
s1.why: With a single agent no handoff is needed. But the moment two or more agents split a task, implicit transfer breaks in two ways: either the sender ships everything (context and cost explode) or it ships "continue" with no context (the receiver asks back or hallucinates). The protocol removes both extremes.
instructions: Find every point in your scenario where one agent hands work to another: supervisor→worker, agent→agent in a pipeline, agent→human→agent.
For each point answer: what is passed today — the whole conversation, a short phrase, or nothing?
Estimate the cost: multiply the size of the passed context by the number of handoffs in a typical task.
State the problem in words: "the receiver redoes work", "context bloats", "constraints get lost".
s1.validate: You can name every handoff point in your scenario and say what goes wrong there without a protocol.
s1.tip: Signal a handoff is broken: the receiving agent repeats the sender's work or loses important constraints. You spot it instantly in duplicated tool calls.

s2.title: What to pass: the 5 package components
s2.why: Passing "everything" or "nothing" are two extremes. The working middle is five mandatory components. They give the receiver exactly enough to continue without questions and without redoing work.
instructions: Task — what specifically must be done (one clear goal statement, not vague).
Context — only the relevant background, not the whole transcript: a short summary plus artifact IDs.
State (completed_steps) — what is already done and what remains, so the receiver does not start over.
Constraints — limits: budget, deadline, tone, forbidden actions, caps.
Success criteria — how to know the task is done and it is safe to stop.
s2.validate: For your task you filled all five fields, and context holds nothing that could be replaced by an artifact reference.
s2.tip: Pass references, not values: a ticket ID instead of the full ticket, an artifact_id instead of the document. The receiver pulls the full content inside a trusted boundary if needed.

s3.title: Structure of the handoff message
s3.why: When the package format is the same for every agent, transfer becomes predictable: equal cost, equal quality, and failures stay localized. The standard schema is a machine-readable object with routing and observability metadata.
instructions: Add routing metadata: from_agent, to_agent — who hands to whom.
Add trace_id — an end-to-end task identifier to stitch logs across all agents.
Fill the body: task, context (with artifact_id instead of data), completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria, open_questions.
Put artifacts in a separate block as references/IDs, not as embedded text.
Wire observability: each handoff is its own log record with package size and timing, see [[node:sys-context-passing|context passing]].
s3.validate: You have a single JSON schema for the package that every agent builds, and it includes trace_id and success_criteria.
s3.tip: If the transcript is still over ~20k tokens, compress it: extract key facts with a separate LLM call and pass the compressed version plus a reference to the raw transcript.

s4.title: How to apply it in practice
s4.why: A schema is useless until it is wired into the transfer code. The goal of this step is to assemble a real handoff in a typical scenario (e.g. customer support: triage→specialist→escalation) and validate it against metrics.
instructions: Describe the package as a data structure (dataclass / typed dict) with the fields from steps 2–3.
In the sending agent: after work, build the package — a summary instead of raw context, artifact IDs instead of values.
In the receiving agent: add to the prompt explicitly "do not redo anything in completed_steps; stop on success_criteria".
Let the receiver pull the full artifact by reference only when it is actually needed.
Hook up metrics: package size, handoff success rate, rework rate.
s4.validate: Running one task through the chain yields a package < 5k tokens, the receiver does not duplicate the sender's work, and metrics are recorded.
s4.tip: Production baseline: package size < 5k tokens, success rate > 95%, rework near zero. Going past these is a reason to fix the protocol, not the agents.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: A handoff protocol introduces its own failure classes: context loss on compression, infinite loops between agents, private data leaking into logs. Close them up front or they surface in production.
instructions: Context loss: when compressing a transcript, always keep a reference to the raw artifact so details can be recovered.
Loops: introduce a hard max-hops (3–5) and on overflow escalate (to a human or supervisor) instead of another round.
Privacy: never put PII/secrets in the package — references only; resolve values inside a trusted boundary.
Observability: verify trace_id is not lost on any handoff — otherwise debugging failures grows by an order of magnitude.
Degradation: decide what the receiver does with an incomplete package — ask, escalate, or work with what it has.
s5.validate: For each risk (context, loops, privacy, trace_id) you have a concrete protection mechanism, not a "hope it won't happen".
s5.tip: The A→B→A→B loop is the most common hidden failure. A hop counter in the trace plus a hard cap is cheaper than any post-hoc log dig.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: Before letting a multi-agent chain run, walk the protocol through a checklist. This is the final filter that catches the most expensive mistakes before they reach production.
instructions: The package contains all 5 components: task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria.
trace_id is end-to-end, max-hops is set, escalation on overflow is configured.
The package holds only artifact references — no PII/secrets and no raw values.
The receiver prompt explicitly forbids repeating completed_steps and sets the stop on success_criteria.
Metrics (package size, success rate, rework) are logged and land on a dashboard.
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, and a test task passes the chain with no rework, no loops, and no context overflow.
s6.tip: Make the checklist part of the scenario's CI check: then a broken handoff never reaches production silently.

sys-tool-orchestration.title: Tool orchestration
sys-tool-orchestration.subtitle: How an agent reliably selects, calls, and combines tools
sys-tool-orchestration.whatItIs: Tool orchestration is managing how one model works with a set of tools: which tool to call, in what order, what to run in parallel, how to handle results and errors. It is the layer between [[node:cap-tools|the ability to call tools]] and a real agent that has 3, 10, or 20 of them. Without orchestration the model confuses similar tools, does everything sequentially, and loops on failed calls.
sys-tool-orchestration.approach: We move from mechanics to reliability. First we understand what physically happens during tool use / function calling (the model requests a call, your code executes it, the result is returned). Then we learn to write descriptions so selection is unambiguous. Next: parallel vs sequential and dependencies between calls. Then handling results and errors in a structured format. After that, boundaries and risks (wrong selection, loops, tool budget). Finally, a checklist and a check on a real tool set.
outcomes: You understand the tool-use cycle: model requests a call → code executes → result returned → next turn
You write tool descriptions so the model picks the right one in >95% of cases
You run independent tools in parallel and cut latency several-fold
You return errors in a structured form so the model chooses retry / fallback / skip deliberately
You set a tool budget and know how to detect wrong selection and loops

applyIn.title: Support agent with multiple sources
applyIn.description: The bot pulls from CRM, email history, and calendar. Independent calls run in parallel, latency drops from 6s to 2s.

applyIn.title: Research assistant with web and internal DB
applyIn.description: Slow web_search sits next to a fast internal DB. Orchestration decides what to parallelize and what depends on a prior result.

applyIn.title: Internal tool with 15+ tools
applyIn.description: With a large set the key is distinct descriptions and a tool budget, otherwise the model gets confused and spams calls.

pitfalls: Vague descriptions: `search_data` and `query_db` are indistinguishable → the model picks randomly, up to 30% wrong calls
No parallel hint: without it the model goes sequential ~70% of the time even on independent tools
Dependent tools without explicit order: get_user → get_orders with no hint causes ordering errors
No tool budget: the model loops and calls one tool dozens of times → cost and latency
Raw errors fed back: "500 Internal Server Error" instead of structured → unpredictable retry or failure

exercises.question: An agent has two tools: search_docs and search_kb. Complaint: the model mixes them up. What do you fix first?
exercises.hint: The problem is not the execution code but how the model distinguishes tools. Look at the field it bases the decision on.

exercises.question: A request makes 4 tool calls, all independent, and latency equals their summed time. How do you cut it?
exercises.hint: Claude can call several tools in one turn. What is missing in the system prompt to make it do so?

exercises.question: A tool sometimes fails with a rate limit. What error-result format helps the model behave predictably?
exercises.hint: Compare "500 Internal Server Error" with an object carrying error_code, retry_after, should_retry.

s1.title: What tool orchestration is
s1.why: Before tuning selection and parallelism you must see the cycle: the model does not execute tools itself — it requests a call, your code executes it, the result goes back. Orchestration manages this cycle when there are many tools.
instructions: Memorize the tool use / function calling cycle: the model returns tool_use → your code executes → the result returns as tool_result → the model takes the next turn
Distinguish orchestration from the bare ability to call tools (see [[node:cap-tools|tool use]]) — orchestration is about selection, order, and resilience across a set of tools
Tie it to the layer above: orchestration is part of building [[node:systems|systems from Claude]] and [[node:ai-orchestration|AI orchestration]]
List your current tool set and note how many there are and which ones resemble each other
s1.validate: You can plainly explain when the model requests a call and who actually executes it.
s1.tip: Orchestration starts to matter from 3 tools — with one or two you can live without it.

s2.title: Describe tools for reliable selection
s2.why: The model selects a tool by its description. Vague or overlapping descriptions cause up to 30% wrong calls — the most common and cheapest-to-fix defect.
instructions: In every description state three things: what it does, when to use, when NOT
Disambiguate similar tools explicitly: "Do NOT use for searching users by email — use search_users for that"
Make input schemas precise — required fields, types, no free text where an enum works
Audit the set for overlap: if two tools can be described by the same phrase, that is future confusion
s2.validate: For any pair of similar tools, the description explicitly says when not to use each.
s2.tip: Test: read only the descriptions, without the names — could you yourself pick the right tool for a task without error?

s3.title: Sequential and parallel calls
s3.why: Claude natively can call several independent tools in one turn. Without a hint it goes sequential ~70% of the time, and latency adds up instead of being the maximum.
instructions: Add an explicit hint to the system prompt: "When tools are independent, call them in parallel in a single turn"
For dependent calls describe the order: "fetch user_id first, then use it for orders" — the model must infer the dependency graph from descriptions
In code, execute parallel tool_use calls concurrently (e.g., collect all calls in one turn and run them at once)
Estimate the gain: 3 independent tools at 2s each are 2s in parallel vs 6s sequential
s3.validate: On independent tools the agent does one parallel turn instead of several sequential ones.
s3.tip: A dependency is when one tool's input comes from another's output. Everything else is a candidate for parallel.

s4.title: Handling results and errors
s4.why: The model decides retry / fallback / skip based on what you return. Raw error text leaves it guessing; a structured result gives it grounds for a deliberate decision.
instructions: Return results structured (JSON), not raw text — easier for the model to extract what it needs
Make errors explicit objects: { error_code, retry_after, should_retry } instead of "500 Internal Server Error"
State a failure policy in the system prompt: "If a tool fails twice, skip it and note in response"
Distinguish transient errors (rate limit → retry) from permanent ones (no permission → skip and report)
s4.validate: When a tool fails the model behaves predictably: it retries, routes around, or reports — it does not hang.
s4.tip: should_retry: true|false in the error response saves the model from guessing and from extra calls.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: Without guardrails orchestration degrades into wrong selection, loops, and tool spamming — dozens of calls to one tool that burn money and time.
instructions: Set a tool budget: a hard limit on total calls per request (usually 5–15), a safeguard against loops from [[node:sys-loop-patterns|loop patterns]]
Scope tool permissions narrowly: broad permissions are both a security risk and a source of confusion (see [[node:sys-auth-patterns|auth patterns]])
Watch for trouble signals: the model skips a required call, latency = sum, 30+ calls per request
For external tools prefer [[node:mcp|MCP]] — standard schemas, auth, and error semantics out of the box
s5.validate: The code has a hard cap on tool calls, and you know which metrics catch wrong selection.
s5.tip: A tool budget is not about saving money but about protection: one looping tool with no cap easily runs a request for minutes and dollars.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Orchestration counts as working not by "it seems to answer" but by measurable metrics of selection, parallelism, and resilience. The final pass closes the gap between "configured" and "works in production".
instructions: Run the checklist: distinct descriptions (when/when NOT), parallel hint, declared dependencies, structured errors, tool budget
Capture metrics via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]: tool-call success rate (>95%), parallel-call ratio, retries per tool, tools-per-request distribution
Run 5–10 real requests and verify: correct tool, parallel where possible, correct reaction to a deliberately triggered error
Record orchestration as part of your agent [[node:m-patterns|patterns]], not a one-off setup
s6.validate: On a test set of requests selection is correct, independent calls run in parallel, errors are handled, the budget is not exceeded.
s6.tip: The key health metric is tool-call success rate >95%. If it is lower, the descriptions (step 2) are almost always to blame.

sys-cost-management.title: How not to go broke on the AI API
sys-cost-management.subtitle: Count, save, and keep the bill under control without losing quality
sys-cost-management.whatItIs: Cost management for the AI API is a set of practices to pay only for what you need: understand where cost comes from (tokens × model price × frequency), measure spend per feature, apply savings levers (right model for the task, caching, context compression), and set limits with alerts. Part of [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] and a subtopic of [[node:systems|Systems thinking]].
sys-cost-management.approach: We move from the nature of the bill to controlling it. First the cost formula, so you know what to push on. Then measuring and attributing spend — without numbers, optimization is blind. Then the three main savings levers. Then defenses — limits and alerts so the bill doesn't quietly spike. A separate step on boundaries: where saving starts hurting the product. Finally, a checklist and a check against real spend.
outcomes: Break any AI bill into tokens, model, and frequency and see where the budget leaks
Measure spend per feature and model, not as one monthly lump sum
Apply three savings levers: right model, caching, context compression
Set limits and alerts that catch an anomaly in hours, not in the end-of-month bill
Cut spend 2-3× without dropping answer quality

applyIn.title: SaaS chat support
applyIn.description: A cheap model classifies the question, simple ones go to Haiku, complex to Sonnet/Opus, FAQs from cache. The bill drops from $4,500 to $1,200/mo at the same quality.

applyIn.title: Bulk document processing
applyIn.description: Thousands of similar calls: pick the minimally sufficient model, cache the shared system prompt, compress input context — batch cost falls several-fold.

applyIn.title: An AI feature inside a product
applyIn.description: A per-user limit and a daily-spend alert keep one loop or abuse from burning the monthly budget overnight.

pitfalls: Using the strongest model "just in case": Opus is ~15× pricier than Haiku, yet on 80% of tasks the difference is invisible
Not caching repeats: if 30% of requests are the same FAQ, you pay for one answer over and over
Watching spend as a single lump number: without per-feature attribution it's unclear what to optimize
Cutting quality silently: downgrade the model and complaints and rework rise — real cost goes up
No limits: a loop or traffic spike burns the budget in hours before you notice

exercises.question: Your feature makes 50,000 calls a day on an expensive model at $0.015. How do you halve the bill within a week without losing quality?
exercises.hint: First measure the share of simple vs complex requests. Simple → cheap model, repeats → cache, long context → compress. Count savings per lever separately.

exercises.question: This morning yesterday's bill came in 10× higher than usual. Which two mechanisms should have warned you earlier, and how do you set them up?
exercises.hint: A daily alert on deviation from baseline and a hard spend/frequency limit. Think in percent-of-normal thresholds, not absolute dollars.

s1.title: Where cost comes from
s1.why: You can't manage what you don't understand. The AI bill is a product of three factors: token count (input + output) × model price per token × call frequency. Each is a lever, but first you must see the formula.
instructions: Break down your model's price: separately for input and output tokens — output is usually several times pricier
Estimate average request length: system prompt + context + history + answer in tokens
Multiply by frequency: how many calls per day/month the feature makes
Compare models: compute the same volume on Haiku, Sonnet, Opus — you'll see the multiple-fold gap
Write the formula per feature: tokens × price × frequency = monthly spend
s1.validate: You can estimate a feature's monthly bill on paper and name which of the three factors contributes the most.
s1.tip: Output tokens are often 4-5× pricier than input — long answers hit the bill harder than long prompts.

s2.title: Measuring and attributing spend
s2.why: A single "$X per month" number is useless for optimization. You need to know which feature, which model, and which request type eat the budget — otherwise you cut blindly.
instructions: Log per call: feature, model, input and output token counts, cost
Tag calls (feature/endpoint/request type) so you can group spend
Build a breakdown: top features by spend, top models, share of simple vs complex requests
Find the 20% of calls driving 80% of the bill — such concentration almost always exists
Fix a baseline: normal daily spend per feature — the basis for alerts in step 4
s2.validate: For any feature you can name its share of the total bill and see where the bulk of spend sits.
s2.tip: Tag attribution matters more than cent-level precision: knowing "classification = 60% of the bill" beats a perfect total.

s3.title: Savings levers
s3.why: Three levers deliver most of the savings: right model for the task, caching repeats, and context compression. Together they often cut the bill 2-3× without losing quality.
instructions: Right model: cheap by default, expensive only where truly needed; add a cheap classifier-router
Caching: serve repeats and FAQs from cache — see [[node:cap-caching|Caching]] and [[node:sys-semantic-cache|Semantic cache]] for similar, not only identical, requests
Context compression: don't drag the whole history and documents into every call — keep only what's relevant
Shrink output tokens: ask for a concise answer, cap max_tokens where length isn't needed
Reuse the system prompt via prompt caching if the model supports it
s3.validate: For each of the three levers you can name a concrete change to your feature and the expected savings.
s3.tip: Start with the lever that hits the "20% of calls = 80% of the bill" found in step 2 — that's the best return on effort.

s4.title: Limits and alerts
s4.why: Savings are useless if one loop, bug, or traffic spike burns the monthly budget overnight. Limits are insurance, alerts are the early signal. This is a core [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] practice.
instructions: Set a hard spend limit per user/key/feature — a ceiling that can't be breached
Cap call frequency ([[node:pl-rate|rate limiting]]) so a loop or abuse can't run up the bill
Configure a daily alert on deviation from the step-2 baseline (e.g., >150% of normal)
Separate environments: dev/test on cheap models and small limits, prod on production ones
Define what happens at the limit: graceful degradation, not a feature crash
s4.validate: Anomalous spend is caught by an alert within hours, and the limit physically prevents breaching the planned budget.
s4.tip: A percent-of-normal alert is more reliable than an absolute threshold: $100 is normal for one feature and an emergency for another.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: Saving at the cost of quality isn't saving — it's shifting the cost. A cheap model where a strong one is needed raises complaints, rework, and churn. True cost = API money + the fallout of bad answers.
instructions: Before downgrading a model, run a quality eval on real requests, not on gut feel
Track quality metrics (complaints, rework, escalations) next to the spend metric
Don't cache what must stay fresh: prices, stock, personal data — the cache will serve stale results
Don't compress context so far that meaning is lost: verify the trimmed input still yields a correct answer
Count full cost: saved $50 on the model but added $500 in support — that's a loss
s5.validate: Every savings decision has a quality check, and you can show the bill dropped while quality did not.
s5.tip: Rule: measure the current model's quality first, then downgrade and compare. Saving without measuring quality is gambling.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Cost management is not a one-off campaign but an ongoing practice. The checklist turns scattered tactics into a system that keeps the bill under control as you grow.
instructions: Run the checklist: cost formula known, spend attributed, levers applied, limits and alerts in place, quality measured
Do a control measurement: bill before vs after, cache hit rate, distribution across models
Confirm the alert actually fires — trigger a test deviation
Assign a regular spend review (e.g., weekly) with anomaly analysis
Document the baseline and thresholds so the next growth phase doesn't catch you off guard
s6.validate: All checklist items are closed, the control measurement shows a lower bill at preserved quality, and alerts are battle-tested.
s6.tip: Put the cost review in the calendar as a recurring task — without cadence the practice quietly dies and the bill starts creeping back up.

sys-monitoring.title: Observability for AI systems
sys-monitoring.subtitle: What to measure in production AI and why uptime is not enough
sys-monitoring.whatItIs: A course on observing the health of production AI: which 5 metrics show the real state of the system (latency, cost, quality, drift, refusals), how to trace a request end-to-end, and how to build dashboards and deviation-based alerts instead of absolute thresholds. This is not the "logs + uptime" of ordinary software — AI fails silently: 100% uptime with 40% garbage answers is invisible to standard monitoring.
sys-monitoring.approach: We move from principle to practice. First we unpack why AI needs a special approach to observability (step 1), then what exactly to measure (step 2) and how to tie the signals into a single request trace (step 3). Next we turn metrics into action: deviation alerts and dashboards (step 4). Separately we fix the boundaries and risks — the main trap of "measure only uptime" (step 5) — and close with a checklist and a readiness test (step 6). Built on the five AI-specific metrics from the Observability node.
outcomes: You understand why APM (CPU/RPS/500-errors) doesn't answer the question "is the AI doing well"
You know the 5 AI-specific metrics and their targets: latency p95/p99, cost per call, output distribution, tool-call success, refusal rate
You can trace a request end-to-end with metadata (model, prompt_version, tokens, tool_calls, refusal_flag)
You build alerts on deviation from a rolling baseline, not on an absolute threshold
You distinguish boundaries: where observability helps and where you need [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|quality evals]]

applyIn.title: Launching an AI feature in production
applyIn.description: From day one you enable latency and cost tracking; from week two you add output distribution and refusal rate once a baseline is collected.

applyIn.title: Operating agents with tool calls
applyIn.description: Tool-call success rate becomes the key metric: 30% failures and retries are a cost spike, latency tail, and quality drop all at once.

applyIn.title: Controlling regressions after a deploy
applyIn.description: The dashboard answers "did it get worse after the deploy" within hours, and rollback goes through a feature flag instead of manually triaging complaints a week later.

pitfalls: Measuring latency only: a fast response can be semantic garbage, and slow model degradation passes silently without refusal rate and output distribution

Logging without aggregation: 50k lines a day is a dumpster, not observability; metrics get aggregated (Datadog/Prometheus), raw logs are for drill-down only (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging patterns]])
Not splitting cost by feature: "$3000/mo on AI" is useless, "compose $0.04/email, summarize $0.002" is actionable (see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]])
Absolute alerts instead of deviation alerts: "p99 > 5s" fires 100×/day from batch jobs; you want "p99 grew 2× vs rolling 1h avg"
Ignoring tool-call metrics on agents — losing the only signal that catches the cost+latency+quality cascade at once

exercises.question: The system shows 100% uptime and p95 latency of 1.2s, yet users complain about quality. Which 2 metrics do you add to catch the problem, and why?
exercises.hint: Quality drifts silently. Think about response length and the share of refusals — what reveals that the model has "drifted" while the API is alive?

exercises.question: An alert "p99 > 5s" fires 100 times a day and everyone ignores it. How do you rephrase the rule so it catches a real regression?
exercises.hint: The problem is the absolute threshold given batch jobs. Compare not against a constant, but against what?

exercises.question: For an agent with tool calls the budget suddenly doubled and so did latency. Which metric do you check first and which hypothesis do you test?
exercises.hint: For agents one signal links cost, latency tail, and quality. What happens when tool calls fail and retry?

s1.title: Why observability for AI differs from ordinary software
s1.why: Standard APM (CPU/RPS/500-errors) shows the API is alive but not that the AI is doing well. You can hold 100% uptime while serving 40% garbage answers — standard monitoring won't catch it. AI fails silently: the model answers, but worse.
instructions: Write down what your current monitoring actually catches: are these infrastructure signals (is the service alive) or model-behavior signals (are the answers good)?

Formulate 3 AI silent-failure scenarios: quality drift (model answers worse while the API is alive), cost spike (one user burns $500/day on long contexts), latency tail (p99 jumped from 3s to 12s — UX is dead for 1%)
Check whether the current system can answer "did it get worse after the deploy or not" — if not, log it as a gap
Connect observability to the operational loop: see [[node:ai-operations|operating AI systems]] and the general [[node:systems|production systems]] node
s1.validate: You can name at least 3 AI problems that 100% uptime does not reveal.
s1.tip: Adopt the mantra: "a green infrastructure dashboard ≠ good AI". That distinction separates AI observability from ordinary APM.

s2.title: What to measure: 5 AI-specific metrics and their targets
s2.why: Without the right metric set you are blind to degradation. Five signals cover system health: latency (speed), cost per call (money), output distribution (drift), tool-call success (reliability), refusal rate (applicability).
instructions: Latency: measure p50/p95/p99 end-to-end (not just the API call, but with tool calls and retries). Target: p95 < 3s for interactive, < 30s for async agents; p99 < 800ms on classification, < 8s on generation
Cost per call: $/request broken down by feature and model. Target: variance < 30% (otherwise runaway prompts — context grows every request). Detail in [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]]
Output token distribution: histogram of response lengths; a sharp shift = the model drifted or the prompt broke
Tool-call success rate: % of successful tool invocations vs schema errors/retries. Target > 95%
Refusal rate: % of responses where Claude refused (safety/ambiguity). Target < 2%, otherwise revise the prompt
s2.validate: You have a table of 5 metrics, each with a concrete target value for your workload type.
s2.tip: Targets are starting reference points (typical for chat/agent as of 2026-05), not law. Calibrate against your own baseline in the first week.

s3.title: End-to-end request tracing
s3.why: Metrics say "something broke", a trace says "where and why". Without an end-to-end trace with metadata you see the aggregate but can't drill down to a specific bad request.
instructions: Implement tracing via middleware at the model-call boundary — one layer, so you don't duplicate instrumentation across the code
Write metadata into every trace: model, prompt_version, user_id, tokens_in/out, latency, tool_calls, refusal_flag
Tie the trace to the step-2 metrics: all 5 signals should aggregate from traces, while the trace itself stays for drill-down
Make sure prompt_version lets you answer "which prompt deploy caused the regression" — the key to fast rollback
Raw traces are for incident analysis, aggregates are for the dashboard; don't confuse their purposes (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging patterns]])
s3.validate: Given one user_id and one prompt_version you can pull every request with its latency, tokens, tool_calls, and refusal flag.
s3.tip: prompt_version in every trace is the cheapest investment: it turns "feels worse after the deploy" into a proven fact in a minute.

s4.title: Alerts and dashboards
s4.why: Metrics and traces are useless if you learn about a problem from a user instead of the dashboard. The goal is to see a regression within minutes. Key rule: alert on deviation from baseline, not on an absolute threshold.
instructions: Build a dashboard from 3 panels: latency (p50/p95/p99 + RPS + error rate), cost ($/day by feature compose/summarize/classify + top-10 expensive users), quality (output length histogram + tool success rate + refusal rate trend)
Set deviation alerts: "p99 grew 2× vs rolling 1h avg", "cost/hour > 2× rolling avg", "refusal rate > 3%"
Avoid absolute thresholds like "p99 > 5s" — they fire 100×/day from batch jobs and people stop reading them
Tie the response to rollback: alert → trace analysis by prompt_version → rollback via feature flag (see [[node:sys-rollback-strategies|rollback strategies]])
Reaction-time goal: from alert to rollback — hours, not days
s4.validate: Each of the 3 key alerts is phrased as a deviation from a rolling baseline, and there is a written alert → trace → rollback path.
s4.tip: If an alert gets ignored, it's either too frequent (absolute threshold) or doesn't lead to action. Every alert needs a runbook: what to do when it fires.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: you can't measure only uptime
s5.why: The most expensive mistake is assuming a green dashboard = a good product. Observability shows symptoms (latency, cost, response length) but does not assess the semantic correctness of an answer. That's the boundary of the method.
instructions: Fix trap #1: a latency-good response can be semantic garbage. Output distribution catches a length shift but not content quality
Fix trap #2: logging without aggregation is a dumpster, not observability; metrics go to Datadog/Prometheus, raw goes to drill-down
Fix trap #3: "$3000/mo on AI" is useless without a per-feature breakdown — otherwise you can't tell what to optimize
Draw the line with quality evaluation: semantic correctness needs [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals and benchmarks]], not latency dashboards
For agents keep tool-call metrics in focus: ignoring them hides the cost+latency+quality cascade at once
s5.validate: You can explain which question observability does NOT solve (semantic correctness of an answer) and where to go for it (evals).
s5.tip: Observability answers "does the system run stably", evals answer "does it answer correctly". These are two distinct disciplines — don't substitute one for the other.

s6.title: Checklist and readiness test
s6.why: The final assembly turns scattered settings into a working observability loop. The checklist guarantees that none of the 5 metrics and none of the layers (metric → trace → alert) dropped out.
instructions: Metrics: all 5 signals are collected (latency, cost per call, output distribution, tool-call success, refusal rate), each with a target
Traces: every request is traced with model, prompt_version, user_id, tokens, tool_calls, refusal_flag, drill-down available
Dashboard: 3 panels (latency, cost by feature, quality) visible on one screen
Alerts: phrased as deviation from baseline, each with a runbook and a rollback path
Boundaries: the team understands that observability ≠ quality evaluation; evals are wired separately for semantic correctness
s6.validate: You passed all 5 checklist items with no gaps: you learn about any regression from the dashboard before users do, and you can roll back within hours.
s6.tip: Test the loop with a synthetic incident: deploy a prompt that cuts response length and time how many minutes until the alert fires. Longer than 15 minutes means your alerts are too sluggish.

sys-logging-patterns.title: What to log for AI
sys-logging-patterns.subtitle: Structured AI-call logs: enough for debugging, safe for compliance
sys-logging-patterns.whatItIs: Logging AI calls is not regular app logging. It's a structured payload per model call (model, prompt_version, tokens, latency, tool_call statuses, hashed user_id) plus a separate sampled store for full prompt/completion. The goal is to reproduce any incident by request_id without drowning the project in storage cost or breaking GDPR. This complements [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]] (metrics and alerts) and [[node:sys-versioning|prompt versioning]] (tying a log to a specific version).
sys-logging-patterns.approach: We move from motivation to implementation: first understand why AI is logged differently, then fix the minimum required payload and sampled layer, handle privacy (redact BEFORE writing), structure logs into hot/warm/cold with retention, draw the boundaries (what must never be logged), and finally assemble a checklist with a verification on a real call. Each step builds on the structure from the [[node:systems|systems layer]] node.
outcomes: You understand how AI logs differ from regular app logs and why metadata + sampled payload is the right pattern
You know the exact minimum required payload and what goes into the sampled store (10-20%)
You can redact PII and secrets BEFORE writing via a field whitelist, not a blacklist
You set retention hot 7d / warm 30d / cold 90d so logs don't cost more than the AI calls themselves
You can reproduce an incident by request_id in minutes instead of saying "can't reproduce"

applyIn.title: B2B product with an AI feature in prod
applyIn.description: Email AI, support, content generation: 100% of requests log metadata, 15% log the full payload to an encrypted store. Customer incidents are resolvable by request_id.

applyIn.title: Team with regulatory requirements
applyIn.description: GDPR/HIPAA environment: redact PII at the SDK layer, fixed retention, audit trail of prompt versions. Logs pass audit without rework.

applyIn.title: Debugging AI quality regressions
applyIn.description: "AI started hallucinating last week" — via prompt_version + git SHA you find which prompt version was active and match it against the sampled completion.

pitfalls: Logging everything to hot storage: 100k requests × 5k tokens = ~2GB/day in prompts alone, $30k+/year in Datadog. Sample full payloads, aggregate metadata.
PII in plaintext — the most common incident. Email AI logs the full body → grabs the customer's email → GDPR violation. Redact BEFORE writing, not after.
Blacklisting tool-arg fields: a new secret in a new tool will leak. Whitelist — log only explicitly allowed fields.
Not logging prompt_version: in 3 months you can't tie a bad answer to a prompt version. Pinning to git SHA is required (see [[node:sys-versioning|sys-versioning]]).
Infinite retention "just in case": GDPR requires deletion, storage grows linearly, value drops exponentially. 7/30/90 is the standard.

exercises.question: Your email AI logs the full email body to hot storage on 100% of traffic. What two problems does this create and how do you fix each?
exercises.hint: Think along two axes: cost (volume × retention) and compliance (PII in plaintext). Fixes are sampling the full payload and redacting BEFORE writing.

exercises.question: Two months later a customer complains about a strange answer from last week. Which log fields do you need to reproduce the incident locally?
exercises.hint: request_id to find it, prompt_version/git SHA for the prompt version, model for the model version, sampled payload for the actual prompt+completion.

exercises.question: A tool call to the database contains {"db_password": "...", "query": "..."}. Why is blacklisting db_password more dangerous than whitelisting query?
exercises.hint: What happens when someone adds a new tool with a new secret field that was never added to the blacklist?

s1.title: Why AI is logged differently
s1.why: AI incidents are only diagnosable from the triad prompt + completion + tool trace. Without them, "AI started hallucinating at customer X" is undiagnosable. Regular app logs (request/response statuses) don't give you that. This is part of the [[node:ai-operations|AI operations layer]].
instructions: Write in your own words the difference: a regular log answers "did the request fail", an AI log answers "what exactly did the model see and generate"
List the 3 questions an AI log must answer: which prompt version, what was the input/output, how much did it cost (tokens/latency)
Fix the dual purpose of logs: enough for debug replay AND safe for compliance — these are two competing requirements
Connect to [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]: metrics tell you WHAT broke, logs tell you WHY
s1.validate: You can explain why a screenshot of a customer's answer is useless for debugging without request_id, prompt_version, and model.
s1.tip: Logs are the "black box" of an AI call. Design them as if in 3 months you'll have to reconstruct an incident you've already forgotten.

s2.title: What to log: required payload and sampled layer
s2.why: A minimum structured payload per call gives 100% metadata coverage without the cost of storing full prompts. Full prompt/completion go into a separate sampled store (10-20%), which provides debug replay without $20k/mo in log storage.
instructions: Fix the required fields (100% of traffic): request_id, timestamp, model, prompt_version, prompt_hash, input/output_tokens, latency_ms, tool_calls[].status, hashed user_id, feature/endpoint
Fix the sampled fields (10-20%): full prompt, full completion, tool_call arguments + responses
Decide WHY the full payload is sampled: storage cost grows with volume × tokens, while a sample suffices for statistics and most incidents
Ensure metadata is written BEFORE the response (latency computed on completion), and tool_call statuses record ok/error per tool
s2.validate: You have two field lists (must-log at 100% and sampled at 10-20%) and each field has a "why it matters for debugging" reason.
s2.tip: prompt_hash (sha256) in the required layer lets you find "identical prompts" even without the full body — cheap incident deduplication.

s3.title: Privacy in logs: PII and secrets
s3.why: Prompts may contain user PII, completions generated PII, and tool_calls secrets (db_password, tokens). Wrong logging = GDPR incident or credential leak. Redaction is done at the SDK/middleware layer BEFORE writing. Details in [[node:pl-privacy|privacy]].
instructions: Build a "never log" list: API keys, OAuth tokens, raw passwords, card numbers, SSN, plaintext PII (email/phone/address)
Put a redactor in middleware BEFORE writing the log: regex for email/phone + a name detector (e.g. Claude Haiku) → replaces with [REDACTED:type]
For tool_call arguments use a field WHITELIST (log only explicitly allowed ones), not a blacklist — otherwise a new secret leaks
Verify redaction fires in BOTH directions: on the prompt (user input) and on the completion (generated text)
s3.validate: You ran a test call with an email and db_password in the input — both are replaced with [REDACTED:...] in the log, no plaintext left anywhere.
s3.tip: Redact BEFORE writing, not after: "we'll clean the logs later" = a window in which PII already leaked into storage and backups.

s4.title: How to structure logs: hot / warm / cold + retention
s4.why: Without structure, logs either cost more than the AI calls themselves or aren't kept long enough for post-mortem. A three-tier model (hot/warm/cold) with retention balances access speed, cost, and compliance.
instructions: Split the tiers: hot 7d (fast debug, expensive storage like Datadog), warm 30d (post-mortem), cold 90d (compliance/audit, cheap storage)
Keep full prompts sampled only and with short retention 14-30d max — longer = GDPR risk and cost spike
Enable encryption at rest for the sampled store with full payloads and a lifecycle policy hot → cold → delete
Pin prompt_version to a git SHA from CI so the log unambiguously connects to the [[node:sys-versioning|prompt version]] in code
s4.validate: Each log tier has a lifespan and a cost, and full prompts are auto-deleted by lifecycle — nothing is kept "forever".
s4.tip: Estimate cost up front: volume/day × retention × storage price. If full prompts are in hot, the number shocks you and the decision to sample becomes obvious.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: what must not be logged
s5.why: Over-logging sensitive data is the main source of incidents. The line between "useful for debug" and "legal risk" runs through PII, secrets, and retention. This is an operational constraint, not a technical detail.
instructions: Draw the red line: everything on the "never" list (step 3) is written to neither hot, sampled, nor cold — regardless of debug usefulness
Fix that retention longer than necessary is a risk, not a safety net: GDPR requires deletion, data value drops exponentially
Separately check tool_call responses: a tool's response may contain someone else's PII (e.g. a DB query result) — it also needs redaction
Agree that any new log field passes a "is there a secret/PII here" review before being added to the payload
s5.validate: The team has an explicit, written list of data forbidden from logging and a rule that a new field is logged only after review.
s5.tip: If in doubt whether to log a field — don't. Adding a field later is cheap; cleaning leaked PII out of backups is nearly impossible.

s6.title: Checklist and verification on a real call
s6.why: The pattern only counts as working when an incident actually reproduces by request_id. The final check catches the gap between "logs configured" and "we can debug an incident".
instructions: Run the checklist: (1) metadata at 100%, (2) sampled full payload 10-20%, (3) redaction BEFORE writing, (4) prompt_version = git SHA, (5) retention 7/30/90, (6) sampled-store encryption
Make a test AI call and find it in logs by request_id — verify all required fields are present
Simulate an incident replay: by request_id pull the sampled payload + metadata + model version and reproduce the answer locally
Verify there's not a single plaintext secret or PII in the logs, and full prompts are deleted by lifecycle
s6.validate: You took a random request_id, reconstructed the prompt/model version and full input-output (from sampled) in minutes, and found no unredacted PII.
s6.tip: Make incident replay part of engineer onboarding: whoever can reproduce an incident by request_id understands why every log field exists.

sys-versioning.title: Prompt and model versioning
sys-versioning.subtitle: Prompts are code: semver, lock files, and an eval gate so "AI worked yesterday, not today" becomes debuggable
sys-versioning.whatItIs: A two-layer discipline. Layer 1 — prompt versions: prompts live in git as files (`prompts/*.yaml`), carry semver, go through PR review, and every request injects `prompt_version`. Layer 2 — model versions: snapshot pinning (`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`) vs alias (`claude-sonnet-4-5`), plus a `models.lock.json` with every pinned snapshot ID — analogous to `package-lock.json`.
sys-versioning.approach: We move from motive to practice: why version at all → what exactly goes into a version (prompt, model, parameters, eval dataset, tool schema) → how to store versions and tie them to results via logs → how to roll back and compare versions → where the limits and desync risks are → a final checklist with verification. Anchored on the [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]] node inside [[node:ai-operations|AI operations]].
outcomes: Every AI response is tied to a (prompt_version, model_snapshot) pair and traceable to a specific commit
Prompts are moved out of code into git-versioned files with semver and PR review
All models are pinned by snapshot ID in a lock file — no aliases in production
An eval gate runs before any model or prompt bump, and regressions are visible before deploy
Rolling back to a working version takes minutes (revert + redeploy or a feature flag), not hours of investigation

applyIn.title: Production service with LLM calls
applyIn.description: 8 prompts in prod: each in its own file with semver, the model pinned by snapshot, prompt_version logged on every call. On a "got worse" complaint you can see which version and model answered.

applyIn.title: Upgrading to a new Anthropic model
applyIn.description: sonnet-4-6 ships: you open a PR bumping models.lock.json, CI runs the eval suite on the new model against baseline, you merge 1-2 weeks after release, not on launch day.

applyIn.title: Investigating a regression
applyIn.description: Answer quality dropped on Wednesday. From prompt_version logs you find the PR that changed the prompt on Tuesday, compare the diff, and roll back with a revert in 5 minutes.

pitfalls: Model alias in production (`claude-sonnet-4-5` without a snapshot) is a ticking bomb: Anthropic updates the alias unannounced and your regression lands overnight
Prompts hardcoded in code (`app.py` line 234) — no diff history, no review, no fast rollback
Bumping the model without an eval gate — you upgrade and pray, then learn about 20% worse answers a week later via NPS
Semver without rules — the team can't tell patch/minor/major apart and doesn't know whether a bump is safe to merge
Tool definitions and parameters (temperature) aren't versioned — schema or temperature changed, the model behaves differently, and the version doesn't show it

exercises.question: Your service references the model as `claude-sonnet-4-5`. Why is this dangerous in production and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: The alias resolves to the latest snapshot. Anthropic can update it at any time — you get a regression with no warning. Pin a concrete snapshot ID in models.lock.json.

exercises.question: A prompt changed, the AI got worse, but nobody remembers which edit is to blame. What minimal set of practices would close this gap?
exercises.hint: Prompts in git files + semver + prompt_version in every call's logs. Then the regression ties to a specific PR and rolls back with a revert.

exercises.question: You want to move to a new model. Describe an eval gate that won't let a regression reach prod.
exercises.hint: An eval suite of 50-200 cases on the new model vs baseline. Pass rate must not drop >2%. A diff report in the PR. Merge only if the threshold holds — see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]].

s1.title: Why version prompts and models
s1.why: Without versions, "AI worked yesterday, not today" is undebuggable: you can't tell whether the prompt changed, the model auto-updated, or Anthropic rolled out a new one. Versioning makes the cause of a failure visible.
instructions: List every source of nondeterminism in your service: prompt edits, model updates, parameter changes
State the goal: every response must trace to a (prompt_version, model_snapshot) pair
Locate your node inside [[node:ai-operations|AI operations]] and treat versioning as ongoing operational discipline, not a one-off task
Assess current pain: can you say right now which prompt and model answered a week ago?
s1.validate: You can name at least 3 reasons AI behavior could silently change without your code changing.
s1.tip: The core idea: a prompt is code. Everything you do for code (semver, review, diff, rollback) a prompt needs too.

s2.title: What to version: prompt, model, parameters, evals, tools
s2.why: A version is incomplete if it captures only the prompt text. Behavior is set by all five: prompt, model snapshot, parameters, eval dataset, and tool schema. Miss one and you get desync.
instructions: Layer 1 — prompt: text in `prompts/*.yaml`, semver (patch = wording/typo, minor = new rules, major = output schema change)
Layer 2 — model: a concrete snapshot ID, not an alias; pinning gives determinism and manual upgrades
Generation parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p) are part of the version: change them and behavior changes
Tool definitions: the tool schema is part of the prompt — lock both schema and version
Eval dataset: version the case set, or version-to-version comparison runs on different rulers — see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]]
s2.validate: For one of your prompts you've written out all 5 versioned elements with their current values.
s2.tip: A prompt major bump (output schema change) = a forced re-eval of all downstream consumers, not just the prompt itself.

s3.title: How to store versions and tie them to results
s3.why: A version not tied to a result is useless. You need to be able to take any prod response and recover exactly which prompt version and model snapshot produced it.
instructions: Put prompts in git: `prompts/email-compose.yaml` with `id`, `version`, `model` (pinned snapshot), `template`
Create `models.lock.json` mapping every model in the system to a concrete snapshot ID — analogous to `package-lock.json`
Inject and log `prompt_version` and `model_snapshot` on every AI call — see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]]
Set up review: a prompt version bump goes through a PR with required review (e.g. 2 reviewers)
Link logs to quality metrics so an NPS drop can be mapped to a specific version
s3.validate: From the log line of one real response you can recover both the prompt version and the model snapshot.
s3.tip: The lock file is the single source of truth for models. Enforce the no-alias-in-production rule with a CI linter.

s4.title: How to roll back and compare versions
s4.why: Versioning pays off the moment a regression hits: you need to revert to a working version fast and understand exactly what changed between "working" and "broken".
instructions: Prompt rollback: `git revert` the PR → CI redeploy in minutes; or instantly via a [[node:sys-rollback-strategies|feature flag]] to the old version
Version comparison: run the eval suite on both versions and produce a diff report (where answers diverged)
Eval gate on bump: the new version's pass rate must not drop more than 2% from baseline — otherwise don't ship
For the model: bump the snapshot in the lock file via a dedicated PR with an eval suite on the new model vs production
Write the rollback procedure down so an on-call engineer can execute it without thinking
s4.validate: You can describe step by step how to roll back both the prompt and the model to the previous working version in 5 minutes.
s4.tip: Don't bump a model on its release day. Merge 1-2 weeks after it passes the eval gate — let it settle.

s5.title: Limits and risks: version desync
s5.why: Versioning creates its own class of bugs — desync. A prompt expects one model but the lock file holds another; evals ran on an old dataset; the tool schema drifted from the prompt. These seams need control.
instructions: Prompt↔model desync: prompt v2.4 was built for a snapshot that got swapped in the lock file — pin the required model right in the prompt file
Evals↔version desync: pass rate was compared on different datasets — version the eval dataset together with the prompt
Tool schema↔prompt desync: the schema changed but the prompt didn't — the model answers differently; lock them together
Mind deprecation: Anthropic supports snapshots ~12 months (as of 2026-05), the window can change — check docs.anthropic.com
Don't spawn versions without cause: too-frequent bumps without evals create noise and the same desync
s5.validate: You've listed at least 3 desync points in your system and for each named how to prevent it.
s5.tip: Any version element that changes separately from the rest is a potential desync. The goal is an atomic bump of all five.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final review turns scattered practices into a working versioning system and catches gaps before they become a prod incident.
instructions: Prompts in git files with semver and PR review — not in code
All models pinned by snapshot ID in `models.lock.json`, aliases banned in production and checked in CI
Every call's logs carry `prompt_version` and `model_snapshot` (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]])
Before any bump (prompt or model) an eval gate runs with a ≤2% pass-rate drop threshold (see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]])
The rollback procedure is documented and tested: revert + redeploy or a [[node:sys-rollback-strategies|feature flag]]
s6.validate: All 5 checklist items are done, and you've run a practice rollback on staging to confirm the procedure actually works.
s6.tip: Set up a deprecate-watch on Anthropic's policy: the snapshot support window can change and the lock file may need updating ahead of time.

sys-rollback-strategies.title: Rollback strategies on regression
sys-rollback-strategies.subtitle: How to restore the previous version in minutes when a new prompt or model answers worse
sys-rollback-strategies.whatItIs: A regression in an AI system is quieter than a bug in regular code: no stack trace, just a drop in answer quality. A rollback strategy is pre-built infrastructure (feature flags, canary, kill switch) that lets you return to the previous prompt or model version in seconds-to-minutes instead of hours of debugging and redeploy. It rests on [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]] (what to roll back) and [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]] (when to roll back).
sys-rollback-strategies.approach: First we pin down why fast rollback matters and what MTTR target to hit. Then we learn to detect regressions via [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]] and [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]. Next come three levels of response: fast flag-based rollback to the previous version, gradual canary rollout to avoid a mass incident entirely, and understanding the limits (no versioning means nothing to roll back to). We finish with a checklist and a game-day test.
outcomes: MTTR from alert to rollback under 5 minutes instead of hours
Every customer-facing AI feature has a flag, canary, and kill switch with a fallback
Regressions are caught automatically by metrics, not by a customer complaint
The team ships more often in smaller batches — per-release risk drops
Rollback is tested in advance, not during a real incident

applyIn.title: A customer-facing AI feature became revenue-critical
applyIn.description: Email-compose, support chatbot, description generation — where a bad answer directly hurts trust and revenue. A flag or canary is mandatory here.

applyIn.title: Updating a prompt or model
applyIn.description: Any prompt_version or model_snapshot bump ships through canary, not straight to 100% of traffic.

applyIn.title: Reviewing an incident that lived for hours
applyIn.description: A past regression lasted 6+ hours before the fix — a signal you need instant-rollback infrastructure.

pitfalls: Feature flag without auto-rollback: a human watches the dashboard and flips by hand — 15-30 minutes lost. Triggers must be automatic.
Canary without statistical significance: 1% × 1 hour = ~50 requests, any difference is noise. Minimum 24h per stage or N ≥ 1000 requests.
Kill switch without a fallback: turn AI off and the user gets a blank screen. You need graceful degradation: template, human queue, cache, explicit 'unavailable'.
Rolling back the prompt only, not the model: if a model bump caused the regression, the flag must toggle both prompt_version and model_snapshot.
Testing rollback only in prod: a broken kill switch surfaces exactly when you need it. Run a quarterly game day.

exercises.question: Take one of your AI features and describe today's rollback path: how many steps from 'we noticed a problem' to 'we restored the previous version', and how many minutes does it take?
exercises.hint: If the answer is 'git revert + redeploy = hours', you found a feature-flag candidate.

exercises.question: Define 3 auto-rollback triggers for your feature with concrete thresholds (e.g. refusal rate +50% vs baseline).
exercises.hint: Lean on metrics from [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]: refusal rate, p99 latency, eval score, cost/request.

exercises.question: Design a kill-switch fallback: what does the user see if the AI feature is turned off entirely?
exercises.hint: A blank screen is a failure. A good fallback: a template response, cache, or an explicit 'temporarily unavailable'.

s1.title: Why you need a rollback strategy
s1.why: Without infrastructure the path detect → debug → fix → PR → CI → deploy takes hours or days. With feature flags: detect → flip → seconds. Time from detection to rollback is MTTR, and for customer-facing AI it must be measured in minutes, because bad answers to customers damage trust.
instructions: List your AI features and mark which are customer-facing or revenue-critical.
For each, estimate current MTTR: how long it actually takes from a complaint to restoring the previous version.
Set a target MTTR under 5 minutes for customer-facing features.
Note that internal tooling can live with git-revert, while customer-facing cannot.
s1.validate: You have a list of features marked 'needs fast rollback' with a numeric target MTTR for each.
s1.tip: If the team is afraid to ship prompt changes, that's a direct symptom of missing rollback: they ship rarely in big batches, which only raises risk.

s2.title: How to detect a regression
s2.why: There's nothing to roll back if you can't see what got worse. AI has no stack trace, so regressions are caught by metrics via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]] on live traffic and [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]] on a fixed case set. Without this a regression lives until the first customer complaint.
instructions: Run every version through [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]] before rollout — the first quality filter.
In prod watch metrics: refusal rate, p99 latency, output length, cost/request, NPS proxy (% who click 'regenerate').
Record a baseline for each metric on the current stable version.
Set alerts on deviation from baseline, not on absolute thresholds.
s2.validate: Each key metric has a recorded baseline and an alert on its degradation.
s2.tip: Evals catch regressions before rollout, monitoring after. You need both: the eval set won't cover every live-traffic edge case.

s3.title: Fast rollback to the previous version
s3.why: Once a regression is confirmed you need to restore the previous version without a full redeploy. A feature flag switches prompt_version or model_snapshot in seconds. This rests on [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]]: to roll back to v2.3.1, that version must be stored and addressable.
instructions: Set up a feature flag that selects the prompt/model version (LaunchDarkly / Unleash / Statsig or homegrown).
Make sure the flag toggles BOTH prompt_version AND model_snapshot — either could have caused the regression.
Configure auto-rollback: when a trigger fires the flag drops to 0% in seconds, with no human in the loop.
Define concrete triggers: refusal rate +50%, p99 latency 2×, eval-score drop >5%, cost/request +30% vs baseline.
Verify the previous stable version is available for rollback (see [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]]).
s3.validate: A simulated trigger moves the flag to the previous version automatically in under 5 minutes with no manual action.
s3.tip: Auto-rollback is critical: a manual flip loses 15-30 minutes on 'human noticed → decided → switched'. The trigger must fire on its own.

s4.title: Canary: gradual rollout against risk
s4.why: The best rollback is the one you never needed at scale. Canary rolls a new version to a small percentage of traffic and expands only if metrics hold. That way a regression hits 1-10% of users instead of everyone, and auto-rollback fires before the incident grows large.
instructions: Set stages: 1% (24h) → 10% (24h) → 50% (24h) → 100%, selecting users by a stable random hash.
Hold each stage under observation for at least 24h or until N ≥ 1000 requests for statistical significance.
Compare the canary group's metrics against a baseline group, not against absolute values.
Wire in the same auto-rollback triggers as step 3 — at any stage the flag drops to 0%.
On Kubernetes you can use Argo Rollouts / Flagger; for AI metrics, custom middleware in the triggers.
s4.validate: A new version passes all canary stages with metrics within baseline; on drift, rollback fires at the current stage.
s4.tip: Don't shorten a stage for speed: 1% × 1 hour = ~50 requests, that's noise. Longer at a small percentage beats a fast rollout to everyone.

s5.title: Limits and risks: no versions, no rollback
s5.why: Rollback doesn't exist in a vacuum. If versions aren't stored ([[node:sys-versioning|versioning]]) there's nowhere to return to. Without a fallback, the kill switch leaves the user with a blank screen. Understanding the limits prevents a false sense of safety.
instructions: Verify each shipped prompt and model version is stored and addressable — otherwise rollback is impossible ([[node:sys-versioning|versioning]]).
For the kill switch, always lay down a fallback path: template response, human queue, cache, or an honest 'feature unavailable'.
Remember statistics: on small traffic metrics are noisy — don't roll back on 10 requests.
Note that external causes (a model-provider outage) aren't fixed by a version rollback but by a kill switch to fallback.
Pin it down: rollback is damage control, it doesn't replace [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]] before rollout.
