s5.validate: For each feature it's confirmed: versions are stored, the kill switch has a fallback, triggers don't fire on noise.
s5.tip: A prompt rollback won't fix a provider problem. Separate two scenarios in your head: 'our version is bad' (rollback) and 'all AI is down' (kill switch to fallback).

s6.title: Checklist and verification via game day
s6.why: A broken rollback mechanism surfaces exactly during an incident — the most expensive moment. A quarterly game day simulates a regression and verifies the whole chain (detection → trigger → rollback → fallback) works within the target under 5 minutes.
instructions: Build a checklist: the feature has a flag, canary stages, auto-triggers, a kill switch with a fallback, and stored versions.
Once a quarter run a game day: artificially introduce a regression and time the rollback.
Separately test the kill switch: turn AI off entirely and confirm the fallback works and UX doesn't fall into null.
Record the actual MTTR and compare to the target under 5 minutes; fix whatever overshoots.
After a real incident run a post-mortem: what worked, which trigger was late, what to add.
s6.validate: The game day showed MTTR under 5 minutes, the kill switch served a working fallback, and the checklist is fully closed.
s6.tip: A game day is insurance you check before the fire. If rollback first runs during a real incident, you'll learn it's broken at the worst possible moment.

sys-rate-limiting.title: Rate limiting and backoff: how not to crash your tier
sys-rate-limiting.subtitle: Managing traffic to the Claude API: 429s, exponential backoff with jitter, Retry-After, queues, and safe retries
sys-rate-limiting.whatItIs: A course on two related layers that protect your Claude API integration. First — backoff on errors: what to do when the API returns a 429 (rate limit) or a 5xx. Second — internal rate limiting: how to cap your own traffic so you never hit [[node:pl-rate|tier limits]] in the first place. Together they keep a single traffic spike from collapsing your whole tier and turning a transient error into a cascade failure.
sys-rate-limiting.approach: We move from symptom to system. First we unpack what a 429 is and why it happens, then build a correct exponential backoff with jitter, learn to respect Retry-After, add queues and throttling on your side, draw the boundaries (what you must not retry), and finish with a checklist verified against a real spike. No theory for its own sake — every step gives concrete numbers and a testable result.
outcomes: Understand how a 429 differs from a 5xx and why a naive retry loop burns your own quota
Implement exponential backoff with ±20% jitter and a justified max retries (3 for interactive, 5-7 for batch)
Parse and respect the Retry-After header as a minimum delay instead of your own formula
Split traffic into priority queues (interactive > batch) and throttle at 80% of the tier limit
Know which calls are dangerous to retry and verify system behavior under 5× load

applyIn.title: Multi-tenant B2B platform
applyIn.description: Several customers share one tier. Without per-user quotas and priority queues, one user or batch job burns the limit and takes everyone else down.

applyIn.title: Chat service with peak load
applyIn.description: A viral spike or marketing campaign delivers 5× traffic. Throttling on your side smooths the peak, interactive users stay stable, batch waits in the queue.

applyIn.title: Evals and classification pipeline
applyIn.description: A large offline volume of calls must not compete with realtime. A separate pool and the Message Batches API give an isolated rate limit and a 50% discount.

pitfalls: Linear retry (1s, 1s, 1s) on a 429 — you burn your own limit and trigger even more 429s. Always exponential + jitter.
Ignoring the Retry-After header: Anthropic suggests the optimal delay, while dumb backoff retries too early and catches a new 429.
Infinite retry: on a transient outage this is $$$ in failed calls and clogged worker threads. Max 3-7 attempts, then fail fast.
One shared rate limit for interactive and batch: batch eats the quota, interactive drops. Minimum two priority pools.
No per-user quotas: one user or a compromised key burns the whole tier in an hour.

exercises.question: The API returned a 429 with Retry-After: 8. Your backoff formula yields a 2-second delay on this attempt. How long do you wait?
exercises.hint: Retry-After is a server directive, not a hint. Use it as a minimum lower bound, not as one of several values to average.

exercises.question: Your interactive chat and a nightly batch classification job both run through one rate limiter. During a daytime chat spike, users started getting 429s. What do you restructure?
exercises.hint: Think about priorities and pool isolation. Which traffic can wait and which cannot? What does Anthropic offer specifically for offline load?

exercises.question: An Anthropic outage is in progress and your service hangs on 30-second timeouts instead of failing fast. What mechanism do you add and what are its states?
exercises.hint: After N consecutive failures you should stop trying and fail instantly, then cautiously probe for recovery. Three states.

s1.title: What rate limits are and why a 429 happens
s1.why: Before building protection, you need to understand how a 429 differs from a 5xx and why a naive retry loop only makes things worse. A 429 means "you exceeded the limit" — retrying immediately is pointless and harmful, unlike a 5xx where a transient glitch may clear.
instructions: Distinguish three response types: 429 (rate limit — your traffic exceeded the tier), 529 (Anthropic overloaded), 5xx (server error). The reaction to each differs.
Find your current RPM/TPM limits in the Anthropic docs and map them to your account's [[node:pl-rate|tier limits]].
Understand the cascade mechanic: one runaway script or viral peak hits the limit → the 429 spreads across the whole tier → even interactive users get errors.
Write down which traffic sources to the API you have (interactive, batch, async jobs) — this is the basis for future queues.
s1.validate: You can explain in words why retrying a 429 request immediately is a mistake, and how that differs from a retry on a 5xx.
s1.tip: A 429 is not an "application error" but a load-management signal. Log it on a separate counter: norm < 0.5%, alert > 2%.

s2.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
s2.why: Linear retry burns your own limit. Exponential backoff stretches the pauses between attempts, and jitter spreads simultaneous retries across time, preventing the thundering herd when thousands of clients retry in sync.
instructions: Implement the formula: delay = min(2^attempt × 1000ms, 60s). Base 1-2 seconds, ceiling 60 seconds.
Add ±20% jitter to each delay — random spread breaks retry synchrony across clients.
Set max retries deliberately: 3 for interactive (better to fail fast), 5-7 for batch (waiting is acceptable).
Log the p95 backoff delay: norm 1-3s, a sharp rise signals congestion on Anthropic's side.
s2.validate: On a simulated series of 429s the pauses grow exponentially (≈2, 4, 8s), each with a random spread, and after max retries the request fails rather than hanging forever.
s2.tip: Jitter is mandatory precisely at scale: without it all clients hit again in the same millisecond after a shared outage.

s3.title: Respecting the Retry-After header
s3.why: Anthropic returns a Retry-After header with the optimal pause. This is the server's knowledge of its own state — more accurate than your formula. Ignoring it means retrying too early and catching another 429.
instructions: Parse the Retry-After header from the response on 429/529 (value in seconds).
Use it as a minimum lower bound: actual delay = max(Retry-After, your backoff delay).
If the header is absent — fall back to your own exponential backoff formula from step 2.
Don't let jitter pull Retry-After downward — jitter is added on top and never reduces the server-specified pause.
s3.validate: When the response carries Retry-After: 10, your client waits at least 10 seconds, even if your own formula would have yielded 4.
s3.tip: Retry-After is a contract with the server. Respecting this header often restores access faster than aggressive retries on your own formula.

s4.title: Queues and throttling on your side
s4.why: Backoff reacts to a 429 that already happened. Internal rate limiting prevents it: you cap your traffic before you hit the limit and split it by priority so batch doesn't take interactive down. This is the move from reaction to prevention.
instructions: Put a token bucket / leaky bucket limiter before every Claude call and hold it at 80% of the tier limit — a buffer for spikes.
Split traffic into at least two priority pools: interactive (high) and batch (low), so offline load doesn't eat the realtime quota.
Add per-user quotas (e.g., 100 req/min for interactive) so one user or key can't burn the whole tier.
For non-realtime volumes use the Message Batches API — a separate rate-limit pool and a 50% discount (see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]]).
s4.validate: On an artificial traffic spike the limiter throttles the excess, interactive requests pass stably, and batch waits in the queue — no 429 reaches the UI.
s4.tip: 80%, not 100% of the limit, is a deliberate margin. The last 20% absorbs micro-peaks that would otherwise turn into a 429 instantly.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: what you must not retry
s5.why: Retry is safe only for idempotent operations. A blind retry of a non-idempotent call (e.g., with a write or billing side effect) on a timeout can execute the action twice. And during a long outage even correct backoff becomes an expensive retry storm.
instructions: Split calls into idempotent (safe to retry) and non-idempotent (double execution is dangerous) — retry the latter only with deduplication.
Add a circuit breaker: after 5 failures / 30s go to open (fail fast) → half-open after 30s → closed after 3 consecutive successes.
Set a cost ceiling: during a prolonged outage a retry storm generates $1000+ in failed calls — the circuit breaker cuts it off.
Tie the behavior to your overall error strategy (see [[node:sys-error-handling|error handling]]): after retries are exhausted — an explicit fallback, not a silent hang.
s5.validate: On a long-outage simulation the circuit breaker opens after the threshold, requests fail fast (rather than hang on timeouts), and non-idempotent calls are not executed twice.
s5.tip: The question "what happens if this call executes twice?" must be asked before wrapping it in a retry, not after a double-charge incident.

s6.title: Checklist and verification under load
s6.why: Protection against rate limits is only proven under a real spike, not in calm mode. The final run confirms that backoff, Retry-After, queues, and the circuit breaker work together, not in isolation.
instructions: Go through the checklist: exponential backoff + jitter ✓, Retry-After respected ✓, max retries set ✓, ≥2 priority pools ✓, per-user quotas ✓, circuit breaker ✓.
Run a load test at 5× usual traffic and confirm interactive users stay stable and 429s at the UI = 0.
Set up a dashboard (see [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]): 429 rate, p95 backoff delay, circuit breaker state, top-10 quota consumers.

Record a deprecate-watch: specific RPM/TPM shift (see [[node:pl-rate|pl-rate]]), but the bucket + backoff + breaker pattern is stable — build it into your system architecture (see [[node:systems|systems]]).
s6.validate: Under 5× load every checklist item holds, the dashboard shows 429 < 0.5% and correct circuit breaker states, and no interactive user got an error.
s6.tip: Test the spike in staging before marketing causes one in prod. A real incident is a bad place for the first test of your backoff logic.

sys-semantic-cache.title: Semantic cache
sys-semantic-cache.subtitle: Queries that mean the same thing → a ready answer, no AI call
sys-semantic-cache.whatItIs:
A semantic cache answers repeating questions phrased differently without calling the model. For an incoming request it computes an embedding ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]]), searches a [[node:af-vector-db|vector DB]] for a similar prior query, and if cosine similarity is above a threshold it returns the existing answer in tens of milliseconds for $0.

It's an infrastructure technique for [[node:ai-operations|running AI in production]]: on FAQ and classification loads 30-40% of queries are rephrasings of the same thing, and an exact cache never catches them.
sys-semantic-cache.approach: Don't confuse it with an exact cache or with [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]]: those cache text, the semantic cache caches meaning. Start with a high threshold (0.95), cache only non-personalized answers, and always design invalidation. Without these three rules the cache starts lying fast.
outcomes: You understand how a semantic cache works: embedding → similar-query search → ready answer
You distinguish exact cache, [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]] and semantic cache — and combine them
You can judge whether a semantic cache pays off for a given workload
You know the risks: false hits, personal-data leakage, staleness
You can run a readiness checklist and validate the cache on real queries

applyIn.title: Support / FAQ bot
applyIn.description: Same questions, different wording, from different users — the cache returns an answer in 50ms instead of 2s.

applyIn.title: Classification and docs search
applyIn.description: A fixed category set and repeating queries give a 50-60% hit rate — most model calls disappear.

applyIn.title: Cutting the AI bill
applyIn.description: On top of prompt caching the semantic cache removes another 30-50% of spend on read-heavy loads — see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]].

pitfalls: Threshold too low: at 0.85 "how do I cancel my subscription" matches "how do I change my subscription" — the customer gets the wrong-meaning answer.
Caching personalized answers: user B gets user A's payment date — a data leak and a GDPR violation.
No invalidation strategy: the knowledge base is updated, but the cache serves stale answers for weeks.
Semantic cache on creative tasks: "write a welcome email" — everyone gets the same text, obviously robotic.
Ignoring the embedding cost itself: at a hit rate < 10% the cache costs more than not having one.

exercises.question: You have a FAQ bot: 20k requests/day, and logs show one question asked in dozens of wordings. Does a semantic cache fit, and why?
exercises.hint: It's a read-heavy load of semantically repeating, non-personalized questions — exactly the case where the cache delivers a 30-40% hit rate.

exercises.question: A marketer asks you to cache answers to "write a welcome email for a new customer." What do you say?
exercises.hint: Creative generation: every answer must be fresh. A cache hit means everyone gets the same text. A semantic cache is contraindicated here.

exercises.question: You set the threshold to 0.95, the hit rate is only 8%, and embedding on every request costs money. What do you check?
exercises.hint: Compute the break-even hit rate: if savings from hits are smaller than the embedding cost across all misses, the cache runs at a loss.

s1.title: What a semantic cache is
s1.why: Without a clear "similar-meaning query → ready answer" model it's easy to expect magic and put the cache in the wrong place.
instructions: Lock in the core: on an incoming request you compute an embedding, search a vector DB for a similar prior query, and above a threshold return the ready answer — the model isn't called.
State the cache's key question: "has anyone asked this in meaning over the last N days?"
Note the two effects of a hit: an answer in 30-80ms instead of 1-5s, and $0 for the model call.
Name the tools: GPTCache, Helicone semantic cache, or custom on [[node:af-vector-db|pgvector]] + Redis.
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how a query becomes a ready answer without a model call.
s1.tip: The semantic cache is an [[node:ai-operations|operations]] layer, not a model property. It wraps the call, it doesn't live inside it.

s2.title: How it differs from exact cache and prompt caching
s2.why: These three mechanisms get confused, which leads people to pick the wrong cache or expect savings where there won't be any.
instructions: Exact cache: byte-for-byte match. "Cancel subscription" and "how do I cancel my subscription" are different keys — no hit.
[[node:cap-caching|Prompt caching]]: caches the repeating prefix (system prompt, knowledge base), but the user query differs for everyone — it doesn't catch rephrasings.
Semantic cache: caches the meaning of the full query, so it catches rephrasings.
Remember: the mechanisms are orthogonal and combine — prompt cache on the prefix + semantic cache on the full query.
s2.validate: You can use one example to show which of the three caches fires and which doesn't.
s2.tip: Enable [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]] first (cheaper and simpler), and only if cost stays high add the semantic cache on top.

s3.title: How it works: embeddings + similarity threshold
s3.why: The similarity threshold is the cache's main dial: it directly sets the balance between number of hits and the risk of returning a wrong answer.
instructions: The query path: text → embedding ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]]) → cosine similarity search in a [[node:af-vector-db|vector DB]] → top-1 candidate.
Compare the candidate's similarity to the threshold: a typical range is 0.92-0.97.
Lock in what the threshold means: 0.97 — strict (few false hits, lower hit rate); 0.92 — risky (you get a similar-but-not-the-same answer); 0.95 — a working recall/precision balance.
On a hit, check the entry's freshness (TTL) before returning the answer.
s3.validate: You can explain what happens to hit rate and error risk if you drop the threshold from 0.95 to 0.85.
s3.tip: Tune the threshold on real logs, not from your head: take pairs of queries that SHOULD and should NOT match, and find the separating boundary.

s4.title: When a semantic cache pays off
s4.why: The cache pays off only on the right workload; on the wrong one it doesn't save anything and just adds embedding cost.
instructions: Look for read-heavy loads with semantically repeating queries: FAQ, support, classification, docs search, translation of popular phrases.
Check the payoff signals: prompt cache miss rate is already low but cost is high; logs show one question, many wordings, many users.
Estimate the ceiling: 30-40% hit rate on FAQ, 50-60% on classification with a fixed category set, < 5% on creative.
Match the savings against the budget goal — see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]].
s4.validate: You can predict the order of magnitude of the hit rate for your load and say whether the cache pays off.
s4.tip: Rough rule: if fewer than 10% of queries in your logs are rephrasings of something already seen, a semantic cache almost certainly won't pay off.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: A semantic cache serves a past answer as a new one — without boundaries that turns into wrong answers, leaks, and stale information.
instructions: False hits: too low a threshold matches close-but-different questions — keep the threshold high and test on real queries.
Personalization: answers that depend on user_context must NOT be cached — otherwise user B gets user A's data (GDPR risk).
Staleness: define an invalidation strategy — TTL (1h volatile / 24h FAQ / 7d stable), event-driven purge on knowledge-base change, or a version-keyed cache key.
Creative and chat with history: each answer is unique or depends on the whole history — semantic matching doesn't work here.
s5.validate: For your scenario you can name which queries must not be cached and how you'll invalidate the cache.
s5.tip: A cache key with prompt_version + knowledge_base_version gives automatic invalidation: bump the version and all stale cache misses.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: A semantic cache silently affects answer quality and the bill, so before turning it on you need an explicit checklist and measurement on real queries.
instructions: Readiness checklist: the load is read-heavy and non-personalized; the threshold is set (start at 0.95); an invalidation strategy is chosen; the personalized branch is excluded from caching.
Run real queries: a set of "should match / should not match" pairs — confirm the threshold separates them.
Turn on metrics: hit rate, latency on hit, share of false hits, embedding cost.
Compute the break-even hit rate and compare the resulting savings to the [[node:sys-cost-management|cost]] goal.
After launch, watch for 1-2 weeks: hit rate, complaints about wrong answers, effect on the bill.
s6.validate: The cache passes the checklist, metrics are collected, and the numbers show real savings without a rise in wrong-answer complaints.
s6.tip: Combining with [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]] on semantic-cache misses often yields 60%+ total cost reduction versus a naive baseline.

sys-api-patterns.title: How AI talks to other systems
sys-api-patterns.subtitle: 4 integration patterns — sync, async, webhook, streaming — and how to pick the right one
sys-api-patterns.whatItIs:
When AI interacts with your software (CRM, email, database) it goes through an API (big topic — [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI Integration Systems]]; the systems themselves — [[node:systems|Systems & Integrations]]). There are 4 standard ways to connect: reply immediately (sync), kick off and report later (async), react to an external event (webhook), stream the answer piece by piece (streaming).

Picking a pattern = answering two questions: "how long does AI take" and "do we need the result right now". It's not about fashion — it's about matching user expectations.
sys-api-patterns.approach: There's no single "correct" way — only the right way for a specific scenario. Don't force everything into sync "because it's simple". First understand the operation's duration and the user's expectation, then pick the pattern. One scenario = one pattern; don't try to serve everything with a single scheme.
outcomes: Distinguish the 4 AI-to-system integration patterns: sync, async, webhook, streaming
Know which signals drive the choice (duration, need for instant answer, who initiates)
Can pick a pattern for a concrete task and justify the choice
See the typical risks: timeouts, unreliable delivery, lost results
Have a checklist to validate the chosen pattern before shipping

applyIn.title: AI feature in a SaaS product
applyIn.description: Short classification — sync; big report — async with notification; long text — streaming. Each button gets its own pattern.

applyIn.title: Reacting to external events
applyIn.description: An email, a submitted form, a new task triggers AI without the user — that's a webhook (see [[node:sys-event-driven|Event-Driven Architecture]]).

applyIn.title: Batch vs realtime processing
applyIn.description: The "now or in the background" choice is a special case of the bigger realtime-vs-batch decision (see [[node:sys-batch-vs-realtime|Batch vs Realtime]]).

pitfalls: Doing everything sync: the user waits 40 seconds, closes the tab, AI finishes anyway — money spent, result useless.
Streaming where the answer is short and fast — it only complicates the code for no value.
Ignoring timeouts: a sync request longer than the server limit gets cut off while AI keeps working for nothing.
Webhook without acknowledgment and retry: the event is lost, AI simply never fires, nobody notices.
Async without notification: the task went to the background, but the user can't tell if it's done.

exercises.question: You have 4 AI operations: (1) detect an email's tone in 1 sec, (2) build a quarterly report in 2 minutes, (3) respond when a customer writes in chat, (4) write a long email in front of the user. Which pattern for each?
exercises.hint: Duration + who initiates + need for instant answer. 1 → sync, 2 → async, 3 → webhook, 4 → streaming.

exercises.question: An operation averages 8 seconds, sometimes up to 40. The user clicks a button and waits. What's wrong with sync here, and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: Think about the server timeout and the user's patience. The threshold is ~5 seconds — beyond that, async with notification.

exercises.question: A webhook from an external service sometimes doesn't arrive. Which two reliability mechanisms must you build in?
exercises.hint: What should the service get back so it doesn't retry? And what to do if there's no response?

s1.title: The four integration patterns
s1.why: Before choosing, you need to know what you're choosing from. Four patterns cover almost every case of how AI exchanges data with other systems via API.
instructions: sync (request/response): the user sends a request and waits for the answer on the same connection. AI replies in 1-3 seconds.
async (kick off and report): the request starts a task, instantly returns "accepted", and the result comes later — via notification or status polling.
webhook (by event): not the user but an external event (email, form, new task) triggers AI.
streaming (piece by piece): the answer is delivered in chunks as it's generated — the user sees AI "typing".
s1.validate: You can describe each of the 4 patterns in one sentence and say who initiates it.
s1.tip: sync and streaming — the user waits here and now. async and webhook — the work goes to the background.

s2.title: When each pattern fits
s2.why: Each pattern covers its own class of tasks. Mixing them up ruins both UX and reliability.
instructions: sync — short, fast operations: classification, simple answer, a check. AI handles it in 1-3 seconds.
async — long operations of 30 seconds or more: document analysis, big report generation. The user starts it and walks away.
webhook — external trigger: an email arrives, a customer submits a form, a task appears (this is event-driven territory — [[node:sys-event-driven|Event-Driven Architecture]]).
streaming — a long answer the user reads as it appears: long text, extended reasoning.
s2.validate: For each pattern you can name at least one real example task.
s2.tip: The line between sync and async sits around 5 seconds of user waiting.

s3.title: How to choose for a concrete task
s3.why: Choosing a pattern isn't a matter of taste — it's the answer to 3 clear questions. Run them and the pattern is almost unambiguous.
instructions: Question 1: who initiates? The user → sync/async/streaming. An external event → webhook.
Question 2: how long does the operation take? Up to ~5 seconds → sync. Longer → async.
Question 3: does the user need visible progress along the way? Yes, and it's a long text → streaming.
Treat "now or in the background" as a special case of the bigger realtime-vs-batch decision (see [[node:sys-batch-vs-realtime|Batch vs Realtime]]).
s3.validate: Take any of your AI operations and name the pattern via the three questions.
s3.tip: If torn between sync and async — pick async: extra waiting annoys more than an extra notification.

s4.title: Example: 4 patterns in one product
s4.why: One real product usually uses all 4 patterns — each for its own case. This shows patterns don't compete, they complement each other.
instructions: sync: "classify the task type" — 1 second, the button returns the answer immediately.
async: "do a full quarterly analysis" — 2 minutes, the user starts it, keeps working, gets a "report ready" notification.
webhook: a customer wrote in support chat → an external webhook triggers AI → AI drafts a reply for the agent.
streaming: "write a long email" — AI types piece by piece, the user sees the process and can interrupt.
s4.validate: You understand why each case took its own pattern rather than one shared one.
s4.tip: The API as the technical foundation for all these exchanges — the node [[node:pl-api|API]].

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: timeouts and reliability
s5.why: Each pattern has a weak spot. Without built-in protection, the system works only while everything is perfect and breaks at the first failure.
instructions: sync: the main risk is a timeout. The server cuts off a long request while AI keeps working for nothing and burns money. Keep sync for fast operations only.
async: the risk is losing the result. You need reliable task status and a notification, otherwise the user never learns it's done.
webhook: the risk is non-delivery. Build in delivery acknowledgment and retry, otherwise the event is silently lost.
streaming: the risk is a dropped connection mid-answer. You need partial-result handling and the ability to reconnect.
s5.validate: For your pattern you can name the main risk and the mechanism that guards against it.
s5.tip: Money and time are spent even if nobody sees the result. Guarding against lost results is guarding the budget.

s6.title: Checklist and validating the choice
s6.why: Before shipping, run the chosen pattern through a short checklist — it catches most mistakes before they reach production.
instructions: The operation's duration is measured (not guessed), and the 5-second threshold is factored into sync vs async.
The initiator is identified correctly: user vs external event → sync isn't confused with webhook.
async has a notification or status polling; webhook has acknowledgment and retry; sync has a timeout within the server limit.
Streaming is used only where the answer is genuinely long; for a short answer, sync is chosen.
Validated on a real scenario: the user sees what they expect ("fast" when fast, "working" when slow).
s6.validate: Every checklist item is a "yes" for your pattern, and one test on a real scenario is done.
s6.tip: If even one item is "no" — it's not a default blocker, but a reason to decide deliberately rather than leave it to chance.

sys-event-driven.title: Event-driven AI architecture
sys-event-driven.subtitle: How to build AI integrations on events instead of synchronous requests
sys-event-driven.whatItIs: Event-driven AI architecture is an approach where AI processing is triggered by events (a webhook from a CRM, a message in a queue, an uploaded file) rather than a synchronous user request. Accepting the event is fast and durable, while the AI processing itself is decoupled: it can scale, retry, and apply backpressure under load without losing events. This is the foundation for scalable AI integrations described in the [[node:sys-event-driven|event-driven AI architecture]] node.
sys-event-driven.approach: We move from idea to practice: first why decoupling ingestion from processing matters, then the event → queue → handler-agent path, then how to avoid processing one event twice (idempotency) and how to handle ordering. Next we build a minimal pipeline on your own case, mark the boundaries and risks (debugging, duplicates, DLQ), and close with a pre-production checklist.
outcomes: Explain why a synchronous webhook → LLM call → 200 breaks on slow and long-running AI tasks
Draw the event path: source → ingestion (fast 200) → queue → worker-agent
Make processing idempotent using an idempotency key and a dedup table
Set up retries with exponential backoff and a DLQ so events are neither lost nor duplicated
Understand the boundaries: where event-driven is overkill and where it is mandatory

applyIn.title: Processing webhooks from external services
applyIn.description: Stripe, Linear, GitHub, Slack send webhooks with a strict timeout. You accept the event, immediately return 200 and enqueue, while a worker does the AI processing separately — no timeouts, no retry storms.

applyIn.title: AI tasks longer than a few seconds
applyIn.description: Ticket classification, a 5-minute research agent, document parsing. Long work goes into a queue and a worker, and the event source does not wait on an open connection.

applyIn.title: Guaranteed processing under spike load
applyIn.description: A 10x traffic spike doesn't bring the system down: the queue absorbs the flow, workers catch up in minutes, and failed events go to a DLQ for review instead of being lost.

pitfalls: AI call inside the webhook handler: a 5s LLM call exceeds the provider timeout (3s) → retry → duplicates. The webhook must ALWAYS just enqueue-and-return-200
No idempotency: webhook delivery is at-least-once, one event gets processed twice → duplicate AI calls and actions. You need an idempotency key and a dedup table check before processing
Ignoring the DLQ: failed events sit for months with no alert and no review. DLQ monitoring and a weekly review are mandatory
One queue for all priorities: batch jobs eat the capacity and interactive processing suffers. Separate queues per priority
Retry without exponential backoff: a transient rate limit → instant retry → another limit → infinite loop. Backoff (1s, 4s, 16s, 64s) is mandatory

exercises.question: A service accepts a Stripe webhook, makes a 6-second LLM call inside the handler, and returns 200. What breaks, and how do you rework it?
exercises.hint: Compare the 6s of processing with Stripe's webhook timeout (~3s). What happens to delivery, retries, and duplicates? What should the handler do instead of the AI call?

exercises.question: Because of a bug, a worker received the same ticket-created event twice and called the AI twice. What mechanism prevents this, and where does it kick in?
exercises.hint: Think about an idempotency key from the event ID and a dedup table. At what point should the worker check the key — before or after the AI call?

exercises.question: Over a week the DLQ grew to 400 events but no one noticed. Which two rules would have prevented this?
exercises.hint: One rule is about an automatic signal on queue depth/growth, the second is about a regular human process.

s1.title: What event-driven is and why AI needs it
s1.why: Without understanding why the synchronous scheme breaks, it's easy to wire an AI call right into the webhook and get a retry storm in production. First we pin down the essence: reacting to events and decoupling ingestion from processing.
instructions: Read the what and why sections of the [[node:sys-event-driven|event-driven AI architecture]] node: what event sources, ingestion, and workers are
List 4 scenarios where the synchronous webhook → LLM call → 200 scheme breaks: slow LLM, downtime, spike traffic, long AI tasks
State the decoupling idea in your own words: accepting the event is fast and durable, AI processing is separate and scalable
Compare with the synchronous API approach from [[node:sys-api-patterns|API patterns]] — understand when request-response is appropriate and when it isn't
s1.validate: You can use a single example (e.g., a Stripe webhook) to explain why a synchronous AI call in the handler leads to timeouts and duplicates, and what decoupling gives you.
s1.tip: The key idea: a webhook is responsible for "accepted and not lost", not for "processed". These are different responsibilities.

s2.title: The event path: event → queue → handler-agent
s2.why: This is the basic skeleton of any event-driven system. Until you see the three links — source, ingestion, worker — you cannot design either scaling or reliability.
instructions: Draw the chain: event source (webhook/queue/CDC) → ingestion endpoint → queue → worker-agent with an AI call
Define the ingestion contract: validation (including verify_signature), enqueue, return 200 in < 100ms — no AI inside
Describe the worker as a separate process: pulls a message from the queue, calls the AI, writes the result, deletes the message
Map the infrastructure choices from the node: Kafka/RabbitMQ (self-hosted) versus AWS SQS/Google Pub/Sub (managed)
Link to the processing modes from [[node:sys-batch-vs-realtime|batch versus realtime]]: a queue lets you combine both
s2.validate: You can draw a three-link diagram and, for each link, name its single responsibility and the target response speed of ingestion.
s2.tip: A worker is always async and scales horizontally: a typical worker delivers 5-20 AI requests/sec, the bottleneck is the AI, not the queue.

s3.title: Idempotency and ordering
s3.why: Event delivery is almost always at-least-once: one event will arrive twice. Without idempotency that means duplicate AI calls and actions — which is real money and corrupted data.
instructions: Study exactly-once via an idempotency key in the impact section of the node: a dedup table check before processing
Build the idempotency key from a stable event identifier (e.g., zendesk_ticket_{id}_{event_id})
Describe the transaction: check the key → call the AI → write the result → insert the key into the dedup table with a TTL
Settle the ordering question: where order matters (use an ordering/partition key) and where events are independent
Link retries and failures to [[node:sys-error-handling|error handling]]: what counts as transient and what as final
s3.validate: You can explain at what point the worker checks the idempotency key, and why a repeated delivery of the same event will not lead to a second AI call.
s3.tip: Idempotency is checked BEFORE the AI call, and the key is written in the same transaction as the result — otherwise a failure between steps allows a duplicate again.

s4.title: How to apply it: build a minimal pipeline
s4.why: Theory only sticks on your own case. A minimal pipeline on a single event source shows all the links in action and surfaces real decisions about priorities and retries.
instructions: Pick one real source: a webhook from Stripe/Linear/Zendesk or a message in a queue
Implement ingestion: verify_signature → send_message to the queue with an idempotency key → return 200
Implement the worker: receive with visibility_timeout, dedup check, AI call, write the result, delete
Add retries with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s, 64s, max 5) and send to the DLQ once attempts are exhausted
Split queues by priority: critical (interactive) > standard > batch, so batch doesn't eat the capacity
s4.validate: Your pipeline processes an event exactly once, does not duplicate the AI call under an artificial double delivery, and puts the event into the DLQ after N failures.
s4.tip: Start with one queue and one worker, then add priority queues as batch load appears — don't over-engineer early.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: debugging, duplicates, DLQ
s5.why: Event-driven is harder to debug than a synchronous request: the flow is async and errors surface late. You need to know the risks in advance and where the approach is overkill.
instructions: Determine when event-driven is NOT needed: pure conversational UI, < 10 events/day, a PoC with no SLA
Examine the debugging risk: tracing an event's path is hard — you need correlation ids and logging at each link
Pin down the anti-duplicate mechanism: idempotency + dedup table — and verify it actually fires on repeats
Set up DLQ monitoring: alert on depth > 100 OR growth > 10/min, plus a weekly DLQ review
Plan for replay: Kafka lets you replay events for recovery, SQS does not, so store events (e.g., in S3)
s5.validate: You can name three situations where event-driven is overkill, and for each risk (debugging, duplicates, loss in the DLQ) point to a concrete protective mechanism.
s5.tip: The DLQ is not a dumping ground but a signal: DLQ growth almost always means a systemic problem (a bug, a changed contract, a downstream outage), not random failures.

s6.title: Checklist and pre-production verification
s6.why: Before launch you need to make sure all the protective mechanisms are in place. One missed item (signature, idempotency, backoff) turns into a production incident.
instructions: Run the checklist: ingestion returns 200 in < 100ms with no AI call inside
Check: verify_signature on the webhook, idempotency key + dedup, retries with exponential backoff, DLQ configured
Make sure queues are split by priority and the worker is async (not blocked on a single AI call)
Run a double-delivery test and an N-failures test → the event must land in the DLQ, not loop forever
Lock in DLQ monitoring and a weekly review plan; link further development to the [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI integration systems]] and [[node:systems|systems layer]] nodes
s6.validate: All checklist items are ticked, the duplicate and DLQ tests pass, and DLQ monitoring is on — the pipeline is production-ready.
s6.tip: Make this checklist a template for every new event-driven integration — most production incidents are exactly the items missed from here.

sys-batch-vs-realtime.title: Batch vs realtime: making the call
sys-batch-vs-realtime.subtitle: How to decide which AI workloads run realtime and which go to batch — to protect UX and cut cost
sys-batch-vs-realtime.whatItIs: A practical course on the most cost-impactful architectural decision in an AI system: where you need realtime (sync, < 5s) and where a task can safely wait an hour and go to batch at a 50% discount. We cover the choice axes (latency, volume), the Anthropic Message Batches API, hybrid and streaming patterns, and build a checklist for real use cases.
sys-batch-vs-realtime.approach: We move from the batch-vs-realtime distinction to selection criteria, then to Batches API specifics and savings, to applying it on your own project, to limits and risks, and finish with a checklist and validation. Each step builds on real numbers from the [[node:sys-batch-vs-realtime|Batch vs realtime]] node and ties into [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]] and [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]].
outcomes: Explain the difference between batch and realtime in terms of latency, volume and cost
Make the realtime/batch/streaming/hybrid call per use case, not globally
Calculate Batches API savings (50% on input+output) for your own workloads
Design hybrid routing: critical path realtime, everything else batch
Avoid the classic mistakes: everything realtime, batch where UX is needed, streaming everywhere

applyIn.title: Bulk classification and extraction
applyIn.description: Thousands of emails/documents per hour go to batch at a 50% discount instead of overloading the realtime rate-limit pool.

applyIn.title: Eval suites and reports
applyIn.description: Running thousands of eval cases and daily/weekly reports are classic batch workloads with no user-facing wait.

applyIn.title: Interactive product with chat
applyIn.description: Chat and autocomplete stay realtime+streaming for fast TTFT, while nightly draft generation goes to batch.

pitfalls: Everything realtime "because it is simpler" — 2x cost and rate-limit problems at peaks
Using the Batches API only for research, ignoring production workloads (reports, drafts, eval)
Batch where the user is waiting for a response — UX disaster and churn
Streaming everywhere, including short answers (< 2s) — needless complexity in error handling and retries
Hybrid without explicit routing — batch exists on paper but everything flows realtime due to a missing classifier

exercises.question: You have 100k requests/day classifying inbound emails, results needed in the CRM by morning. Realtime or batch, and why?
exercises.hint: Ask: is the user waiting right now? What is the volume and what is the saving from the 50% discount on input+output?

exercises.question: In chat a user asks a question and the answer takes 8 seconds to generate. How do you make the UX feel fast without reducing total time?
exercises.hint: Think about streaming and TTFT (300-800ms) — perceived 2-3x faster at the same total time.

exercises.question: A team says "we have both realtime and batch," but 95% of load goes realtime. Where is the hybrid broken?
exercises.hint: Look for routing logic: by which signal (tag/source/priority) is a request sent to the right path?

s1.title: The difference between batch and realtime
s1.why: Without a clear distinction, every workload drifts into realtime by inertia, which doubles cost and loads rate limits.
instructions: Lock in the definitions: realtime — sync, low latency (< 5s), the user waits; batch — async, throughput-optimized, results in 5min—24h
Name the two key choice axes: latency budget (is the user waiting) and volume (dozens vs thousands per hour)
Add streaming as the middle ground: first token in 300-800ms, full response slow, UX feels fast
Write down 3 example tasks for each mode from your own project
s1.validate: You can take one of your use cases and explain which mode it belongs to and on which axis (latency or volume).
s1.tip: Realtime protects UX, batch protects money — not "better/worse" but different tools.

s2.title: When to choose what: latency vs cost/volume
s2.why: The decision is per use case, not global — the same product contains both realtime and batch workloads.
instructions: For each use case ask: do you truly need a < 5s response, or can the email/report arrive in an hour?
Realtime — chat, autocomplete, search, critical path (ticket triage, fraud detection), conversational flow
Batch — eval suites, bulk classification/extraction, daily/weekly reports, re-indexing, A/B data generation
Streaming — long generation (> 5s) with a UI; hybrid — realtime first pass + batch refinement
Build a table of your workloads with a "mode" column and a rationale
s2.validate: Every workload in your table has a mode and a one-line rationale (latency or volume/cost).
s2.tip: If a task is user-facing and the user actually waits — that signals realtime; everything else is a batch candidate.

s3.title: The Batch API and its savings
s3.why: The Anthropic Message Batches API gives a 50% discount on input+output and a separate rate-limit pool — a cost game changer.
instructions: Memorize the parameters (2026-05 baseline): 50% discount on input+output, up to 100k requests per batch (jsonl), latency 5min—24h (often 1-2h), separate rate-limit pool
Study the flow: messages.batches.create(requests=[...]) → poll/wait → messages.batches.results(batch.id)
Compute the saving on an example: 10k requests, 5k input + 1k output, Sonnet — realtime $300 vs batch $150
Estimate the scale: 100k requests/day → saving ~$4,500/mo
Tie it to [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]] and [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]]
s3.validate: You can state the 50% discount, the 100k/batch limit, the latency window, and compute the saving for your volumes.
s3.tip: The separate rate-limit pool means batch does not eat interactive quota — realtime peaks stay protected.

s4.title: How to apply it on your project
s4.why: Knowing the modes is useless without explicit routing: a request must land on the right path automatically.
instructions: Split the endpoints: a realtime handler for lead scoring/chat, a batch job for nightly draft generation
For batch add a cron pickup: check processing_status == 'ended', collect results, mark complete
For interactive long generation enable streaming via messages.stream and StreamingResponse
Introduce explicit routing by a signal (tag/source/priority), not "realtime by default"
Add batch SLA monitoring: alert if processing exceeds the usual 1-2h
s4.validate: You have a scheme: which request → which path, and a cron that picks up batch results when ready.
s4.tip: Lean on [[node:sys-api-patterns|API patterns]] and [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI integration systems]] — batch/realtime is part of the broader integration architecture.

s5.title: Limits and risks
s5.why: The costliest mistakes are choosing realtime where batch would have done, and batch where the user is waiting.
instructions: Realtime by inertia: check which workloads truly need < 5s and which landed there "just because" (2x cost)
Batch where realtime is needed: "let the user wait an hour" = churn; batch only without a user-facing wait
Streaming everywhere: for short answers (< 2s) it is overkill and complicates error handling/retries/caching
Ignoring TTFT with streaming: TTFT 5s = terrible UX; optimize prompt size, model, [[node:cap-caching|caching]] of the first section
Mind the deprecate-watch: Batches API pricing/limits evolve, 50% is the 2026-05 baseline
s5.validate: You can point to at least one workload on your project worth moving from realtime to batch.
s5.tip: Ask not "can this be realtime" but "must this be realtime" — the default should be batch for non-user-facing tasks.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: A final review turns scattered decisions into a reproducible mode-selection policy.
instructions: Checklist per workload: is the user waiting? what volume? what batch saving? is streaming needed?
Confirm that batch was considered and savings computed for all non-user-facing workloads
Confirm explicit routing and batch SLA monitoring with alerts
Run through the pitfalls list: no "everything realtime," "batch where the user waits," "streaming everywhere," "hybrid without routing"
Record the final mode table as an architecture decision
s6.validate: Every workload has a deliberate mode, batch savings are computed, and routing and SLA monitoring are in place.
s6.tip: Return to the checklist for each new use case — the mode choice is made anew, not inherited by habit.

sys-data-sync.title: Data sync for AI context
sys-data-sync.subtitle: A fresh index without a full re-sync every time
sys-data-sync.whatItIs: An AI agent is only as good as how fresh its context is. If answers are built on data from CRM, Linear, Notion, or Slack, that data must stay current in your own operational store rather than being fetched from the source on every request. This course covers how to sync reliably: full vs incremental sync, handling deletes and conflicts, scheduling and triggers, and guarding against a stale index and drift. The topic extends [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI integrations with systems]] and builds on [[node:sys-event-driven|event-driven architecture]].
sys-data-sync.approach: Don't do a fresh fetch on every AI request — it kills latency and hits the source's rate limits. Read fast from a local store, update the store asynchronously. Webhooks as primary, polling on a cursor as fallback, weekly full sync as insurance against drift. Every sync explicitly tracks the cursor and time — without that you cannot prove freshness.
outcomes: You understand why to sync data into your own store instead of calling the source directly
You distinguish full from incremental sync and know when each is needed
You can handle deletes and conflicts across multiple sources
You set up scheduling and triggers: webhooks + polling + weekly snapshot
You see the risks of a stale index and drift, and you measure sync lag

applyIn.title: AI sales assistant
applyIn.description: Context from Salesforce + Linear + Slack: deal status is always fresh, answers never cite three-day-old data.

applyIn.title: Internal knowledge agent
applyIn.description: A fresh index over Notion and tickets, so the agent answers "what did the team decide" from the current state, not a week-old cache.

applyIn.title: RAG over live systems
applyIn.description: Incremental sync keeps the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG index]] fresh without an expensive full reindex every time.

pitfalls: Calling the source API on every AI request — rate limits and degradation under load
Webhooks only, no polling fallback — one missed event and data is stale forever
Ignoring delete events — a record removed at the source, yet the AI cites a "ghost" from the store
No conflict-resolution policy — two sources give different values and the AI gets confused
No drift detection or lag monitoring — sync is broken, the AI answers from week-old data, no one knows

exercises.question: You have a source without webhook support, data changes every few minutes, and AI requests run ~50/hour. Which sync strategy do you pick and why?
exercises.hint: Without webhooks, polling on a cursor is what's left. Think about the interval relative to required freshness and about the source's rate limits.

exercises.question: Webhooks and polling both work, but the weekly full sync shows 0.5% discrepancies with the store. What does that mean and what do you do?
exercises.hint: That's drift — some events get lost silently. The full sync exists precisely to catch this before users do; find out where events are being lost.

exercises.question: A record is deleted in the CRM. Describe what happens in your store by default and how to fix it.
exercises.hint: Most sync pipelines only upsert. You need explicit delete tracking, usually a soft delete in the operational store.

s1.title: Why sync data for AI context
s1.why: Without sync the AI answers from stale data: "the deal is in Prospecting" when it was Closed Won three days ago. Trust breaks in days. And a fresh fetch on every request gives 2-5x latency and hits the source's rate limits.
instructions: Pin down your case: does data change regularly? Are AI requests > 10/hour? Does the source have rate limits? Is accuracy critical?
If at least three "yes" — you need your own operational store the AI reads from fast, updated asynchronously.
Write down freshness requirements per data type: critical (< 1 min), standard (< 15 min), reference (< 24 h).
Decide the store is separate from the source — so AI traffic doesn't load the CRM.
s1.validate: You can state a concrete freshness requirement for each data type and justify why you don't call the source directly.
s1.tip: If data is static (docs weekly) or the AI is called once a day — you don't need sync, a direct call is fine. Don't build a pipeline you don't need.

s2.title: Full vs incremental sync
s2.why: A full sync pulls the entire set every time — simple, but costly and slow at volume. An incremental sync pulls only changes since the last cursor — fast and cheap, but it can miss events. You need both, in different roles.
instructions: Incremental: a query like `WHERE updated_at > last_cursor`; after processing, save the new cursor.
Set up sync state tracking: a sync_cursors table (source, entity_type, cursor, last_sync_at).
Full snapshot: a periodic full pass for reconciliation — not a replacement for incremental, a complement.
Pick a store with millisecond read latency for the AI (Postgres / DynamoDB); simplify the schema to the fields the AI actually needs.
s2.validate: You have a working incremental, cursor-based sync and understand why a periodic full snapshot is needed on top.
s2.tip: Don't make the store schema a 1:1 copy of the source schema — extra fields bloat the store and slow queries. Normalize for AI needs, not source needs.

s3.title: Handling deletes and conflicts
s3.why: An incremental sync on updated_at can't see deleted records — they silently stay in the store and the AI cites a "ghost." And when two sources hold one field with different values, without an explicit policy the AI gets a contradiction.
instructions: Track deletes explicitly: handle deleted events and soft delete in the operational store (mark, don't lose history).
If the source doesn't send delete events — catch deletions via reconciliation during the weekly full sync.
Choose a conflict policy: last-write-wins by timestamp (simple but lossy), source priority ("CRM is truth for X, Linear for Y"), or a manual reconciliation queue.
Send conflicts that can't be resolved automatically to a manual review queue instead of silently overwriting.
s3.validate: A record deleted at the source correctly disappears (or is marked) in the store, and on a value mismatch between sources there's an explicit rule for who wins.
s3.tip: For multi-source you almost always need source priority: decide up front which source is truth for each field. That removes 90% of conflicts.

s4.title: Scheduling and triggers
s4.why: A single sync mechanism is fragile: webhooks are fast but lose events on failures; polling is reliable but lags; full sync catches drift but is heavy. A combination gives both freshness and reliability.
instructions: Webhooks as primary: the source sends events on change, you enqueue a sync job. Latency in seconds.
Polling on a cursor as fallback (e.g., every 5 minutes) — catches missed webhooks, gives eventual consistency.
Weekly full sync on a schedule (e.g., Sunday night) — reconciliation and a drift report.
Sync worker per event: pulls the full record from the source, normalizes it, upserts it to the store with a synced_at mark.
s4.validate: Three layers run: webhooks (primary), polling (fallback), weekly full sync (insurance), and every update is stamped with a sync time.
s4.tip: The polling fallback is mandatory even with good webhooks: a network glitch or source bug, and without a fallback the data goes stale forever.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: stale index and drift
s5.why: Sync can break silently: webhooks and polling formally work, yet the data still diverges from the store. If you don't measure this, the AI answers from a stale index for weeks, and users find out before you do.
instructions: Failure handling: a missed webhook is caught by the next polling; a failed polling — exponential backoff and an alert after > 3 fails ([[node:sys-event-driven|event-driven]]).
Measure sync lag per source (norm < 15 min p95) and alert when it's exceeded.
Weekly full sync with a diff report for drift detection: count drift (norm < 0.1%).
Watch the webhook delivery rate (alert if < 95%) and protect PII: encrypt at rest, redact before AI calls ([[node:sys-document-pipelines|data pipelines]]).
s5.validate: For each source you see sync lag, drift count, and webhook delivery rate, and each metric has a threshold with an alert.
s5.tip: Drift almost always exists, even when webhooks and polling are "green." The weekly full sync is the only way to catch it before users do.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Before production you must confirm the pipeline covers all four problems: freshness, deletes, conflicts, and drift. One uncovered item and the index silently rots.
instructions: Freshness: the AI reads from the store (not the source), latency requirements are set and measured.
Deletes and conflicts: delete events are handled (soft delete), a conflict policy is chosen and applied.
Triggers: webhooks + polling fallback + weekly full sync are enabled, sync_cursors is populated.
Observability: sync lag, drift count, webhook delivery rate are monitored with alerts; PII is encrypted.
Run: change a record at the source and confirm it appears in the store within the target lag; delete a record and confirm the AI no longer cites it.
s6.validate: All five checklist groups are covered, and a manual run (change + delete a record) confirms freshness and correct delete handling.
s6.tip: The final check is always a real change at the source with a measurement of the time until it shows up in the AI's answer. Green dashboards without such a run prove nothing.

sys-auth-patterns.title: Auth patterns for AI integrations
sys-auth-patterns.subtitle: How AI safely accesses external services: keys, OAuth, rotation, isolation
sys-auth-patterns.whatItIs: A course on managing identity and permissions for AI agents and MCP servers that call external services. The AI acts on behalf of a user or a service account, often with short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials — harder than standard web auth. We cover API keys, OAuth 2.0, service accounts, secret storage, least privilege, rotation, and the boundaries of risk.
sys-auth-patterns.approach: We move from motivation to practice: first why careful auth is critical specifically in AI scenarios, then the mechanism types and how to choose, then secret storage and least privilege with rotation, and finally the boundaries of risk (key leak, prompt injection) plus a readiness checklist with verification. Grounded in the 2026 production baseline and the [[node:sys-auth-patterns|auth patterns]] node.
outcomes: Understand why overly broad permissions for AI mean a huge blast radius on compromise
Choose the right mechanism (API key / OAuth / service account) for a given scenario
Store secrets in env/vault rather than in code and logs, and know why
Apply least privilege (minimal scopes) and token rotation
Assess boundaries and risks — key leak, prompt injection stealing access — and pass a readiness checklist

applyIn.title: AI assistant on behalf of a user
applyIn.description: Gmail/Calendar assistant via OAuth 2.0: authorization code flow with PKCE, refresh with rotation, minimal scopes, revocation on disconnect.

applyIn.title: MCP servers with tools
applyIn.description: Local servers — filesystem-scoped credentials and OS keychain; remote servers — mandatory OAuth, scoped per resource. See [[node:mcp|mcp]].

applyIn.title: Multi-tenant SaaS
applyIn.description: Per-tenant credential isolation: tenant A's credentials are never reachable by code serving tenant B; API keys and service accounts per function, not one for everything.

pitfalls: API keys / tokens in code and git — history is forever; you need pre-commit hooks (gitleaks) and secret scanning
Overly broad scopes ("full Gmail access because it is easier") — on compromise the AI reads everything
One service account and admin rights for everything — a breach becomes full org compromise
No rotation and plain-text token storage — a leaked token means an enormous exploit window
No audit trail and no revocation process — after a breach you cannot determine scope, and a removed user is still reachable by the AI

exercises.question: An AI assistant only needs to read the user's calendar. Which scope do you request and why not "full access"?
exercises.hint: Least privilege: request exactly what is needed (read calendar), no more. On compromise the blast radius is smaller, and the user trusts you more.

exercises.question: A team stores customers' OAuth refresh tokens in a plain DB table in cleartext. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: A database breach makes every token usable. You need encryption at rest, access logs on retrieval, and refresh-token rotation on each use.

exercises.question: Via prompt injection an attacker makes the agent call a tool with someone else's rights. Which two barriers limit the damage?
exercises.hint: Minimal scopes (the agent physically cannot do more) and per-tenant isolation + audit trail to catch and investigate the anomalous call.

s1.title: Why careful auth matters in AI integrations
s1.why: Standard web auth does not cover AI cases: the AI wants to read your Gmail at 3am while you are away — how do we refresh the token? An MCP server exposes a tool any user's agent can call — how do we scope it? Without proper auth the blast radius on compromise is huge.
instructions: State on whose behalf your AI acts: a specific user or the system itself (service account)
List which external services it calls and which data it touches
Assess the blast radius: what breaks / leaks if this credential is compromised
Note whether you are at the first integration — auth is designed in from the start, not "added later"
s1.validate: You can name the AI system's identity and the worst-case scenario if its access leaks.
s1.tip: Alarm signals: "one API key for all customers" or "the AI has admin permissions because it is easier" — a future catastrophe.

s2.title: Mechanism types and where each fits
s2.why: Three base patterns cover different scenarios. Mixing them up means either over-engineering (OAuth where an API key suffices) or under-protecting (a shared key where you need user-delegated access).
instructions: API key — simple server-to-server without user context (Anthropic API key, OpenAI key)
OAuth 2.0 — when the AI acts on behalf of a specific user (access to their Gmail, Calendar): authorization code flow with PKCE, refresh, revocation
Service account — a dedicated identity for the AI system itself (a Slack bot, a GCP service account), not the developer's personal account
Short-lived tokens / STS — tokens issued for an hour to a day with automatic rotation, as a security best practice
For MCP: local servers — local credentials and OS keychain; remote servers — mandatory OAuth (see [[node:mcp|mcp]])
s2.validate: For each of your integrations you can justify the chosen mechanism.
s2.tip: Heuristic: a specific user and their personal data → OAuth. System to system with no user → API key or service account.

s3.title: Secret storage: env/vault, not code or logs
s3.why: API keys and tokens in code / git are the classic leak: GitHub history is forever. Plain-text storage in a DB means a database breach hands over every token at once.
instructions: Keep secrets in a managed store: AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / HashiCorp Vault
Never put secrets in env files that land in git, and never write tokens to logs
Encrypt tokens at rest and enable access logs on every secret retrieval
Add pre-commit hooks (gitleaks) and secret scanning to catch keys before commit
s3.validate: There is no secret anywhere in the repository, and store access is logged.
s3.tip: If a secret ever landed in git history, treat it as compromised and rotate it — deleting the commit does not help.

s4.title: Least privilege and rotation
s4.why: Overly broad scopes and non-rotated tokens are the two main damage amplifiers. Minimal rights bound what a compromised AI can do at all, and rotation shrinks the exploit window of a leaked token.
instructions: Request only the scopes you need ("read calendar," not "full Gmail access")
One service account per function (least privilege), not one for everything
Rotate refresh tokens: each use issues a new one, typically every 24h on modern APIs
Rotate API keys every 90 days (sooner for high-stakes) and run a permission audit every quarter
s4.validate: Each credential has the minimum necessary rights and a defined rotation schedule.
s4.tip: On refresh with rotation, immediately persist the new refresh token to the store — otherwise the next call breaks.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: key leak, prompt injection
s5.why: AI widens the attack surface: prompt injection can make the agent call a tool with someone else's rights, and multi-tenant without isolation hands tenant A's credentials to code serving tenant B. Understanding the boundaries decides where to place barriers.
instructions: Enforce strict per-tenant credential isolation: A's credentials are unreachable from code handling B
Minimize scopes so prompt injection cannot reach extra rights
Keep an audit trail of every credential use (who, what, when, from where, success/fail) — integrate with [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging patterns]]
Build a working revocation process: disconnect in the UI → revoke at provider + delete from store
For MCP, scope tools and rely on OS-level permissions; never grant unbounded filesystem access
s5.validate: You can show exactly how the damage from a leaked key and from prompt injection is bounded.
s5.tip: Revoking only in your own UI without revoking at the provider is an illusion — the provider's token still works.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final check turns scattered rules into a reproducible baseline. This is what separates "seems safe" from production and compliance readiness.
instructions: Secrets: nothing in code/logs, everything in a vault, encrypted at rest, gitleaks in pre-commit
Scopes minimal, service accounts per-function, rights audited quarterly
Rotation set up: refresh ~24h, API keys ~90d, the new refresh token persisted
Per-tenant isolation, audit trail on all auth events, a working revocation process
Metrics and alerts: failed auth rate (>1%), token rotation success rate, scope creep
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, metrics are wired up, and alerts fire on anomalies.
s6.tip: deprecate-watch: OAuth 2.1 supersedes 2.0 (PKCE becomes mandatory) — adapt as it lands.

sys-error-handling.title: Error handling and fallbacks in AI systems
sys-error-handling.subtitle: Make a failed AI call something other than a visible failure for the user
sys-error-handling.whatItIs: A course on graceful degradation: when an AI call fails (rate limit, provider downtime, malformed output, tool error, network glitch), the user must not see a 500 or a blank page. Instead of crashing, the system switches to a backup path — a different model, a cache, a partial answer, or an honest message. The topic of the node [[node:sys-error-handling|Error handling and fallbacks]] is broken into steps: what errors occur, retry vs fallback, graceful degradation, how to tell the user, where the limits and risks are, and a final checklist.
sys-error-handling.approach: We move from classifying errors to a working fallback chain. First we learn to tell transient errors (5xx, 529, timeout) apart from intentional ones (refusal) and from format errors (invalid JSON) — each has its own policy. Then we build a degradation ladder: retry with backoff, then a fallback model, then cache, then a canned response. Separately — UX: what to show the user and how. And always — limits: a circuit breaker against infinite retries, logging and metrics against hidden failures. Every step is technically concrete and grounded in the real playbook from the node.
outcomes: Classify AI-system errors by category (rate limit, 5xx, 529, invalid JSON, context limit, refusal, tool failure) and assign each its own policy
Tell retry (repeating the same operation) apart from fallback (switching to a backup path) and apply them in the right order
Build a graceful degradation chain: reduced context → fallback model → cache → canned response
Word clear user-facing degradation messages instead of a silent fail or a generic "something went wrong"
Set limits: circuit breaker, timeout budgets, logging and metrics on every fallback

applyIn.title: Production AI chatbot
applyIn.description: When the primary model is unavailable (5xx/529), the request automatically travels the fallback chain to reduced context, then Haiku, then the semantic cache — the user sees only a slight delay instead of an error.

applyIn.title: Agent with several tools
applyIn.description: If 1 of 5 tools fails, the agent returns a partial answer from the 4 working sources with a note "1 source unavailable" rather than failing the whole request.

applyIn.title: An AI feature inside a large app
applyIn.description: When AI is temporarily unavailable, only that block breaks with an explicit "AI temporarily unavailable" message, while the rest of the page keeps working.

pitfalls: No fallback at all — "let it crash": a 5-minute provider outage = your service down for 5 minutes. The minimum is one layer (a canned response).
Infinite retry without a circuit breaker: provider downtime turns into a retry storm that burns through the rate limit again on recovery.
Silent fallback without logs and metrics: you fell back to Haiku, quality dropped, and you do not know why complaints are growing.
Treating refusal as an error: the model intentionally declined — retry will not help, fallback is irrelevant, you need a separate user-friendly path.
Timeout too high: 30s on an interactive request → the user decides "it broke" after 5s and refreshes, creating 6 parallel requests.

exercises.question: The Anthropic API returned 529 (overloaded). What do you do — retry with backoff or fall back to a backup model immediately? Why?
exercises.hint: Look at the policy table in the node: 529 = the system is overloaded, retrying the same model makes it worse. Compare with 5xx, where retry is appropriate.

exercises.question: The model returned invalid JSON instead of the expected schema. Is this a transient error, a format error, or a refusal? What policy applies?
exercises.hint: A format issue can be fixed with a corrective prompt — it is not downtime and not an intentional refusal. How many times should you retry before falling back?

exercises.question: In your system the fallback invocation rate has risen to 8%. What does this signal, and what threshold counts as alarming?
exercises.hint: The monitoring section of the node has an alert threshold. If too many requests go to fallback, the problem is not the fallback but the reliability of the primary.

s1.title: What errors occur in AI systems
s1.why: Without classification, all errors get treated the same way (usually "retry or crash"), but each category has its own correct reaction. First you need to see the full map of failures: provider API errors, bad model output, timeouts, tool failures.
instructions: Write out the error categories from the node [[node:sys-error-handling|Error handling and fallbacks]]: rate limit (429), server error (5xx), overloaded (529), invalid JSON output, context limit, refusal, tool failure.

Split them into three groups: transient (will pass on its own — 5xx, 529, timeout), format/content (fixable with a prompt — invalid JSON, context limit), and intentional (refusal — the model declined deliberately).
For each category, note what the user currently sees in your project if you do nothing.
Find the AI-call and tool-call sites in your code — these are the points where any of these errors can surface.
s1.validate: You have a table: error category → group (transient / format / intentional) → current behavior. No category is simply marked "crash."
s1.tip: Refusal is not a bug. It is the model's intentional output under policy. Confuse it with an error and you will retry forever something that will never pass.

s2.title: Retry vs fallback: when to repeat, when to switch
s2.why: Retry and fallback are often confused. Retry is repeating the same operation (helps with transient failures). Fallback is switching to a backup path (needed when a repeat is pointless or exhausted). The wrong choice either deepens the outage or needlessly degrades quality.
instructions: Assign each category from step 1 a policy: 5xx → retry 2× with jitter, then fallback; 529 → fallback immediately (repeating is useless); 429 → backoff + retry; invalid JSON → retry 1× with a corrective prompt; refusal → no retry and no fallback, a separate path.
State the transition rule: how many times to retry and on what trigger to move to fallback.
Add jitter (a random addition to the pause) to the backoff so client retries do not synchronize into a single storm.
Link the backoff/retry policy to the node [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]] — that is where limits and the circuit breaker live, on which retry relies.
s2.validate: For each error category it is explicitly written: retry or not, how many times, and under what condition to move to fallback. 529 goes to fallback immediately, refusal is not retried.
s2.tip: The key rule: retry cures "the provider blinked," fallback cures "the provider went down or the answer is bad." If repeating the same operation clearly will not help, do not spend timeout budget on it.

s3.title: Graceful degradation: a chain of backup paths
s3.why: One fallback is better than nothing, but real resilience comes from a degradation ladder: each next level is cheaper/simpler than the previous, and the user almost always gets at least some useful answer.
instructions: Build the chain from the node: Primary (full context + tools) → reduced context (last N messages) → fallback model Haiku (faster, cheaper) → semantic cache → canned response.
Make sure the fallback model has a compatible signature — it can be swapped in without rewriting the call (swappable).
For an agent with tools, add a partial response: if 1 of N tools fails, return the result from the working ones plus a note, not a total failure.
Assign timeout budgets: interactive — 10s total (primary 5s, fallback 3s, network buffer 2s); async — 60s+ acceptable.
Decide which level of the chain is acceptable for each scenario: where a partial response is fine, and where a full answer is required.
s3.validate: The fallback chain is written top to bottom with transition conditions and a timeout at each level. The last level is always a guaranteed answer (canned); the chain cannot "fall into the void."
s3.tip: Failure of the last level is unacceptable: the canned response must always work, with no network calls and no dependencies that can themselves go down.

s4.title: How to tell the user
s4.why: Even perfect technical degradation is useless if the user does not understand what happened. A silent fail breeds distrust, a generic "something went wrong" is useless. The message must be honest and suggest an action.
instructions: For each chain level, decide whether to tell the user: light degradation (reduced context, Haiku) — usually silent; partial response — with an explicit note; full exhaustion — with a clear message.
Replace generic text with specific, actionable text: instead of "Something went wrong" → "AI is currently slow — try again or contact support if urgent."
For refusal, make a separate user-friendly message explaining that the request cannot be fulfilled — without the technical details of the exception.
Implement graceful UI degradation: on an AI-feature failure only its block breaks with an explicit "AI temporarily unavailable," the rest of the page stays alive.
s4.validate: No failure state shows the user a stack trace, a 500 code, or a blank page. Every message explains what happened and suggests the next step.
s4.tip: Write the message as if a tired user is reading it at 2 a.m.: what broke, what to do now, where to write if it is urgent.

s5.title: Limits and risks: where fallback does harm
s5.why: Wrong error handling is more dangerous than none. Infinite retries take the provider down again, a hidden fallback masks quality degradation, a high timeout provokes a refresh avalanche. These risks must be limited explicitly.
instructions: Add a circuit breaker: after a series of primary failures, temporarily stop calling it to avoid a retry storm on recovery (the mechanics are in [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]]).
Make every fallback visible: a log + a metric on each trigger. Alert if the fallback invocation rate > 5% (primary is unreliable) and if the cascade failure rate grows (all levels are failing).
Measure the fallback model's quality: compare primary vs Haiku on an eval set so a quiet quality drop does not go unnoticed.
Keep the interactive timeout budget < 10s so the user does not refresh and spawn parallel requests.
Remember cost: retry amplification can double spend during an outage; falling back to Haiku is usually cheaper and smooths spikes. Metrics — via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]].
s5.validate: There is a circuit breaker, every fallback has a log and a metric, alerts are set on the fallback share and cascade failure, the interactive timeout is within budget. A quiet quality drop is impossible — the eval comparison catches it.
s5.tip: If fallback triggers often and quietly, that is not a success but a disguised outage. A high fallback share always means the primary needs fixing.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: The final run-through pulls everything together and proves the system really degrades gracefully. Without testing on real failures, error handling stays theory that gets tested in production for the first time during an actual outage.
instructions: Run the checklist: (1) every error category has a policy; (2) retry and fallback are separated and ordered; (3) the degradation chain ends with a guaranteed answer; (4) the user gets a clear message; (5) there is a circuit breaker, logs, metrics, and alerts; (6) timeout budgets are respected.
Simulate failures: force a 5xx, 529, invalid JSON, refusal, and a single tool failure — verify the system takes the right branch.
Check the edge case: what the user sees when the entire fallback chain is exhausted (it must be a specific canned response, not a crash).
Look at metrics after the simulation: success rate per level, fallback distribution (norm ~95% primary), full-exhaustion rate (alert > 0.1%) — via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]].
Connect the result to the system level as a whole — see [[node:systems|AI systems]] and [[node:ai-integration-systems|integrating AI into systems]].
