s6.validate: All 6 checklist items are checked, each failure type is replayed and takes the expected branch, chain exhaustion yields a specific canned response, metrics and alerts work. Error handling is verified before production, not during it.
s6.tip: Once a quarter, run a "fire-drill outage" — deliberately take the primary down in staging. A fallback never tested under load most likely will not work in the real moment.

cc-tty-sessions.title: Sessions and history in Claude Code
cc-tty-sessions.subtitle: Keep context, resume work in seconds, manage several projects
cc-tty-sessions.whatItIs: Every claude launch creates a session — a saved record of your conversation with the model. You can save it, continue the last one, or pick any past session. It's memory across breaks: context isn't lost, and you don't need to re-explain the task.
cc-tty-sessions.approach: We go from understanding what a session is to practice: start a new one, continue a prior one with --continue and --resume, read history, trim context with /compact, and keep several parallel sessions per project. We finish with common mistakes and a skill check.
outcomes: You understand that a session = saved conversation history tied to a project folder
You start a new session or return to a prior one with a single command
You distinguish --continue (the latest) from --resume (pick from a list)
You manage context size with /compact without losing the gist
You run several sessions in parallel across different tasks and projects

applyIn.title: A long task across several sittings
applyIn.description: A big refactor spread over days. You close the terminal at night, continue in the morning from the same spot — the model remembers everything you discussed.

applyIn.title: Parallel branches and features
applyIn.description: Two independent tasks in one repository. You keep two sessions and switch between them without mixing context.

applyIn.title: Resuming after an interruption
applyIn.description: A call dropped in or the terminal crashed. --continue instantly brings back the last conversation, with nothing to recall by hand.

pitfalls: Starting from scratch every time instead of --continue — you lose context and burn tokens on re-briefing
Confusing --continue (silently takes the latest) with --resume (lets you pick from a list) — you open the wrong session
Not running /compact on a long session — context overflows and answers degrade
Running --continue from a different folder and being surprised it's the wrong history — sessions are tied to the project directory
Expecting /compact to keep everything verbatim — it condenses into a summary, so small details can be lost

exercises.question: What's the difference between claude --continue and claude --resume?
exercises.hint: Think about which command asks no questions and which shows a list to pick from.

exercises.question: Why does --continue in folder project-a bring up history different from what you expected in project-b?
exercises.hint: Sessions are tied to the directory you launched claude from.

exercises.question: When should you run /compact, and when is it better to start a new session?
exercises.hint: Compare: same topic but bloated context — versus the task has changed entirely.

s1.title: What a session and history are
s1.why: Without grasping that each launch creates savable history, you'll re-brief the model every time and lose context.
instructions: Run claude in a project folder — this creates a new session
Do some work: ask a couple of questions, request a file change
Notice: the whole dialogue is the session history, tied to the current folder
Close the terminal — the session is saved automatically, nothing to do by hand
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words: a session = saved conversation history tied to a project directory.
s1.tip: A session lives where you launched it: one folder's history doesn't mix with another's.

s2.title: New session or continuation
s2.why: Returning to work in seconds instead of re-explaining the task is the main payoff of sessions. You need to know which command resumes.
instructions: For a fresh start, just run claude — a new clean session
To silently bring up this folder's latest session — claude --continue
To pick a specific past session from a list — claude --resume
Remember the rule: --continue = no questions, the latest; --resume = pick from a list
s2.validate: You resumed yesterday's dialogue with --continue and continued from the same spot, no re-briefing.
s2.tip: If you don't recall which session is the latest, use --resume — it shows a list with descriptions.

s3.title: Viewing history
s3.why: To pick the right session out of many and recall where you left off, you must be able to view the list and scroll the history.
instructions: Run claude --resume — a list of past sessions with brief descriptions opens
Pick the one you need by topic or time and open it
Inside the session, scroll the dialogue up to see the full exchange history
Confirm the model remembers earlier discussion — ask about something from the start
s3.validate: You found the right session in the --resume list and confirmed its context is intact.
s3.tip: The description in the --resume list helps tell sessions apart — give tasks clear opening messages.

s4.title: /compact and managing context
s4.why: On a long session context overflows and answers degrade. /compact condenses history into a summary and frees room while keeping the gist.
instructions: In a long session, type /compact
Wait for the history to fold into a brief summary of key facts and decisions
Keep working — the model holds the gist but uses less context
If the task changed entirely — better start a new session rather than compact the old one
s4.validate: You ran /compact on a bloated session, and the dialogue continued without losing the main thread.
s4.tip: /compact condenses into a summary rather than storing verbatim — small details can be lost, so restate what matters.

s5.title: Several sessions and projects
s5.why: Parallel tasks need separate context. Sessions are tied to the folder, so each project keeps its own history apart.
instructions: Open two project folders in separate terminal tabs
Run claude in each — you get two independent sessions
Switch between tabs: one's context doesn't leak into the other
To return, use --continue in the right folder — it brings up that folder's latest session
s5.validate: You run two parallel sessions in different folders, and their contexts don't overlap.
s5.tip: The folder binding is your friend: one task = one directory = one session line.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a check
s6.why: Knowing the antipatterns, you won't burn tokens on re-briefing or open the wrong session. The final check locks in the skill.
instructions: Stop starting from scratch: instead of a fresh launch, get used to --continue
Don't confuse --continue (the latest, silently) with --resume (pick from a list)
Run --continue from the correct folder — otherwise the wrong history comes up
On a long session, run /compact in time; when the topic changes — a new session
Test yourself: resume yesterday's work, compact the context, start a second session in another folder
s6.validate: You went through the whole cycle: --continue → /compact → a second session in another folder — without losing context or tokens.
s6.tip: If you're unsure you'll resume the right session — --resume and the list settle it in a second.

cc-tty-files.title: Files in the Claude Code chat
cc-tty-files.subtitle: How to give Claude the right files without copy-paste: @-mentions, attachments, code references
cc-tty-files.whatItIs: A course on passing files into Claude Code's context in the terminal: via @-mention, drag-and-drop, and attachments. Claude reads the file itself with the Read tool — you don't need to paste its contents into the chat manually.
cc-tty-files.approach: We move from motivation to practice: first why you give a file rather than its text; then three ways to pass it (@, drag-and-drop, attachments); then precise addressing of code fragments; and we finish with managing context limits and the typical mistakes plus how to verify.
outcomes: You understand why a file reference beats pasting its text into chat
You can attach files via @-mention with path autocomplete
You attach images and PDFs by dragging them in or as attachments
You point at the exact code fragment instead of the "whole file"
You control context size and avoid stale data

applyIn.title: Working with code
applyIn.description: You attach a specific module via @path and ask Claude to analyze or change exactly that, without retelling its contents.

applyIn.title: Reading logs and configs
applyIn.description: You pass a log or config file by reference — Claude reads the current version and finds the issue from real data.

applyIn.title: Screenshots and documents
applyIn.description: You drag an error screenshot or a spec PDF straight into the chat so Claude sees the visual context.

pitfalls: Copying file contents into chat manually — it bloats the context and goes stale fast
Attaching a whole huge file when only one code section is needed
Forgetting that @ references a path relative to the project's working folder
Dropping in dozens of files at once — the context overflows and the answer loses focus
Assuming Claude "remembers" a file after an edit — once changed, it must be re-read

exercises.question: Why is the reference @src/App.jsx better than pasting the whole file's code right into the message?
exercises.hint: Think about two things: context size and how current the content stays after edits.

exercises.question: You need to show Claude an error visible only in an interface screenshot. How do you pass it into the chat?
exercises.hint: A text reference won't do here — you need a visual input channel.

exercises.question: A 5000-line file, but the question is only about one function. How do you narrow the context?
exercises.hint: Address the specific section, not the entire file.

s1.title: Why give a file, not its text
s1.why: The core idea of the course: you pass a reference to a file, not its contents. Claude reads the current version itself with the Read tool. This saves context and rules out working from a stale copy.
instructions: Open Claude Code in the terminal inside your project folder
Compare two approaches: pasting all the code into the message vs. pointing at the file path
Remember the rule: a file's contents are not what you type, but what Claude reads itself
Grasp the benefit: fewer tokens go to "here's my code", more to the task itself
s1.validate: You can explain why pasting code manually is an anti-pattern in Claude Code.
s1.tip: The less wrapping in your message, the more room and attention left for the request itself.

s2.title: @-mentioning files
s2.why: The @-mention is the main way to attach a file. You type @ and the path, Claude reads the file automatically and factors it into the answer.
instructions: In the input field type the @ symbol and start typing the file name
Use path autocomplete to avoid mistakes: @src/App.jsx
Remember the path is counted from the project's working folder
You can mention several files in one message — each with its own @
State the task next to the reference: "@src/App.jsx — find the extra re-render"
s2.validate: Claude has read the mentioned file and refers to its real contents instead of asking you to paste the code.
s2.tip: Autocomplete after @ noticeably reduces the chance of a path typo.

s3.title: Drag-and-drop and attachments
s3.why: Not everything is passed as text. Images, screenshots, and PDFs are added by dragging the file into the window or as an attachment — that gives Claude visual context.
instructions: Drag the file from the file manager straight into the terminal window with Claude Code
For an error screenshot use an image — a text reference won't convey the visual
Attach a spec or document PDF as an attachment
After adding it, describe in words what exactly to do with the attachment
s3.validate: The image or PDF appears in the context, and Claude comments on what it sees in it.
s3.tip: A screenshot often explains a visual problem faster than a long text description.

s4.title: How to reference parts of code
s4.why: Often you need not the whole file but a specific section. Precise fragment addressing saves context and focuses the answer on the right place.
instructions: If the question is about one function — name it and the file, don't attach a giant file whole
Give landmarks: a function name, a class, or a line range
For a large file, state which fragment matters: "in @utils.js — the parseDate function"
Ask Claude to first read only the needed part before changing it
s4.validate: Claude works with exactly the specified fragment instead of retelling the whole file.
s4.tip: The more precise the fragment address, the more precise and shorter the answer.

s5.title: Context and limits
s5.why: Context is not infinite. Dozens of large files at once overflow it, and the answer loses focus. Give exactly what the task needs.
instructions: Attach only files relevant to the current question
For a large file, prefer an addressed fragment (see step 4) over the whole volume
Watch the size: the more clutter in the context, the vaguer the answer
If there really are many files — split the work into several steps with different sets
s5.validate: Only relevant files are in the context, and answers stay precise and focused.
s5.tip: Fewer files in context means higher density of attention on your real task.

s6.title: Mistakes and verification
s6.why: The final step cements the habits: don't paste code manually, remember to re-read after edits, and verify Claude sees the current version.
instructions: Never copy a file's contents into chat by hand — use @ or an attachment
After a file has changed, let Claude re-read it
Check the path: @ is counted from the project's working folder
Don't dump everything in — extra files only get in the way
Make sure the answer relies on the real contents, not a stale copy
s6.validate: You pass files only by reference or attachment, control the size, and work with current versions.
s6.tip: If the answer looks like Claude sees old code — ask it to re-read the file.

cc-tty-modes.title: Claude Code terminal operating modes
cc-tty-modes.subtitle: Normal, auto-accept edits and plan mode: which to use when and how to switch
cc-tty-modes.whatItIs: Claude Code in the terminal runs in one of several permission modes: normal (every action needs confirmation), auto-accept edits (file edits apply without asking) and plan mode (read and plan only, no edits). The mode sets how much freedom the agent has and how much control you keep.
cc-tty-modes.approach: We walk through the three modes one by one: what each does, what risk it carries and what work rhythm it creates. You learn to switch them mid-session with Shift+Tab and pick the right mode per task — from safely exploring unfamiliar code to fast routine edits.
outcomes: Understand the difference between normal mode, auto-accept edits and plan mode
Switch mode on the fly with Shift+Tab without interrupting the session
Pick the mode per task: plan for recon, auto-accept for routine, normal by default
Recognize the danger of bypass mode and why it must not be enabled carelessly
Avoid both extremes: confirming everything by hand or allowing everything blindly

applyIn.title: Exploring unfamiliar code
applyIn.description: Turn on plan mode so Claude reads and proposes a plan but physically never touches files — safe recon before any change.

applyIn.title: Routine mass edits
applyIn.description: Renames, formatting, small fixes in a trusted project — auto-accept edits removes the stream of confirmations and speeds things up.

applyIn.title: Critical changes
applyIn.description: Editing prod configs, migrations, deleting files — normal mode, where every action passes through your confirmation.

pitfalls: Staying in one mode forever: either slow (everything by hand) or dangerous (everything allowed)
Enabling auto-accept edits in an unfamiliar or prod project and missing a destructive edit
Confusing plan mode with normal: in plan, edits are not applied, so you may wait for a result in vain
Carelessly enabling bypass permissions — the agent runs everything with no questions, including risky commands
Forgetting which mode is active and being surprised why edits do (or do not) apply

exercises.question: You were handed someone else's repo and need to grasp the architecture without breaking anything. Which mode and why?
exercises.hint: You need a mode where Claude reads and plans but physically does not change files.

exercises.question: You are doing 30 similar renames in your own trusted project and are tired of pressing confirm. What do you enable?
exercises.hint: A mode where file edits apply without confirming each one separately.

exercises.question: Why is bypass permissions more dangerous than auto-accept edits?
exercises.hint: Consider what each mode actually allows: only file edits, or any action at all, including commands.

s1.title: What the modes are and why
s1.why: Without a map of the modes you either stall on confirmations or accidentally give the agent extra freedom. Understanding the three modes is the basis of safe and fast work.
instructions: Memorize the three core modes: normal (confirm every action), auto-accept edits (edits without asking), plan mode (read and plan only, no edits)
Grasp the main axis: a mode tunes the balance of "control ↔ speed"
Keep bypass permissions in mind separately — an extreme mode with no confirmations, for special cases
Tie mode to task risk: the more dangerous the edit, the more control you need
s1.validate: You can name the three core modes and describe in one word what each allows.
s1.tip: Think of modes like gears: not "which is best" but "which fits the current road".

s2.title: Normal mode — confirm every step
s2.why: This is the default and safest mode: no file edit or command runs without your "yes". Start here in any unfamiliar context.
instructions: Launch Claude Code in a project — by default you are already in normal mode
Give a task that requires a file edit and wait for the confirmation prompt
Read exactly what is proposed before you confirm
Reject one proposal and confirm the edit was not applied
s2.validate: Before each edit you see a prompt and can accept or reject it.
s2.tip: Don't confirm on autopilot — reading the diff before "yes" is the whole value of this mode.

s3.title: Auto-accept edits — edits without asking
s3.why: When the task is routine and the project familiar, the stream of confirmations only gets in the way. Auto-accept edits applies file edits automatically, giving you speed instead of clicks.
instructions: Enable auto-accept edits by switching mode (Shift+Tab)
Give a series of similar edits: formatting, renames, small fixes
Notice that file edits apply immediately, without separate confirmation
Remember: this mode only removes asking about file edits, it does not make the agent all-permissive
s3.validate: File edits apply automatically and you understand this only concerns edits.
s3.tip: Enable auto-accept only where you trust both the project and the nature of the task — routine in familiar code.

s4.title: Plan mode — planning only, no edits
s4.why: Before a large or risky change it helps to get a plan first, not edits. Plan mode lets Claude read code and propose a strategy while physically changing nothing.
instructions: Switch to plan mode (Shift+Tab) before a large task
Ask it to study a section of code and propose a plan of changes
Confirm Claude responds with a plan and files stay untouched
Once you approve the plan, leave plan mode and switch to a mode where edits apply
s4.validate: In plan mode you get a plan and no file is changed until you leave the mode.
s4.tip: Plan mode is the best recon before an architectural step or a mass edit: it's cheap to be wrong on paper.

s5.title: Switching modes with Shift+Tab
s5.why: A mode is not a whole-session setting: you change it on the fly to fit the current step. Shift+Tab cycles through modes without interrupting the conversation.
instructions: Press Shift+Tab in a session and watch the active-mode indicator change
Go through the cycle: normal → auto-accept edits → plan mode → back
Before each task quickly check which mode is currently active
Build the habit: recon → plan, routine → auto-accept, risk → normal
s5.validate: You switch mode in one keystroke and always know which one you're in.
s5.tip: Task first, then mode: ask yourself "how risky is this?" and switch to fit the answer.

s6.title: Which when, the bypass danger and checking
s6.why: The main mistake is getting stuck in one mode. The final step cements picking the mode per task and warns about bypass permissions, where the agent acts with no confirmations at all.
instructions: Form the rule: unfamiliar/risky → plan or normal, routine in familiar code → auto-accept
Grasp the danger of bypass permissions: any action is allowed, including commands, with no questions
Don't enable bypass on prod, in someone else's code, or when you don't control the consequences
After each switch double-check: edits apply / don't apply exactly as you expect
If a mode behaves unexpectedly — stop and check the active-mode indicator
s6.validate: For three different tasks you name the right mode and explain why bypass is not a default option.
s6.tip: Bypass is like a wheel with no brakes: occasionally needed, but not for daily driving or crowded places.

cc-tty-keys.title: Claude Code terminal hotkeys
cc-tty-keys.subtitle: Keyboard-driven session control: interrupt, modes, input, history and help
cc-tty-keys.whatItIs: The set of Claude Code terminal shortcuts that control a session without a mouse: stop generation (Esc), exit (Ctrl+C), switch mode (Shift+Tab), enter multiline text, scroll history (↑/↓, Ctrl+R) and autocomplete paths (Tab).
cc-tty-keys.approach: We go by meaning, not alphabet: first why hotkeys matter at all, then groups by task — stopping, modes, input, history, help. Each step is practiced by hand in a live session until the combo becomes muscle memory.
outcomes: Stop generation and exit a session calmly and without a mouse
Switch Claude Code work modes with a single Shift+Tab
Enter long multiline prompts without sending them by accident
Find and reuse past commands via ↑/↓ and Ctrl+R
Open the built-in hotkey help and self-check without a cheat sheet

applyIn.title: Interrupting a long answer
applyIn.description: Claude went off track — Esc stops generation instantly without killing the session.

applyIn.title: Switching mode for the task
applyIn.description: Shift+Tab toggles the mode (e.g. auto-accept) mid-flow, no restart needed.

applyIn.title: Repeating and editing commands
applyIn.description: ↑ brings back the last prompt, Ctrl+R searches history — no retyping long prompts by hand.

pitfalls: Confusing Esc (interrupt the answer) with Ctrl+C (exit the session) — Ctrl+C twice closes Claude Code
Pressing Enter mid-multiline and accidentally sending an unfinished prompt
Using the mouse in the terminal — you lose the main CLI advantage and speed
Not knowing Shift+Tab and manually restarting the session just to change mode
Ignoring Ctrl+R and retyping long commands instead of searching history

exercises.question: What is the difference between Esc and Ctrl+C while Claude Code is working?
exercises.hint: One stops the current answer and keeps the session alive, the other exits Claude Code itself.

exercises.question: You need to repeat a 5-line prompt you entered 10 prompts ago. What is faster than retyping it?
exercises.hint: Think history: scrolling ↑/↓ or substring search.

exercises.question: How do you enter a multi-line prompt without sending it too early?
exercises.hint: Enter sends; a line break needs a different input — check the hotkey help.

s1.title: Why terminal hotkeys
s1.why: Without hotkeys every action means reaching for the mouse and retyping. That breaks flow and doubles your time in the terminal.
instructions: Open Claude Code and run one normal session the way you usually do — with mouse and manual typing
Roughly count how often you reached for the mouse or retyped something you had already entered
Remember the principle: hands stay on the keyboard — terminal work flows
State the course goal: stopping, modes, input, history and help — all from the keyboard
s1.validate: You can name at least 3 moments in your session where the mouse or retyping slowed you down.
s1.tip: An hour in the terminal on hotkeys becomes 30 minutes — the gain is not cosmetic.

s2.title: Interrupt and stop: Esc and Ctrl+C
s2.why: Claude often goes off track. Being able to stop an answer instantly is control over the session and saved time.
instructions: Give Claude any task and during generation press Esc — the answer stops, the session stays alive
Confirm that after Esc you can immediately type a new prompt — no restart needed
Press Ctrl+C once — note that it is an exit signal, not just a stop
Remember the difference: Esc interrupts the answer, Ctrl+C exits Claude Code
s2.validate: You stopped generation with Esc and continued working without restarting the session.
s2.tip: If you only want to stop the answer — always Esc. Save Ctrl+C for exiting.

s3.title: Switching modes: Shift+Tab
s3.why: Different tasks need different work modes. Changing them with one key inside the session is faster than restarting.
instructions: In an active session press Shift+Tab — the work mode switches, the indicator changes
Press Shift+Tab a few times and watch how the behavior and mode label change
Pick the mode that fits the current task and keep it
Remember: changing mode needs no restart — it is an on-the-fly toggle
s3.validate: You switched mode with Shift+Tab and can see the changed mode indicator.
s3.tip: Pick the mode before starting a big task — fewer interruptions along the way.

s4.title: Input and multiline
s4.why: Long multi-line prompts are normal. Without correct input, Enter sends unfinished text and breaks your train of thought.
instructions: Start typing a prompt and notice: Enter sends the message
Open the hotkey help (see step 6) and find the combo for a line break
Enter a 3-4 line prompt using line breaks, and only then send with Enter
Confirm the multiline text was sent whole, not in pieces
s4.validate: You sent one multi-line prompt without breaking it with an accidental Enter.
s4.tip: If the prompt is long — type the whole text first, send only at the very end.

s5.title: History and autocomplete
s5.why: Retyping long commands by hand is wasted time. History and Tab return what you already typed in seconds.
instructions: Enter several different prompts, then scroll history with ↑ and ↓
Press Ctrl+R and start typing a piece of a past command — search finds it by substring
Type the start of a file path and press Tab — the path autocompletes without typing the name
Try Tab after @src/ — autocomplete suggests the files inside
s5.validate: You found a past command with Ctrl+R and autocompleted a file path with Tab.
s5.tip: ↑ — for the last couple of commands, Ctrl+R — when it was long ago and you only recall a fragment.

s6.title: Hotkey help and self-check
s6.why: Memorizing it all at once is impossible. The built-in help is a cheat sheet at hand until the combos become muscle memory.
instructions: Open the built-in Claude Code hotkey help and review the full list
Cross-check everything you practiced: Esc, Ctrl+C, Shift+Tab, line break, ↑/↓, Ctrl+R, Tab
Run one full session without a mouse, leaning on the help when you stall
Mark the combos not yet automatic and repeat them every session
s6.validate: You ran a full session without a mouse and can name from memory the hotkey for each of the 6 course tasks.
s6.tip: After a week of daily practice all these combos become muscle memory — you no longer need the help.

cc-cfg-settings.title: Project settings.json in Claude Code
cc-cfg-settings.subtitle: Shared team rules in the repository: permissions, hooks, env
cc-cfg-settings.whatItIs: The .claude/settings.json file in the project root is the team configuration for Claude Code: permissions, automated actions (hooks), and environment variables (env). It is committed to the repository, so every team member gets the same rules for working with the agent.
cc-cfg-settings.approach: We move from understanding the file's purpose to its structure and key fields, then cover why it is committed to git and how it combines with global and local settings levels. We finish with the main mistake — secrets in settings.json — and validation.
outcomes: You understand that .claude/settings.json defines shared team rules and lives in the repository
You know the file structure and the three key blocks: permissions, hooks, env
You can set base permissions and a hook that runs after editing a file
You understand the difference between the global, project, and local settings levels
You keep secrets and API keys out of settings.json and can validate the config

applyIn.title: Onboarding new developers
applyIn.description: A new person clones the repo and immediately gets the same permissions and hooks as the whole team — no "set it up per my instructions".

applyIn.title: A unified agent standard
applyIn.description: Everyone runs Claude Code with the same permissions and automated actions, so the agent behaves predictably for each member.

applyIn.title: Automating routine via hooks
applyIn.description: Formatting, linting, or tests run automatically after the agent's actions because the hook is declared in the shared project file.

pitfalls: Storing personal secrets or API keys in settings.json — the file goes to git and is visible to everyone
Putting personal preferences in the project file instead of the local settings.local.json
Forgetting to commit settings.json, so the team ends up working with different rules
Overly broad permissions.allow (for example, allowing everything) — confirmations lose their meaning
Invalid JSON (trailing comma, wrong quotes) — Claude Code cannot read the config

exercises.question: Why must an API key not go into .claude/settings.json, but into an env variable or a local file instead?
exercises.hint: Recall where settings.json is committed and who sees it after git push.

exercises.question: How does the project .claude/settings.json differ in purpose from .claude/settings.local.json?
exercises.hint: One is shared with the team and goes to git, the other is personal and stays out of git.

exercises.question: Which entry in permissions.allow lets the agent run tests without confirmation?
exercises.hint: The format is a tool with a command pattern, e.g. Bash(npm test).

s1.title: What .claude/settings.json is and why
s1.why: Without a shared settings file each team member configures the agent their own way, and Claude Code behaves differently from machine to machine.
instructions: Open the project root and find (or create) the .claude folder
Inside it lives settings.json — the team configuration for Claude Code
Remember the three jobs of the file: permissions, hooks, and environment variables (env)
The file is shared: Claude Code reads it for everyone who cloned the repository
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence: settings.json defines shared team rules for working with the agent.
s1.tip: It is most convenient to create the file right after /init, once the base project structure is described.

s2.title: File structure
s2.why: Claude Code reads settings.json as JSON: understanding the structure lets you add settings without breaking the file.
instructions: The file is a single JSON object with curly braces at the top level
Inside are named blocks: permissions, hooks, env, and others (for example statusline)
Values are objects, arrays, or strings depending on the block
Follow JSON syntax: double quotes, commas between fields, no trailing comma at the end
s2.validate: A minimal valid file { } reads without errors, and you can see where to add blocks.
s2.tip: Check syntax in an editor with JSON highlighting — it will flag an extra comma instantly.

s3.title: Key fields: permissions, hooks, env
s3.why: These three blocks cover the team's main needs: what the agent is allowed to do, what runs automatically, and what environment it sees.
instructions: permissions.allow — an array of allowed actions, e.g. Bash(npm test) and Edit(./src/**)
permissions.deny — what is explicitly forbidden, even if it would match allow
hooks — automated actions on events, e.g. PostToolUse:Write runs prettier after a file write
env — project environment variables (not secrets) the agent sees
s3.validate: The file has a permissions block with a non-empty allow, and you know how to add a simple hook.
s3.tip: Start minimal: allow frequent safe commands, leave the rest to confirmation.

s4.title: Commit it to the repository
s4.why: The whole point of the project settings.json is shared rules for everyone; they work only if the file is in git.
instructions: Make sure .claude/settings.json is not excluded in .gitignore
Add the file to the index: git add .claude/settings.json
Commit it together with the rest of the project setup
After git push, teammates get the same permissions and hooks on their next pull
s4.validate: git status shows settings.json as tracked, and after a clone another member has the same rules.
s4.tip: Agree as a team that changes to shared rules go through normal review, just like code.

s5.title: Relation to global and local levels
s5.why: Settings layer by level: personal preferences must not land in the shared file, while project settings should override global ones.
instructions: Global level — user settings shared across all projects on your machine
Project level — .claude/settings.json, shared with the team and committed to git
Local level — .claude/settings.local.json, personal and NOT committed (usually in .gitignore)
Keep personal secrets and preferences in the local file or environment, not in the project file
s5.validate: You understand which level to pick for a team rule versus a personal setting.
s5.tip: If a rule is needed only by you, that is a signal it belongs in settings.local.json, not settings.json.

s6.title: Mistakes: secrets in settings.json + validation
s6.why: The most dangerous mistake is putting a secret into a file that is committed: after push the whole team and git history see it.
instructions: Never write API keys or passwords in .claude/settings.json — it goes to git
Pass secrets via environment variables or a local file outside git
Verify the JSON is valid (no trailing commas or single quotes)
Run Claude Code in the project and confirm permissions and hooks took effect
s6.validate: There is no secret in settings.json, the file is valid JSON, and the rules you set actually work.
s6.tip: If a secret already landed in a commit, deleting it is not enough — the key must be revoked and rotated.

cc-cfg-local.title: settings.local.json: personal Claude Code settings
cc-cfg-local.subtitle: Personal configuration that never lands in the shared repository
cc-cfg-local.whatItIs: settings.local.json lives in the .claude folder next to the project's settings.json. It has the same fields, but it is not committed to git: it stays local and holds whatever is specific to your machine only — personal permissions, paths, ENV variables, experiments.
cc-cfg-local.approach: We move from understanding how the local file differs from the shared one, through filling it correctly and excluding it from git, to its priority over project settings and a breakdown of common mistakes (committed the local file, leaked a secret). Every step is technically accurate and grounded in the Claude Code config model.
outcomes: You understand the purpose of .claude/settings.local.json and how it differs from settings.json
You know what belongs in local versus the shared project file
You can exclude the local file from git via .gitignore
You understand the priority order: local overrides project settings
You avoid leaking secrets and desyncing with the team

applyIn.title: Personal command allow-lists
applyIn.description: Allow commands you personally trust in local without forcing them on the whole team via the shared settings.json.

applyIn.title: Machine-specific paths and ENV
applyIn.description: Store local paths and environment variables of your machine that will differ for your colleagues.

applyIn.title: Experiments without risk to the repo
applyIn.description: Try new settings and permissions without polluting commit history or touching the shared config.

pitfalls: Committing settings.local.json — it lands in the repo and breaks the idea of a 'personal' file
Putting secrets or API keys somewhere they might leak into a commit
Duplicating in local what should be in the shared settings.json — desync with the team
Forgetting the priority: local silently overrides project settings, and behavior changes 'for no clear reason'
Putting team-wide settings in local — colleagues won't receive them

exercises.question: You have an API key needed only on your machine. Which of the two files should hold it, and why?
exercises.hint: Think about which file goes into the shared repository and which stays local.

exercises.question: The team complains that a permission works for you but not for them. Where could the cause be?
exercises.hint: Check whether the needed rule lives only in your local file instead of the shared settings.json.

exercises.question: How do you make sure settings.local.json definitely won't end up in a commit?
exercises.hint: Look at .gitignore and check git status.

s1.title: What settings.local.json is and why you need it
s1.why: Without understanding its purpose it's easy to confuse local with the project file and put settings in the wrong place.
instructions: Open the .claude folder in the project root — settings.local.json may sit next to settings.json
Remember: the fields in local are the same as in settings.json — the structure is identical
Key difference: local does NOT go to git; it holds configuration for your machine only
Use it for personal permissions, local paths, ENV variables, and experiments
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why a separate local file is needed instead of just the shared one.
s1.tip: If the file doesn't exist — that's fine: Claude Code creates it on the first write of local settings.

s2.title: How local differs from settings.json
s2.why: The boundary between 'shared' and 'personal' is the foundation of the whole topic; mix it up and you either leak a secret or the team misses something it needs.
instructions: settings.json — shared: committed to git and applies to the whole team
settings.local.json — personal: not committed, applies only to you
The fields are identical; the difference is scope and whether it lands in the repository
Rule: shared for the team → settings.json; personal for the machine → settings.local.json
s2.validate: For any setting you can say which of the two files it should go into.
s2.tip: If unsure 'shared or personal', ask: should colleagues receive this? Yes → settings.json.

s3.title: What to put in settings.local.json
s3.why: Correct content makes local useful; wrong content turns it into a source of desync.
instructions: Put personal allow-lists for commands that only you trust
Put local paths and ENV variables specific to your machine
Put experimental settings you don't want to impose on the team
Do NOT put here what should work for everyone — that's the shared settings.json's job
s3.validate: Your local holds only what is specific to your machine and nothing team-wide.
s3.tip: Personal allow-lists are the most common case: they spare you extra confirmations without touching the team.

s4.title: .gitignore — don't commit the local file
s4.why: The whole point of local rests on it not landing in the repository; without excluding it from git the protection doesn't work.
instructions: Open the project's .gitignore and confirm settings.local.json is listed there
If the line is missing — add the path to the local file to .gitignore
Run git status and verify settings.local.json is not shown as modified/new
If the file is already tracked by git — that signals it was committed earlier (covered in step 6)
s4.validate: git status does not show settings.local.json among files to commit.
s4.tip: In Claude Code project templates the local file exclusion is often already in place — but checking won't hurt.

s5.title: Priority of local over project settings
s5.why: If you don't know that local overrides settings.json, behavior will change 'for no clear reason'.
instructions: Remember: when fields overlap, settings.local.json takes priority over settings.json
This lets you locally override a shared setting for yourself without touching the shared file
When debugging behavior, look at local first — it may have silently overridden the project value
Don't duplicate fields needlessly: a duplicate in local hides the value from settings.json
s5.validate: You understand which value applies when a field is set in both local and the project file.
s5.tip: If something is 'not like in settings.json', first look for that field in settings.local.json.

s6.title: Mistakes and verification: committed the local file / leaked a secret
s6.why: The two main mistakes of this topic are costly: a secret in git and desync with the team; you need to find and prevent them.
instructions: Mistake 1: settings.local.json is committed — add it to .gitignore and remove it from git tracking (without deleting the file itself)
Mistake 2: a secret/key landed in a commit — treat it as compromised, revoke and replace the key
Mistake 3: a team setting duplicated in local — move it to the shared settings.json
Verification: git log and git status contain no local file and no secrets; the team gets shared settings via settings.json
s6.validate: Git history contains neither settings.local.json nor secrets, and team settings live in the shared file.
s6.tip: Treat any key that ever entered git history as leaked — simply deleting the commit isn't enough, the key must be rotated.

cc-cfg-global.title: Claude Code global settings
cc-cfg-global.subtitle: Personal defaults for all projects via ~/.claude/
cc-cfg-global.whatItIs: The ~/.claude/settings.json file holds your personal Claude Code settings that apply to every project on this machine: language, response format, Statusline, command permissions. Alongside it lives a global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with behavior rules you want everywhere. This is the base layer that project-specific settings sit on top of.
cc-cfg-global.approach: We go from meaning to practice: first understand what the global layer is and why it exists, then what exactly to put there, add a global CLAUDE.md, master the precedence of layers (global < project < local), learn to notice when global settings get in the way, and close with common mistakes plus a checkout. After this course you set up a new machine once and stop copy-pasting configs across projects.
outcomes: Understand the purpose of ~/.claude/settings.json and the global CLAUDE.md
Know what belongs in the global layer and what to leave to the project
Can set personal defaults: language, allow for safe commands, Statusline
Understand layer precedence: global < project < local
Notice when a global setting hurts a specific project and fix it

applyIn.title: Setting up a new machine
applyIn.description: Set language, favorite tools and baseline permissions in ~/.claude/ once — and all future projects immediately follow your rules.

applyIn.title: A consistent way of working
applyIn.description: A global CLAUDE.md sets habits (response format, tone, preferred approaches) that follow you across every repository without duplication.

applyIn.title: Saving on confirmations
applyIn.description: A global allow for safe Bash commands (ls, git status, npm test) removes routine confirmation prompts in every project.

pitfalls: Putting project-specific settings in the global settings.json — junk and risk of conflicts with project settings
A global allow on dangerous commands (rm -rf, git push --force) removes protection everywhere at once
Expecting a global setting to win over a project one — in reality the project and local layers override it
Editing settings.json with broken JSON (extra comma, quotes) — the whole file stops being read
Forgetting the global CLAUDE.md as a source of unexpected behavior when a rule seems to come out of nowhere

exercises.question: You want Claude to answer in English everywhere and not ask for confirmation on git status. Where do you put this?
exercises.hint: These are project-independent rules → the global ~/.claude/ layer. Language/style go in CLAUDE.md, the command allow goes in settings.json (permissions.allow).

exercises.question: In one project a global allow on npm test is a problem because tests there are slow and costly. What do you do?
exercises.hint: The project layer overrides the global one. Add a stricter rule or deny in that project's .claude/settings.json — it wins without touching the global config.

exercises.question: After editing ~/.claude/settings.json, Claude Code stopped applying your settings. First thing to check?
exercises.hint: Most likely broken JSON — an extra comma or an unclosed quote. Validate the file with a JSON validator; on error the whole file is ignored.

s1.title: What ~/.claude/settings.json is and why
s1.why: Without understanding the purpose of the global layer you'll copy-paste the same configs into every project and won't understand where a given behavior comes from.
instructions: Open your home folder and find the ~/.claude/ directory — it's created on first use of [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]].
The ~/.claude/settings.json file is your personal defaults for all projects on this machine: language, response format, Statusline, permissions.
Remember the principle: this is where anything project-independent that should work everywhere goes.
If the file doesn't exist that's fine — you can create it manually as a valid JSON object {}.
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words how the global settings.json differs from settings inside a project.
s1.tip: The global layer is about you as a user, the project layer is about a specific repository. Keep that distinction in mind.

s2.title: What to put in global settings
s2.why: Filling the global layer correctly saves time across all projects at once; filling it wrong clutters the config and creates conflicts.
instructions: Put your preferred response language and general format here — what's the same across all your projects.
Put a global allow for safe Bash commands (ls, git status, npm test) — this removes routine confirmations.
Put the Statusline setting and favorite tools if you need them everywhere.
Do NOT put project-specific things: paths, service names, project deploy commands.
More on config fields — see [[node:cc-config|Claude Code configuration]].
s2.validate: For each item in your config you can answer: is this needed in ALL projects or just one?
s2.tip: Simple test: if a setting makes sense on someone else's machine with different projects — it's global. If not — it's project-level.

s3.title: The global CLAUDE.md
s3.why: settings.json sets technical permissions, while the global CLAUDE.md sets behavior rules — tone, habits, approaches you want in all projects.
instructions: Create a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file next to settings.json.
Write your personal behavior rules there: communication language, summary format, preferred coding approaches.
Keep it short — it's a base layer, not a place for project specifics.
Remember: for the structure and purpose of CLAUDE.md see [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]].
s3.validate: The global CLAUDE.md contains only rules appropriate for any of your projects, with no mention of specific repositories.
s3.tip: settings.json = 'what's allowed', CLAUDE.md = 'how to behave'. Don't mix the two roles.

s4.title: Layer precedence: global < project < local
s4.why: Without understanding precedence you'll be surprised why a global setting 'doesn't work' in a project — in fact a narrower layer overrides it.
instructions: Remember the order of strength: global (~/.claude/) is weakest, project (.claude/settings.json in the repo) is stronger, local (.claude/settings.local.json) is strongest.
A narrower layer overrides a wider one when the same parameter conflicts.
The local layer (settings.local.json) is personal tweaks for one project, usually not committed.
Use this deliberately: keep the general settings global, set exceptions at the project or local level.
s4.validate: You can predict which value applies if one parameter is set both globally and in the project.
s4.tip: Think of layers as filters: each next one refines the previous, it doesn't wipe everything out.

s5.title: When global settings get in the way
s5.why: A global setting that's handy in most projects sometimes harms a specific one — you need to spot it and work around it without breaking the shared config.
instructions: Sign of trouble: in one project Claude behaves differently than expected for no visible reason — look for a global rule.
If a global allow is dangerous for this project (slow/costly tests, sensitive deploy) — add a stricter rule at the project level.
A project deny overrides a global allow — this is the standard way to make an exception.
Don't edit the global config for one project — it'll break the others; fix it at the project level.
s5.validate: You made an exception for one project without changing ~/.claude/, and confirmed other projects are unaffected.
s5.tip: Rule: change the global only if the problem repeats across all projects. A single case is cured at the project layer.

s6.title: Common mistakes and the checkout
s6.why: Most problems with global settings are broken JSON and inappropriate content; a quick check saves hours of confusing behavior.
instructions: Verify settings.json is valid JSON: an extra comma or unclosed quote disables the whole file.
Make sure the global layer has no project-specific junk and no dangerous allow entries.
Check that the global CLAUDE.md has no rules conflicting with project ones.
Restart the Claude Code session and confirm the settings applied as expected.
If something behaves oddly — walk the layers top to bottom: local → project → global.
s6.validate: settings.json parses as valid JSON, the global layer is clean of project specifics, and Claude's behavior matches your expectation.
s6.tip: Keep the global config minimal: the fewer rules in it, the fewer unexpected conflicts with projects.

cc-cfg-statusline.title: Statusline in Claude Code
cc-cfg-statusline.subtitle: Your own status line: model, branch and context always in view
cc-cfg-statusline.whatItIs: Statusline is a custom terminal bottom line in Claude Code that you populate yourself via the statusLine setting in settings.json. It shows session context: current model, git branch, remaining context, project path, and any markers of yours. Under the hood it's a shell command that receives session JSON on stdin and prints the status line to stdout.
cc-cfg-statusline.approach: We move from understanding to practice: first grasp why the line matters and what people put in it, then enable the built-in statusLine, then write your own script, pick the genuinely useful fields, watch performance, and close with error handling and verification. Each step yields a working result visible right in the terminal.
outcomes: You understand what statusline is and what session context it exposes
You can enable and configure statusLine via settings.json
You can write your own status line script that reads the session JSON
You know which fields are truly useful and which are just noise
You keep the line fast so it doesn't slow down every edit

applyIn.title: Working on projects in parallel
applyIn.description: Branch and project path in the status line stop you from committing to the wrong place when switching repos.

applyIn.title: Tracking context usage
applyIn.description: Remaining context in view hints when it's time to compact history or start a new session.

applyIn.title: Picking the model for the task
applyIn.description: A visible model in the line reminds you which model you're on before sending an expensive request.

pitfalls: A heavy script in statusline — it runs often and slows down every edit
Network calls or external API requests inside the status script
Too many fields: the line becomes unreadable and gets truncated by the terminal
The script crashes or writes to stderr — the status line silently disappears
Hardcoded paths and assuming git is always available in the directory

exercises.question: Why must the statusLine script be lightweight and free of network calls?
exercises.hint: Recall how often the line is redrawn and that Claude Code caches it only for ~300ms.

exercises.question: Where does the statusline script get data about the current model and session?
exercises.hint: Claude Code passes JSON on the script's stdin — model, path, version, etc.

exercises.question: What happens to the line if the script exits with an error?
exercises.hint: Consider whether the error is visible to the user and whether you should add fallback output.

s1.title: What statusline is and why it matters
s1.why: Before configuring, understand the problem the line solves: session context (model, branch, remaining context) stays visible without running commands.
instructions: Open Claude Code and look at the bottom of the terminal — by default the status line is minimal
Decide what context you actually need at hand: model, git branch, path, remaining context
Note the scenario where it matters most — e.g. switching between several projects
Remember: a statusline is not a command but a persistent state indicator
s1.validate: You can name 3-4 fields you want in the line and explain why each one is there.
s1.tip: Think of statusline as a dashboard: put only what you actually glance at while working.

s2.title: How to enable and configure statusLine
s2.why: The line is defined via the statusLine key in settings.json — the basic way to bind any command to the status line.
instructions: Open settings.json (user or project level)
Add a statusLine block with type: "command" and a command field — a shell command that prints the line
Start with a simple command, e.g. echo "hello statusline"
Restart or refresh the Claude Code session and confirm the line shows at the bottom
s2.validate: Your test line appears at the bottom of the terminal instead of the default one.
s2.tip: Start with a trivial echo — that separates a config problem from a script problem.

s3.title: A custom statusline script
s3.why: Real value appears when your script builds the line: it gets session JSON on stdin and prints a meaningful status.
instructions: Create a separate script (e.g. statusline.sh) and make it executable
In the script, read stdin — Claude Code passes session JSON there (model, path, etc.)
Parse the needed fields (e.g. with jq) and assemble the output line on stdout
Set statusLine.command to the path of this script
Confirm the line updates and shows data from the JSON
s3.validate: The status line shows real session data assembled by your script.
s3.tip: Debug the script in isolation: echo '{...}' | ./statusline.sh — you see the output without restarting Claude Code.

s4.title: What is useful to show
s4.why: The line's value is in choosing fields well. Extras clutter; the right ones save switches and prevent mistakes.
instructions: Add the git branch (via git rev-parse or from the passed path) — an anchor against committing to the wrong place
Show the current model from the session JSON — a reminder before expensive requests
Add remaining context or a short project path if you work across several projects
Drop anything you don't look at — the line must read in a fraction of a second
s4.validate: The line holds only the 3-4 fields that genuinely affect your decisions while working.
s4.tip: Separate fields with a short symbol and use color sparingly — the eye should instantly find branch and model.

s5.title: Performance: the script must not slow you down
s5.why: The line is redrawn often and cached only for ~300ms — a heavy script makes every edit slow.
instructions: Remove network calls and external API requests from the script
Minimize subprocess launches — every git/jq call costs time
Measure it: time (echo '{...}' | ./statusline.sh) — aim for tens of milliseconds
Cache rarely changing data if you truly need it, instead of fetching it every time
s5.validate: The script runs in tens of milliseconds and working in Claude Code doesn't lag.
s5.tip: Any operation in statusline runs on every update — treat it like code in a hot loop.

s6.title: Errors and verification
s6.why: The line script fails silently: on error the line just disappears. You need resilience and a final check.
instructions: Guard the script against missing git/jq and empty stdin — don't crash, print a fallback instead
Don't write extra noise to stderr — it can break rendering
Test behavior outside a git repo and on a slow disk
Run the line in a real session across several projects and confirm the data is correct
Validate the JSON in settings.json — a syntax error disables statusLine entirely
s6.validate: The line displays correctly in all tested scenarios, including outside git and with empty data.
s6.tip: Add a default placeholder string in the script: even on failure the user sees something rather than emptiness.

cc-grp-session.title: Session management in Claude Code
cc-grp-session.subtitle: The slash-command group for controlling context, restoring state, and switching devices
cc-grp-session.whatItIs: Sessions in Claude Code are persistent: you can pause, resume, fork, export, and move them to another device. The Session management command group gives you full control over context and conversation history — from clearing and compacting to rolling back code and continuing from your phone.
cc-grp-session.approach: We go from general to specific: first understand what the group is and why it exists, then break the commands down by meaning (context, conversation, devices, exit) — one or two commands per step with a 'what it does / when' breakdown. Finally we learn to combine commands and avoid common mistakes. Always verify commands with /help — the list reflects exactly your version.
outcomes: Understand the difference between /clear and /compact and never lose context by accident
Restore past sessions with /resume and undo mistakes with /rewind
Manage the conversation: rename, branch, recap, export
Move work between terminal, Desktop, claude.ai, and phone
Check available commands with /help instead of guessing

applyIn.title: Long coding session
applyIn.description: A multi-hour task with growing context: compact the history in time with /compact so you don't hit the limit, while keeping the conclusions.

applyIn.title: Risky refactor
applyIn.description: Before a dangerous change run /branch, experiment freely, and if it fails the main session stays untouched.

applyIn.title: Switching devices
applyIn.description: Started in the terminal, continued in Claude Desktop via /desktop or on claude.ai via /teleport — with no loss of progress.

pitfalls: Using /clear when you meant /compact: /clear erases all context, /compact compresses it and keeps the conclusions
Forgetting /rewind after a bad change and rolling back code by hand
Closing the terminal without /background, losing a long background task
Guessing commands from memory instead of checking the live list with /help
Not branching risky experiments with /branch and corrupting the main conversation

exercises.question: Context has grown and you're about to hit the limit, but you need the conclusions from the discussion. Which command do you pick, and why not /clear?
exercises.hint: Compare what /compact does to the conversation history versus what /clear does.

s1.title: What this command group is
s1.why: To use sessions deliberately you must first understand: a session in Claude Code isn't a one-off run but a persistent state you can manage. The group's commands fall into four meaningful blocks.
instructions: Remember the idea: a session is persistent — you can pause, resume, fork, export, and move it

Split the commands into blocks: context control (/clear, /compact, /resume, /rewind), conversation control (/rename, /branch, /recap, /export, /copy), switching devices (/background, /desktop, /teleport, /remote-control), exit (/exit)
Open Claude Code and type /help — see which session commands are actually available in your version
s1.validate: You can name the four command blocks and found them in the /help output
s1.tip: The command list changes between versions — /help always shows the live set for you.

s2.title: Context control: /clear and /compact
s2.why: This is the most important pair and the source of the most common mistake. Both free up context, but in fundamentally different ways.
instructions: /clear — what it does: starts a new session from scratch, deleting context. When: the task is done and you start something unrelated
/compact — what it does: compresses history while keeping conclusions. When: context has grown but the discussion must continue
Remember the key difference: /clear deletes context, /compact compresses it
Try both commands on a test conversation and compare the result
s2.validate: You can explain when to use /clear versus /compact and why they must not be confused
s2.tip: When in doubt, /compact is almost always the answer: it's safer because it doesn't lose conclusions.

s3.title: Restoring: /resume and /rewind
s3.why: These commands save you from lost work and from the consequences of mistakes — two different recovery scenarios.
instructions: /resume — what it does: continues the previous session. When: you return to a task the next day or after restarting the terminal
/rewind — what it does: rolls code and chat back to a previous state. When: a change turned out to be wrong and you need to go back
Distinguish them: /resume is about continuing where you stopped; /rewind is about rolling back in time
Test both scenarios: close and continue a session with /resume; make an edit and roll it back with /rewind
s3.validate: You understand the difference between continuing a session (/resume) and rolling back state (/rewind)
s3.tip: /rewind rolls back both code and chat — a real time machine, not just undoing the last message.

s4.title: Conversation control: /branch, /rename, /recap, /export, /copy
s4.why: These commands treat the conversation itself as an object: you can name it, fork it, summarize it, save it, and copy a response.
instructions: /branch — what it does: forks the conversation at the current point. When: you want to experiment without touching the main line
/rename — name the conversation; /recap — short session summary. When: you organize and quickly recall what was discussed
/export — save the conversation to a file; /copy — copy the last response. When: you need to take the result outside
Try /recap in the middle of a long session to see a short summary
s4.validate: You forked with /branch and got a summary with /recap
s4.tip: /branch is the best friend of risky experiments: the main conversation stays untouched.

s5.title: Switching devices and exit
s5.why: Work isn't tied to one terminal: you can push it to the background, move it to Desktop, the web, or control it from a phone — then exit cleanly.
instructions: /background — keep working after closing the terminal; /exit — close the CLI. When: you leave but the task must continue / you finish the work
/desktop — move to Claude Desktop; /teleport — continue from claude.ai. When: you change devices but want the same context
/remote-control — control from a phone. When: you need to watch a task away from the computer
Try /background before closing the terminal on a long task
s5.validate: You can match each switching command to its destination device
s5.tip: Before closing the terminal on a long task, run /background first, or the work will stop.

s6.title: Combining, mistakes, and checking with /help
s6.why: The power of the commands shows in chains. The final step locks in working combinations and guards against common mistakes.
instructions: Experiment chain: /branch → experiment → if it goes wrong, the main session is intact (or /rewind to roll back)
Long-session chain: /compact as context grows → /background before you leave → /resume the next day
Device-switch chain: /export or /desktop → continue elsewhere
The main mistake — /clear instead of /compact: remember /clear deletes, /compact compresses
Always check with /help instead of guessing — the set depends on the version
s6.validate: You assembled at least one meaningful command chain and know how to check availability with /help
s6.tip: Don't invent commands by analogy — if it's not in /help, it's not in your version.

cc-grp-context.title: Context and code in Claude Code
cc-grp-context.subtitle: The slash-command group that controls what Claude sees and where its attention goes
cc-grp-context.whatItIs: "Context and code" is a group of built-in Claude Code slash commands: /add-dir, /context, /memory, /diff, /focus, /goal, and /init. They all operate on a single resource — the context window — and help you precisely control which files and folders Claude keeps in view, how context is being spent, and what the work is focused on.
cc-grp-context.approach: We move from the general to the specific: first understand why the group shares one resource — the context window — then go through the commands in pairs (what it does / when to use it), and finally learn to combine them in a real session and verify the result. Commands come straight from the node, nothing invented; for the full list always go to /help.
outcomes: Understand that every command in the group manages one resource — the context window
Know what each command does: /add-dir, /context, /memory, /diff, /focus, /goal, /init
Be able to add only the needed folders to context instead of the whole repo
Monitor context usage with /context and focus the session with /focus and /goal
Review uncommitted changes with /diff and find the full command list with /help

applyIn.title: Large codebase
applyIn.description: Use /add-dir to add only the relevant folders (e.g. src/components) instead of the entire repo, so you don't waste context.

applyIn.title: Long session
applyIn.description: Check /context periodically to see how much context is used, and /focus to strip extra noise from the output.

applyIn.title: Starting a new project
applyIn.description: Run /init to generate CLAUDE.md, then edit memory with /memory as the project grows.

pitfalls: Adding the whole repo with /add-dir when one folder is enough — wastes context and slows Claude down
Not watching /context in a long session and hitting the context-window limit unexpectedly
Guessing commands from memory instead of checking the current list with /help
Inventing non-existent flags or commands — the group has exactly the seven commands from the node
Ignoring /diff and losing track of which uncommitted changes are already in place

exercises.question: You have a large monorepo but only work in src/api. Which command adds just that folder to context, and why not add the whole repo?
exercises.hint: The node command starts with /add — it adds a directory. Recall that the context window is finite.

exercises.question: A session has run long and answers got slower. Which command shows how much context is used, and which one strips extra tool output?
exercises.hint: One command visualizes context usage as a grid, the other shows only the prompt, tool summary, and final response.

exercises.question: You don't remember the exact command list for this group. Where do you look to see the current set without inventing commands?
exercises.hint: The built-in help command in Claude Code.

s1.title: Why the "Context and code" group exists
s1.why: The context window is finite. Before going into individual commands, grasp the shared idea: the whole group exists to control what Claude sees and where its attention goes.
instructions: Memorize the group's members: /add-dir, /context, /memory, /diff, /focus, /goal, /init — seven commands from the node.
Get the common principle: they all manage one resource — the context window.
Realize the effect: the more precise the context, the better the answers, fewer hallucinations, and faster responses.
Open /help to see the full current list of slash commands in your version.
s1.validate: You can name all seven commands and explain in one sentence which shared resource they control.
s1.tip: Don't memorize flags — hold the idea of "managing Claude's attention" and look up details with /help.

s2.title: /add-dir and /context — what's in context and how much
s2.why: The base pair: one command adds the needed folders to context, the other shows how much context is already used. Conscious management starts here.
instructions: /add-dir — adds a directory to Claude's working context. Use it when Claude needs to see a specific folder in full.
Example: /add-dir src/components → Claude reads all components automatically without referencing each file.
/context — visualizes current context usage as a grid. Use it in long sessions to know your headroom.
Add only the needed folders, not the whole repo — this saves context.
s2.validate: You added one target folder with /add-dir and used /context to see how context filling changed.
s2.tip: If /context shows high filling early in a session, you probably added unnecessary directories with /add-dir.

s3.title: /memory and /init — project memory
s3.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's persistent memory that Claude reads automatically. This pair creates and edits it.
instructions: /init — generates CLAUDE.md for the current project. Use it when starting with a new repo.
/memory — opens the memory files (CLAUDE.md) for editing. Use it to extend or fix project rules.
Run /init first for the base file, then /memory as the project accumulates conventions.
Check /help for exactly how both commands are invoked in your version.
s3.validate: The project has a CLAUDE.md created via /init, and you have opened it for editing with /memory.
s3.tip: Memory is "long" context: whatever is in CLAUDE.md is considered every session without re-running /add-dir.

s4.title: /diff and /focus — track code and cut noise
s4.why: During active work you need to see what changes in the code without drowning in extra output. This pair handles change review and a clean focus.
instructions: /diff — shows uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs. Use it to control what has already been applied.
/focus — shows only the prompt, tool summary, and final response. Use it when output gets noisy.
Use /diff before committing to confirm the changes are exactly what you wanted.
Turn on /focus in long sessions where detailed tool logs are distracting.
s4.validate: You reviewed current changes with /diff and switched output to compact mode with /focus.
s4.tip: /diff doesn't replace git — it's a quick in-session view; still do the final check with your own tools.

s5.title: /goal — set a goal and work to the result
s5.why: Sometimes you need to direct the whole session at one task, not just see context. /goal focuses work on meeting a condition.
instructions: /goal — sets a goal and keeps working until it's met. Use it for tasks with a clear done condition.
Phrase the goal verifiably: it's clear by what sign it's achieved.
Combine with /context to see whether there's enough context for the path to the goal.
Check /help for the exact syntax of /goal in your version.
s5.validate: You set a verifiable goal with /goal and understand by what sign Claude knows it's reached.
s5.tip: A vague goal ("make it better") prevents /goal from knowing when to stop — phrase it measurably.

s6.title: Chaining commands, mistakes, and verification
s6.why: The commands shine in combination. The final step: assemble a working scenario and lock in how to avoid common mistakes and check yourself.
instructions: Build a chain: /init → /add-dir the needed folders → /context to monitor → /goal on the task → /diff before committing.
Avoid the main mistake: don't add the whole repo with /add-dir when one folder is needed.
In a long session, check /context regularly so you don't hit the limit unexpectedly.
Don't invent commands or flags — the seven-command list is fixed; see the current set with /help.
Verify the result: after /diff confirm exactly the intended changes are in place.
s6.validate: You ran the full scenario from /init to /diff on a real task and never guessed commands — only from the node or /help.
s6.tip: A good habit: start the session with /context so you immediately see how much context headroom you begin with.

cc-grp-model.title: Model and limits in Claude Code
cc-grp-model.subtitle: The slash-command group for choosing a model, controlling effort, and tracking spend
cc-grp-model.whatItIs: A set of Claude Code slash commands that control which model runs your session, how hard it thinks, and how much you spend: /model, /fast, /effort, /advisor, /upgrade, /usage, /status, /extra-usage.
cc-grp-model.approach: We move from the big picture to specifics: first why the group exists, then the model- and mode-switching commands, then the spend and status commands, and finally we tie it all into a 'right model for the task' strategy verified with /usage.
outcomes: You know which command in the group to use in each situation
You can switch model and effort level mid-session without losing context
You track token spend with /usage and avoid surprise bills
You diagnose connection and account issues with /status
You build a personal strategy for picking a model by task type

applyIn.title: Mixed development session
applyIn.description: Quick edits on /fast, a tricky algorithm on a stronger model via /model, then back — no session restart.

applyIn.title: Budget control
applyIn.description: Regular /usage checks through the month so spend stays predictable and limits never hit you by surprise.

applyIn.title: Troubleshooting
applyIn.description: When Claude Code acts strange, /status shows version, model, account, and API connectivity.

pitfalls: Never checking /usage — and getting a surprise bill at the end of the month
Keeping a strong model on for the whole session, including trivial edits — wasted spend
Forgetting /fast for routine work like writing tests or cleaning up code
Ignoring /status during failures and blaming the model instead of a connection issue
Running /upgrade blindly without first checking real spend in /usage

exercises.question: You write repetitive tests, then move to a tangled algorithm, then clean up code. Which commands do you use, and in what order?
exercises.hint: Recall the node's example: routine — fast mode, hard work — switch model, then back.

exercises.question: At the end of the week you want to know whether you're nearing your plan limits. What do you run?

exercises.question: Claude Code stopped responding. Before changing the model, what do you check?
