s1.title: What this command group is
s1.why: Before pressing commands, grasp the idea: different tasks need different models, and switching mid-session saves cost without losing context. The Model and limits group gives you levers for model choice, effort level, and spend control.
instructions: Open Claude Code and type /help — review the list of available slash commands
Find the group's commands in the list: /model, /fast, /effort, /advisor, /upgrade, /usage, /status, /extra-usage
Group them mentally: model and mode (/model, /fast, /effort, /advisor), plan and limits (/upgrade, /extra-usage), control (/usage, /status)
s1.validate: You can name which command handles switching the model, which one tracks spend, and which one shows connection status.
s1.tip: /help is the main entry point — it always shows the current command set for your exact version.

s2.title: Switching the model: /model and /fast
s2.why: These are the two core selection commands. /model switches the model for the current session for heavier work; /fast toggles fast mode (Haiku) for routine work. Session context is preserved either way.
instructions: Type /fast to enable fast mode — it uses Haiku and suits simple edits
Type /model to switch the session model to a stronger one for architecture or complex work
Make a simple change on /fast, then switch via /model and notice the context is not lost
s2.validate: You switched between fast mode and a stronger model in one session without losing the conversation history.
s2.tip: /fast for quick edits, /model for architecture work — the base rule from the node.

s3.title: Fine-tuning: /effort and /advisor
s3.why: Sometimes you don't need to change the model itself — just tune how hard it thinks (/effort) or pull in a stronger model at a key moment (/advisor). This balances quality against spend.
instructions: Type /effort and set the model's effort level for the current task
Use /advisor when you want to consult a stronger model at an important moment without switching the whole session
Compare: for one tough decision — /advisor once; for sustained heavy work — /model
s3.validate: You understand the difference between a one-off consult (/advisor), tuning effort (/effort), and a full model switch (/model).
s3.tip: /advisor is cheaper than keeping the whole session on a strong model for just a couple of hard spots.

s4.title: Limits and plan: /upgrade and /extra-usage
s4.why: When you hit plan limits there are two routes: /upgrade — move to Max for higher limits, and /extra-usage — configure extra usage when limits hit. This is about managing the ceiling, not a specific session.
instructions: Type /upgrade to look at moving to Max for higher limits
Type /extra-usage to configure extra usage when limits are hit
Decide for yourself: do you need a permanently higher limit (upgrade) or a one-off buffer (extra-usage)
s4.validate: You know which command raises the plan permanently and which adds usage on a one-off basis.
s4.tip: Don't upgrade blindly — first check your real spend in /usage (next step).

s5.title: Spend control: /usage and /status
s5.why: Your main defense against a surprise bill. /usage shows token spend, plan usage, and activity stats. /status shows your Claude Code version, model, account, and API connectivity — useful for both money and diagnostics.
instructions: Type /usage and review token spend and plan usage for the session
Type /status to see the current model, account, and API connection state
Make /usage a habit — for example, at the end of each working day
s5.validate: You can check at any moment how much you've spent and which model you're running.
s5.tip: /usage to track spend, /status to diagnose connection issues — the direct rule from the node.

s6.title: Strategy, mistakes, and verification
s6.why: Now tie the commands into a workflow: the right model for the task plus regular control. The main mistake is never checking /usage and getting a surprise bill at the end of the month.
instructions: Build a route for a typical session: /fast for routine → /model for complex → back to /fast
Add /advisor for one-off hard decisions and /effort to fine-tune effort
Lock in the habit: periodic /usage, /status on failures, and only then /upgrade or /extra-usage if you hit a limit
Test yourself on the node's example: /fast for writing tests → /model Opus for the tricky algorithm → back to /fast for cleanup
s6.validate: You can assemble a command sequence for a mixed session unaided and name how you control spend.
s6.tip: The most common mistake is not looking at /usage. Make the spend check a habit, not a reaction to a bill.

cc-grp-ui.title: Claude Code interface and appearance
cc-grp-ui.subtitle: The slash-command group for theme, color, rendering, and session comfort

Verify command availability and exact names via /help

applyIn.description: In projects with private data, enable the sandbox via /sandbox and review /privacy-settings to limit execution and data sharing.

pitfalls: Allowing all bash commands globally via 'Bash(*)' — a serious security risk. Be specific: 'Bash(npm run *)'.
Not knowing the full command list and configuring blindly instead of using /help.
Confusing /config (the overview panel) with /update-config (natural-language editing of settings.json).
Ignoring /permissions and suffering constant approval prompts.
Changing /privacy-settings or /sandbox without understanding the security and data-sharing consequences.

exercises.question: What is the difference between /config and /update-config?
exercises.hint: One shows a settings overview, the other edits settings.json via a natural-language description.

exercises.question: Why is the rule 'Bash(npm run *)' safer than 'Bash(*)'?
exercises.hint: Think about what each rule allows and which set of commands Claude can run without confirmation.

exercises.question: How do you see the full list of configuration-group commands without memorizing them?
exercises.hint: There's a built-in command that prints all available slash commands.

s1.title: What the group is and how to see all commands
s1.why: Before configuring anything you need to know the group's members and how to view the current list — it depends on your CLI version.
instructions: Memorize the group's members: /config, /keybindings, /permissions, /privacy-settings, /update-config, /sandbox, /remote-env.
Type /help in Claude Code to see the full current list of slash commands.
Find the configuration commands in the output and read their short descriptions.
Note which ones relate to security (/permissions, /sandbox, /privacy-settings).
s1.validate: You can name at least 5 commands in the group and explain each one's purpose in a phrase.
s1.tip: The /help list is the source of truth: commands may be added between versions.

s2.title: Tool permissions: /permissions
s2.why: Permissions are the foundation of safe, fast work. Without them every action needs confirmation, and overly broad rules are dangerous.
instructions: Type /permissions to open the allow and deny rule management.
Add a specific allow rule, e.g. 'Bash(npm run *)'.
Make sure you don't use broad patterns like 'Bash(*)'.
Save and run an allowed command — Claude executes it without asking.
s2.validate: An allowed tool runs without confirmation while others still ask.
s2.tip: Example: /permissions → allow 'Bash(npm run *)' → npm scripts run without asking every time.

s3.title: Keybindings: /keybindings
s3.why: Convenient keybindings speed up daily work and remove small friction like an awkward submit.
instructions: Type /keybindings to open or create the keybindings config file.
Find the submit-message action and bind it to, e.g., Cmd+Enter.
Save the file and return to the chat.
Test the new combination in real input.
s3.validate: The assigned combination works as expected (e.g. Cmd+Enter submits the message).
s3.tip: Only change keys that actually bother you — leave the rest at their defaults.

s4.title: Settings panel and natural-language config: /config and /update-config
s4.why: These two commands are the main entry to general settings: one shows an overview, the other lets you edit settings.json with a plain description.
instructions: Type /config to open the settings panel and see current parameters in one place.
Review the available options without changing them right away.
Type /update-config and describe the desired settings.json change in plain words.
Verify the change was applied as you described.
s4.validate: /config shows the current settings, and /update-config correctly edits settings.json from your description.
s4.tip: /config is to look, /update-config is to change. Don't mix up these roles.

s5.title: Privacy, sandbox, and environment: /privacy-settings, /sandbox, /remote-env
s5.why: These commands govern execution safety and data sharing — configure them deliberately, especially in sensitive projects.
instructions: Type /privacy-settings to view and, if needed, update privacy settings.
Type /sandbox to configure the sandbox for tool execution in an isolated environment.
Type /remote-env to set the default remote environment if you work remotely.
Change only what you're sure about; leave the rest at defaults.
s5.validate: You understand what each of the three commands does and changed settings only deliberately.
s5.tip: Sandbox and privacy affect security — don't toggle them at random.

s6.title: Mistakes and verifying the setup
s6.why: A final check catches the most common mistakes — overly broad permissions, command confusion, and unsafe settings.
instructions: Check your /permissions rules: no broad patterns like 'Bash(*)'.
Make sure you're not confusing /config (overview) and /update-config (editing).
Use /help to confirm you're using real group commands, not invented ones.
Run an allowed tool and confirm there are no extra approval prompts.
s6.validate: Permissions are specific, commands are used for their intended purpose, there are no extra confirmations, and sensitive settings are deliberate.
s6.tip: If unsure about a rule, make it narrower, not broader. Safety beats a couple of extra confirmations.

cc-grp-integrations.title: Slash Commands: Integrations
cc-grp-integrations.subtitle: Connecting Claude Code to your IDE, MCP, GitHub, Slack, browser, and plugins
cc-grp-integrations.whatItIs: The Integrations slash-command group embeds Claude Code into your real development workflow. These are /mcp, /ide, /chrome, /hooks, /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, and /web-setup. Each one owns a connection point: the IDE, MCP servers, the browser, tool events, plugins, agents, and external services.
cc-grp-integrations.approach: We move from overview to practice. First we view the whole group via /help, then break the commands down by purpose: editor connection (/ide, /chrome), data via /mcp, extension via /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, and /hooks, and reaching external services (/install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup). We finish with common mistakes and verifying that an integration is actually active.
outcomes: You know which commands belong to integrations and what each one does
You connect Claude Code to your IDE via /ide and to data via /mcp
You manage plugins and agents via /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents
You set up external services: /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
You can verify an integration is active and diagnose it when it isn't

applyIn.title: Working in the IDE
applyIn.description: After installing the VS Code extension you run /ide, and Claude automatically sees your open files and diagnostics right in the editor.

applyIn.title: Connecting data and APIs
applyIn.description: Via /mcp you add MCP servers for access to a database or external API, so Claude works with your real data sources.

applyIn.title: Team automation
applyIn.description: Via /install-github-app and /install-slack-app you bring Claude into GitHub Actions and Slack so the whole team uses it in shared workflows.

pitfalls: Not calling /reload-plugins after adding a plugin — it won't activate until the next session
Calling /ide before installing the IDE extension — there's no integration, so the command does nothing
Confusing /mcp (managing servers) with /hooks (tool events) — they are different connection points
Assuming /install-github-app sets everything up instantly — it launches a wizard you must finish
Not checking status after connecting and assuming the integration works by default

exercises.question: You want Claude to see your open files and errors right inside VS Code. What steps and which command?
exercises.hint: First the IDE extension, then the integrations command that shows status and activates the link.

exercises.question: You added a new plugin, but Claude doesn't 'see' it. What did you forget?
exercises.hint: The group has a dedicated command that activates pending plugin changes without restarting the session.

exercises.question: Your team needs to invoke Claude in a GitHub pull request and a Slack channel. Which two setup commands do you run?
exercises.hint: Both start with /install-...

s1.title: What the Integrations group is
s1.why: Before connecting anything, you need to understand the group's makeup and purpose: integrations embed Claude Code into your full workflow — IDE, GitHub, Slack, browser — instead of running alongside it.
instructions: Start Claude Code and type /help to see the list of all commands
Find the integration group commands: /mcp, /ide, /chrome, /hooks, /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
Read the short description next to each — note which is for the editor, which for data, which for external services
Remember the core idea: Claude works inside your tools, not next to them
s1.validate: You can name at least 6 commands in the group and say what each one connects.
s1.tip: /help is your map: integration commands always appear there with the up-to-date description for your version.

s2.title: Editor connection: /ide and /chrome
s2.why: The most common integration is the editor. /ide links Claude Code to VS Code or JetBrains, and /chrome manages Claude in Chrome settings. This lets Claude see context where you actually work.
instructions: Install the Claude extension in VS Code or JetBrains (done inside the editor itself)
In Claude Code run /ide — the command shows integration status and activates the link
Confirm Claude sees your open files and inline diagnostics
If you work in the browser, run /chrome for Claude in Chrome (beta) settings
s2.validate: After /ide the status shows an active integration, and Claude references your open file without you giving the path.
s2.tip: /ide requires the IDE extension to be installed first — without it there's nothing for the command to connect.

s3.title: Connecting data: /mcp
s3.why: /mcp manages MCP servers: add, remove, and list them. Through MCP Claude gains access to databases and external APIs — it's the main way to give it your real data sources.
instructions: Run /mcp to see the list of already connected MCP servers
Via /mcp add the server you need — for example, access to a database or external API
Check that the server appears in the list and is marked active
Ask Claude to reach the connected source and confirm it answers with real data
s3.validate: In the /mcp output your server is visible and active, and Claude successfully retrieves data from it.
s3.tip: Connect only the MCP servers you need: extra ones grow the context and tool list with no benefit.

s4.title: Extending capabilities: /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /hooks
s4.why: These commands extend Claude Code's behavior. /plugin manages plugins, /reload-plugins activates their changes, /agents manages agent configurations, and /hooks shows hook configurations for tool events (pre/post-execution).
instructions: Run /plugin to view and configure plugins
After adding or changing a plugin, always run /reload-plugins — otherwise the changes won't apply
Use /agents to view and configure agent setups
Run /hooks to see which hooks fire before and after tools
s4.validate: After /reload-plugins the new plugin is available in the current session, and /hooks shows your configured hooks.
s4.tip: The most common mistake is forgetting /reload-plugins: without it a new plugin only activates in the next session.

s5.title: External services: /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
s5.why: These commands take Claude beyond your local machine. /install-github-app sets up Claude GitHub Actions, /install-slack-app installs Claude in Slack, and /web-setup sets up Claude Code on the web — so the whole team works with Claude in shared services.
instructions: Run /install-github-app and finish the wizard to connect Claude to GitHub Actions
Run /install-slack-app to install the Claude app in Slack
Run /web-setup to set up Claude Code on the web
After each command go through to the final confirmation — the wizard doesn't finish on its own
s5.validate: The GitHub app responds in a pull request, the Slack app is installed in the workspace, and web access is set up.
s5.tip: These commands launch setup wizards — skipping any step leaves the integration incomplete.

s6.title: Mistakes and verification
s6.why: Integrations often 'don't work' not because of a bug but because of a skipped step. A final check saves time: you confirm each connection is actually active.
instructions: After adding a plugin, confirm you called /reload-plugins and that it's active
Before /ide make sure the editor extension is installed, otherwise there's no integration
Via /mcp check that the servers you need are listed and active, not just added
For /install-github-app and /install-slack-app confirm the wizard was completed
If something didn't connect — go back to /help and compare the command's description with what you did
s6.validate: Each needed integration is explicitly confirmed active (via /ide status, /mcp list, the GitHub/Slack app's action), not assumed to work.
s6.tip: Rule: after any integration command, check status immediately — don't assume everything connected by default.

cc-grp-automation.title: Automation and AI tasks in Claude Code
cc-grp-automation.subtitle: The group of slash commands that turn Claude into an autonomous background worker
cc-grp-automation.whatItIs: The "Automation and AI tasks" command group is a set of Claude Code slash commands (/plan, /tasks, /background, /loop, /schedule, /batch, /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview) that turn Claude from a chat assistant into an autonomous worker. They run work in the background, on a schedule, or in parallel — while you focus elsewhere.
cc-grp-automation.approach: We go from simple to advanced: first understand what the group is and where to see its list (/help), then break down the commands in pairs by role — background and parallelism, schedules and loops, goals and web agents. We finish with safe-automation rules and verifying that tasks actually complete.
outcomes: Understand which commands belong to the automation group and where to find the list
Launch background and parallel tasks via /background, /tasks and /batch
Set up recurring and scheduled runs via /loop and /schedule
Set goals and review PRs autonomously via /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultrareview
Avoid common automation mistakes — such as running /batch without /plan first

applyIn.title: Large-scale refactor
applyIn.description: Split a uniform change across dozens of files with /batch — parallel agents, each opening its own PR.

applyIn.title: Nightly automation
applyIn.description: Use /schedule to run a remote agent on a schedule: nightly checks, reports, dependency updates.

applyIn.title: Release quality control
applyIn.description: Before a major release, run /ultrareview for deep bug finding and /autofix-pr to auto-fix PR issues.

pitfalls: Running /batch without /plan first — parallel agents start working from an unapproved plan
Using /ultrareview on every small PR — it's a paid command ($5-20), overkill for routine work
An uncontrolled /loop with no stop condition — the command runs forever and burns resources
Not knowing the current group lineup — the command list changes, always verify via /help
Confusing /loop (local recurring interval) with /schedule (remote agent on cron) — different tools

exercises.question: You need to add JSDoc comments to all functions in a large src/ folder. Which command fits, and what must you do before it?
exercises.hint: Think about parallelism across dozens of files. And recall the key safety rule from the node about /plan.

exercises.question: You need to run a dependency check every night without your involvement. Which command do you pick and how does it differ from /loop?
exercises.hint: Schedule and remote agent versus local recurring interval.

exercises.question: How do you quickly find the full current list of automation commands in your version of Claude Code?
exercises.hint: One built-in command shows all available slash commands.

s1.title: What the group is and where its list lives
s1.why: Before automating, understand the tool's boundaries: which commands belong to the group and how Claude shifts from conversationalist to background-task executor.
instructions: Grasp the group's idea: automation commands run work in the background, on a schedule, or in parallel while you focus elsewhere.
Open the full command list via /help — it shows the current set of slash commands for your version.
Find the automation commands in the list: /plan, /tasks, /background, /loop, /schedule, /batch, /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview.
Note that some commands run locally and some (e.g. /ultraplan, /ultrareview) run on the web and are paid.
s1.validate: You can name at least 5 commands from the group and explain in one sentence how an autonomous worker differs from a chat assistant.
s1.tip: The group's lineup evolves with Claude Code — /help always shows what is actually available now.

s2.title: Background tasks: /background and /tasks
s2.why: The foundation of automation is sending work to the background and tracking it. Without this, the other commands lose their point.
instructions: Use /background to continue the current session in the background and free up your chat for other work.
Open /tasks — this lists and manages background tasks: you see what's running and what's done.
Through /tasks, monitor status and, if needed, stop or return to a task.
Remember the pairing: /background sends to the background, /tasks controls what runs there.
s2.validate: You launched a task in the background via /background and found it in the /tasks list.
s2.tip: Background doesn't mean "forget": check /tasks so background agents don't run pointlessly.

s3.title: Parallelism and planning: /batch and /plan
s3.why: Large uniform changes are faster with dozens of parallel agents. But parallelism is dangerous without an approved plan.
instructions: First call /plan — plan mode — so Claude drafts the change plan before executing it.
Approve the plan: this is the key safety rule before any parallel run.
Run /batch for a large-scale change — it spreads work across 5-30 parallel agents, each opening its own PR.
Example: /batch 'add JSDoc to all functions in src/' → 20 agents, each taking its file group.
s3.validate: You understand why /batch always follows an approved /plan, and you can describe what parallel agents return (a PR per file group).
s3.tip: The clearer the plan, the fewer divergences between parallel agents — a plan saves time sorting results.

s4.title: Schedules and loops: /schedule and /loop
s4.why: Many tasks repeat. /loop and /schedule remove the routine: runs on an interval or on a schedule without your involvement.
instructions: Use /loop to run a command on an interval — for recurring local tasks.
Use /schedule to create scheduled remote agent routines — e.g. nightly automation.
Draw a clear line: /loop is a local recurring interval, /schedule is a remote agent on a schedule (cron).
For /loop, keep a stop condition in mind so the loop doesn't run forever.
s4.validate: You can pick the right command for the task: "repeat locally" → /loop, "nightly remote" → /schedule.
s4.tip: Nightly automation via /schedule is the most underrated scenario: checks and reports get done while you sleep.

s5.title: Goals and web agents: /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview
s5.why: The highest tier of automation is setting a goal and driving the task to completion, while offloading heavy reviews to web agents.
instructions: Use /goal to set a completion condition and keep working until the goal is met.
Use /autofix-pr to monitor a PR and automatically fix issues found.
To align on a large plan, use /ultraplan — the plan draft is prepared on the web for editing and approval.
Before a major release, run /ultrareview — deep bug finding on the web (paid, $5-20).
s5.validate: You can state which of these commands are paid and run on the web (/ultraplan, /ultrareview) and which set the work mode (/goal, /autofix-pr).
s5.tip: /ultrareview saves money when run selectively — before a release, not on every small PR.

s6.title: Automation mistakes and verification
s6.why: An autonomous worker is dangerous without discipline: parallelism without a plan, endless loops, and needless paid runs quickly turn benefit into harm.
instructions: Top rule: never run /batch without a prior, approved /plan.
Don't overuse paid commands: /ultrareview is only for important checks, not routine.
For /loop, always keep a stop condition so the command doesn't spin pointlessly.
Regularly verify the current command list via /help — the group's lineup changes.
Verify results: open /tasks to confirm background tasks completed correctly.
s6.validate: You can list at least 3 common automation mistakes and, for each, name how to avoid it.
s6.tip: The discipline of "plan → run → verify via /tasks" makes automation reliable rather than risky.

cc-grp-quality.title: Code quality and review
cc-grp-quality.subtitle: The Claude Code slash-command group for checking code quality and security before shipping
cc-grp-quality.whatItIs: A group of Claude Code commands that act as quality gates: /review analyzes a pull request, /security-review hunts for vulnerabilities, /simplify strips out over-engineering, /diff shows uncommitted changes, /debug enables session diagnostics, and /fewer-permission-prompts reduces permission interruptions. Claude catches what linters miss: logic errors, security issues, and over-engineering.
cc-grp-quality.approach: We move from the big picture to specifics: first understand why the group exists as a whole, then walk through the commands one or two per step on real code, then wire the checks into your working cycle (before merge, before deploy, after a long session), and finish with common mistakes and a self-check. Each command is practiced on your own uncommitted change, with /help kept handy as a reference.
outcomes: Know which command does what: PR review, security, simplification, viewing changes, diagnostics
Run /review and read its output by severity (Critical / Warning / Info)
Run /security-review before deploy and understand the vulnerability report
Wire quality checks into a steady cycle: before merge, before deploy, after a session
Avoid treating review as a rubber stamp and confirm results with a self-check

applyIn.title: Before merging a pull request
applyIn.description: Run /review before merging the branch — Claude lists issues by severity, and you fix Critical items before the code reaches the main branch.

applyIn.title: Before deploying to production
applyIn.description: Run /security-review over the branch changes to catch risks like SQL injection or leaked secrets before they reach users.

applyIn.title: After a long development session
applyIn.description: Use /simplify so Claude finds the duplication and over-engineering that piled up during the session and suggests cleaner code.

pitfalls: Using /review as a rubber stamp — read the output carefully, especially Critical items
Running /security-review only at the end of a big release instead of regularly before every deploy
Confusing /simplify (quality cleanup) with bug hunting — /simplify does not find logic errors, /review does
Skipping /diff before review and not knowing exactly which changes go into the check
Forgetting /help and guessing command flags instead of reading the built-in reference

exercises.question: You have an uncommitted change on a branch. Which command gives you a structured breakdown by severity before merging?
exercises.hint: It's the core PR-review command of the group; output is split into Critical / Warning / Info.

exercises.question: Before deploy you must confirm the changes carry no security risks. Which command is it, and how does its output differ from a normal review?
exercises.hint: The command is specifically about security; it looks for vulnerabilities like injections and leaked secrets, not general quality.

exercises.question: How do you find the exact list and purpose of the group's commands right inside Claude Code, without guessing from memory?
exercises.hint: The built-in reference command, shared by all slash commands.

s1.title: What the group is and why it exists
s1.why: Before running commands, understand their shared role: they are quality gates before shipping. Without that picture it's easy to treat review as a formality and skip critical issues.
instructions: Open Claude Code in a project with uncommitted changes or an active branch
Run /help and locate the group commands: /review, /security-review, /simplify, /diff, /debug, /fewer-permission-prompts
Read the short description of each command in the /help output
Phrase the group's role for yourself: catch what linters miss — logic, security, complexity
s1.validate: You can name all six group commands and say which is for review, which for security, and which for simplification.
s1.tip: /help is your first source of truth about the commands: it shows the current set without guesswork.

s2.title: /review — structured review of changes
s2.why: /review is the group's central command. It analyzes changes and lists issues by severity, making review repeatable and independent of your mood and fatigue.
instructions: First run /diff to see which uncommitted changes will go into the review
Run /review
Read the output by level: Critical, Warning, Info
Start with Critical items — for example, a SQL injection risk — and decide what to fix immediately
Mark Info items as future improvements if they don't block the merge
s2.validate: You got a list of issues split by severity and understand which items are Critical versus recommendations.
s2.tip: Example output: Critical (SQL injection risk), Warning (no error handling), Info (rename for clarity).

s3.title: /security-review — security check before deploy
s3.why: A general review doesn't replace a dedicated security check. /security-review deliberately hunts for vulnerabilities in the branch changes to catch them before the code reaches users.
instructions: Make sure the changes going to deploy are on the current branch
Run /security-review
Read the vulnerability report — watch for injections, leaked secrets, unsafe input handling
Compare its focus with a regular /review: here the priority is security, not general quality
Fix the identified risks before deploy
s3.validate: You ran the security check and can explain how its report differs from /review output.
s3.tip: Run /security-review regularly before every deploy, not just at the end of a big release.

s4.title: /simplify and /diff — code cleanliness and change control
s4.why: After a long session, code accumulates duplication and over-engineering. /simplify cleans up quality, and /diff gives a clear picture of exactly what you're changing and sending into review.
instructions: Run /diff to see the full list of uncommitted changes
Run /simplify so Claude finds reusable pieces and over-engineering
Read the suggestions and apply the ones that improve the code without losing clarity
Remember the split: /simplify is about quality, not bug hunting; /review handles logic
Run /diff again after the edits to see the final state
s4.validate: You received simplification suggestions from /simplify and can see via /diff how the code changed.
s4.tip: Use /simplify at the end of a long session — that's when extra complexity piles up.

s5.title: /debug and /fewer-permission-prompts — diagnostics and fewer interruptions
s5.why: Two helper commands remove friction: /debug helps you understand what went wrong in a session, and /fewer-permission-prompts cuts the stream of permission requests so quality checks run without constant pauses.
instructions: If a session behaves oddly, run /debug to enable debug logging for diagnostics
Study the extra detail that appears in the output once diagnostics are on
Run /fewer-permission-prompts — it scans transcripts and builds an allowlist of frequent safe actions
Review the proposed allowlist before accepting: only allow what is genuinely safe
Run /review or /simplify again and notice there are fewer permission interruptions
s5.validate: You understand when /debug is needed and ran /fewer-permission-prompts after deliberately reviewing the proposed permission list.
s5.tip: Don't allow everything via /fewer-permission-prompts — add only verified read-only actions to the allowlist.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a self-check of the cycle
s6.why: The commands only pay off when wired into a steady cycle and not turned into a formality. The final step cements the habit and helps you check yourself.
instructions: Fix your cycle: /diff → /review before merge, /security-review before deploy, /simplify after a session
Check you don't use /review formally: re-read the Critical items of your last review
Make sure /security-review runs regularly, not once per release
If unsure about flags or the command set — open /help instead of guessing
Write yourself a short checklist of the commands and when to apply each
s6.validate: You have a clear personal quality-check cycle and can name the main mistake of each command and how to avoid it.
s6.tip: The group's main mistake is treating review as a stamp. The value is in actually reading and fixing the Critical items.

cc-grp-help.title: Help, learning and account in Claude Code
cc-grp-help.subtitle: The group of slash commands that help you learn, diagnose problems and manage your account — without leaving the CLI
cc-grp-help.whatItIs: This is the set of utility slash commands in Claude Code covering three jobs: onboarding and learning (/help, /powerup, /release-notes, /skills, /team-onboarding), help mid-task (/btw, /insights), and managing your account and installation health (/login, /logout, /feedback, /doctor, /mobile). They all run straight from the input line without leaving your current task.
cc-grp-help.approach: First understand what the group is for, then work through the commands in logical pairs: learning, help mid-task, skills and team onboarding, account, diagnostics. At each step you try a command live and learn to read its output. The base entry point is always /help: it shows the current list of what's actually available in your version.
outcomes: Know which slash commands handle help, learning and account
Can ask a side question with /btw without losing the main task's context
Can diagnose installation issues yourself with /doctor
Understand how to sign in and out of your account (/login, /logout)
Know where to find new features and the list of skills (/release-notes, /skills)

applyIn.title: Starting work on a new project
applyIn.description: Run /powerup for interactive lessons and /help to refresh the list of available commands before diving in.

applyIn.title: A question mid-task
applyIn.description: In the middle of a refactor, use /btw to ask a quick clarification without breaking your main line of work.

applyIn.title: Something broke
applyIn.description: The CLI behaves strangely — run /doctor, which catches 90% of common installation issues instantly.

pitfalls: Not running /doctor when the CLI behaves strangely — it fixes most common issues right away
Interrupting your main task with a plain question instead of a lightweight /btw, losing context
Ignoring /insights — analyzing session patterns shows where your time goes
Forgetting /release-notes and missing new features, working the old way
Not signing out with /logout on a shared or borrowed device, leaving the account active

exercises.question: You're mid-way through a big task and want to quickly clarify what a pattern does without interrupting your work. Which command do you use and why?
exercises.hint: Look for the command for a side question without interrupting the main task.

exercises.question: The CLI started behaving strangely after an update. Which command do you start the diagnosis with?
exercises.hint: This command checks installation health and catches up to 90% of common issues.

exercises.question: How do you find the full, current list of commands in your specific version of Claude Code?
exercises.hint: The most basic command of the group, the entry point to help.

s1.title: What this command group is
s1.why: Before dissecting individual commands, it's important to see the whole group: that it covers three different jobs — learning, help mid-task and account — and why they're grouped together.
instructions: Remember the group's three areas: learning (/help, /powerup, /release-notes, /skills, /team-onboarding), help mid-task (/btw, /insights), account and health (/login, /logout, /feedback, /doctor, /mobile)
Open the Claude Code input line and type / — you'll see the list of available commands
Find the commands from this group in the list and note which ones you know and which you don't
Remember that the entry point to all help is the /help command
s1.validate: You can name the group's three areas and at least one command in each.
s1.tip: Don't try to memorize every command — it's enough to know that /help always shows the current list.

s2.title: Learning: /help and /powerup
s2.why: These are the two main commands for getting into Claude Code: /help gives you a map of all commands, and /powerup teaches features through short interactive lessons.
instructions: Run /help and review the full list of available commands
Find the commands we'll cover next in the /help output to confirm they exist in your version
Run /powerup and complete one interactive lesson on Claude Code features
Note what the lesson taught you — this is how continuous learning works
s2.validate: After /help you see the full command list, and after /powerup you completed at least one lesson.
s2.tip: /powerup is handy at the start of work — a couple of minutes of lessons saves hours of trial-and-error on features.

s3.title: Help mid-task: /btw and /insights
s3.why: These are the group's underused gems: /btw lets you ask a side question without interrupting the main task, and /insights shows your session patterns weekly.
instructions: In the middle of any task, type /btw and ask a short question, for example about an unfamiliar pattern
Confirm that Claude answered briefly and the main task continued without losing context
Run /insights and look at the analysis of your session patterns
Make a habit of running /insights weekly to analyze where your time goes
s3.validate: You asked a question via /btw without interrupting the task and opened /insights at least once.
s3.tip: /btw alone saves dozens of context-breaking interruptions per day — it's the fastest way to clarify a small thing.

s4.title: Skills and onboarding: /skills, /team-onboarding, /release-notes
s4.why: These commands help you see available skills, quickly get a team up to speed, and keep track of new Claude Code features.
instructions: Run /skills and look at the list of available installed skills
Run /release-notes and see what's new in Claude Code
Run /team-onboarding to generate a guide for onboarding your team
Compare the skills list from /skills with what was there before — that's how you spot new capabilities
s4.validate: You saw the skills list via /skills, learned what's new via /release-notes, and generated an onboarding guide.
s4.tip: Check /release-notes periodically — otherwise you'll keep working the old way, unaware of new features.

s5.title: Account: /login, /logout, /mobile
s5.why: These commands manage your access: signing in and out of your account, plus linking the mobile app via a QR code.
instructions: Run /login if you need to sign in, or confirm you're already signed in
Remember the /logout command — it's useful on a shared or borrowed device
Run /mobile to get a QR code for the mobile app
Scan the QR code with your phone if you want to link the mobile app
s5.validate: You understand how to sign in and out, and you got a QR code via /mobile.
s5.tip: On a shared computer, always end your session with /logout so the account doesn't stay active.

s6.title: Diagnostics and mistakes: /doctor and /feedback
s6.why: The final step reinforces the group's main rule: whenever the CLI behaves strangely you run /doctor first, and you send notable issues to Anthropic via /feedback.
instructions: Run /doctor and read the report on your installation's health
Remember the main rule: when the CLI behaves strangely, run /doctor first — it catches 90% of common issues instantly
If you found a problem or have an idea — send it to Anthropic via /feedback
Repeat to yourself: /help is the command map, /btw is a quick question, /doctor is diagnostics
s6.validate: You ran /doctor, read its report, and know how to send /feedback.
s6.tip: The main mistake is not running /doctor when things break. Make it your first reflex, not a last resort.
